Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 1:

(Surat Maryam

It is well known by this name, and it has been related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). al-Tabarani, Abu Nu'aym and al-Daylami narrated through the route of Abu Bakr ibn Abd Allah ibn Abi Maryam al-Ghassani, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "I came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) and said: 'A girl was born to me tonight.' He said: 'And tonight there was revealed to me Surat Maryam.'"

It has also come in what is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it is named Surat Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad. It is Meccan, as related from Aisha, Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them all. Muqatil said: it is likewise, except the verse of prostration, which is Medinan, revealed after the emigration of the believers to Abyssinia. In al-Itqan, the exception of the verse ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾ is also mentioned. According to the Iraqis and the Syrians it has ninety-eight verses, according to the Meccans ninety-nine, and the Medinans have two opinions. The link between it and Surat al-Kahf lies in its containing wonders of a similar kind, such as the story of the birth of Yahya and the story of the birth of Isa, peace be upon them both, and for this reason it is mentioned after it. It has also been said that the People of the Cave will be raised before the Hour and will perform Hajj with Isa, peace be upon him, when he descends. So, in mentioning this surah after that one, along with this (if it is established), there is an evident connection. This is strengthened by what has been said, that they were from his people, peace be upon him. Other things have also been said.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad﴾

Ibn Mardawayh related from al-Kalbi that he was asked about this, and he narrated from Abu Salih, from Umm Hani, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Kaf, Ha, 'Alim (the Knowing), Sadiq (the Truthful)." The reports from Ibn Abbas differ. In one report he said: Kaf is from Karim (the Generous), Ha is from Hadi (the Guide), Ya is from Hakim (the Wise), 'Ayn is from 'Alim (the Knowing), and Sad is from Sadiq (the Truthful). In another report he said: it means Kabir (the Great), Hadi (the Guide), Amin (the Trustworthy), 'Aziz (the Mighty), Sadiq (the Truthful). In another he said: it is an oath that Allah swore by, and it is one of the names of Allah. In yet another he used to say: Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn, Ha-Mim, Ya-Sin and the like is the Greatest Name of Allah. This is supported by what Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi, Ibn Majah and Ibn Jarir narrated from Fatimah bint Ali, who said: Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, used to say: "O Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn, forgive me."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and a number of the Companions that they said: Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad is the disjoined letters: the Kaf is from al-Mulk (the Sovereign), the Ha is from Allah, the Ya and the 'Ayn are from al-'Aziz (the Mighty), and the Sad is from al-Sadiq (the Truthful) or al-Musawwir (the Fashioner).

He also narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b something similar, except that he did not mention the Ya, and said: the Sad is from al-Samad (the Eternal Refuge).

He also narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Anas that he said concerning this: "O You who protect and are not protected against." Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah that it is one of the names of the Qur'an. It was also said that it is the name of the surah, and a group holds this view. It was said that they are letters enumerated in the manner of counting, and this is attributed to a group of the people of verification. Some entrusted the knowledge of the reality of this to the Presence of the Knower of the Unseen.

The full discussion of this and similar matters has already been given at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, so recall it.

The majority read Kaf with a sukun on the fa'. It is related from al-Hasan that it was read with a damma. Nafi' read with imalah, intermediate between the two pronunciations, and made the dal of Sad clear and did not assimilate it into the dhal that follows; this is the view of most.

al-Hasan read the Ha with a damma; and from him also the Ya with a damma and the Ha with a kasra. From 'Asim, the Ya with a damma, and from him also both with a kasra. From Hamzah, the Ha with a fatha and the Ya with a kasra. Abu al-Fadl Abd al-Rahman ibn Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Muqri al-Razi said in the book al-Lawami': the damma in these letters is not on its real basis, otherwise the alifs following them would have to be turned into waws. Rather, the intended meaning is that these alifs are inclined toward the waw, according to the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and this is what is called the alif of tafkhim (emphasis), the opposite of imalah. This rendering is like how they rendered the imalah fatha, which leans toward the kasra, with a kasra, because the alif after it draws near to the ya. End of quote. The basis of imalah and tafkhim is that since these alifs have no original root, they were treated as derived from waw at times and from ya at other times, so both are permitted, to avoid arbitrariness.

Abu Ja'far read by separating these letters and isolating each from the others, which requires the last of them to be unvowelled; meeting of two unvowelled letters is tolerated in pause. Abu 'Amr assimilated the dal of Sad into the following dhal. Hafs, from 'Asim, and a group, made the nun of 'Ayn clear, while the majority hid it.

Opinions differ about its i'rab (grammatical analysis). It was said, on the view that each letter of a divine name has no place in the i'rab, nor does the whole combination have any i'rab. It was also said that each letter, if taken in full, is a predicate of an omitted subject: i.e., he is Kaf, he is Ha, and so on; or the first is taken in full on this basis, and the rest are predicates after predicate. According to what was related from al-Rabi', it was said: it is a vocative, being one of the names of Allah, meaning "the One who protects and is not protected against." It was also said that it has no place in the i'rab, and that it is a word said in the position of calling upon Allah by that title, like "mahyam" said in the position of asking about a state; and this, as you see, is weak. On the view that they are letters enumerated in the manner of counting, they said: they have no place in the i'rab.

And His saying, ﴿Dhikru rahmati rabbika﴾ ("A mention of the mercy of your Lord"), according to these opinions, is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "This recited (matluww) is (dhikr) etc." It is said that according to the last view, which is that it is a composition of the same kind as these separate letters, meaning the surah itself, (dhikr) etc. It is also said that it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "In what is recited to you is (dhikr) etc." According to the view that it is the name of the surah, it is said that its position is in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "This is Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad," i.e., it is named by it. The pointing to it was valid even though its mention had not preceded, because by virtue of its being on the wing of the mention (dhikr), it became like something present and witnessed, as it is said in the phrase "this is what so-and-so bought."

There are two possibilities regarding (dhikr): that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and that it is a subject whose predicate is omitted. It is also said that its position is in the nominative, as a subject, and (dhikr) etc. is its predicate, meaning: "The one named by it is a mention (dhikr) etc.," for the mention of that, since it was the opening of the noble surah and the main content that it encompasses, was treated as if it were the very mention of it. Or the attribution is by way of inclusion (ishtimal). Or it is with an omitted modifier, meaning "possessor of a mention etc.," or by interpretation, "a mention in which is the mercy of your Lord."

According to the view that it is the name of the Qur'an, it is said that what is meant by the Qur'an is that which applies to a part, and what is meant is the surah, and the grammatical analysis (i'rab) is the same i'rab, and in that case there is no contradiction between the two views. It is also said that what is meant is the apparent meaning, which is that it is a subject whose predicate is (dhikr) etc., and the attribution is by way of inclusion, or by estimation, or by interpretation.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿'abdahu﴾ ("His servant"), is the object of ﴿rahmati rabbika﴾, on the basis that the verbal noun (rahmah) is the object of what is attributed to it. It is written thus with the taa' and not as a marker of singularity, so that it would be prevented from acting, because the form of singularity is not the form from which the verb is derived, and the verb does not indicate singularity. Therefore the verbal noun does not act like the verb for this reason except anomalously, as the grammarians have stated explicitly. It is also said that it is the object of (dhikr), on the basis that it is a verbal noun attributed to its agent in an extended sense. The meaning of the mention of mercy is its reaching and befalling, as one says: "Your kindness mentioned me," meaning, "reached me."

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿Zakariyya﴾ ("Zakariyya"), is an appositive to it, either as a substitution of the whole for the whole, or as an explanatory apposition to it, or it is in the accusative by an implied "I mean" (a'ni). His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿idh nada rabbahu﴾ ("when he called out to his Lord"), is an adverbial of time for ﴿rahmati rabbika﴾. It is also said that it is for (dhikr), on the basis that it is attributed to its agent, not according to the first view, because the meaning would be corrupt. It is also said that it is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from Zakariyya, as in His saying, ﴿And mention in the Book Mary, when she withdrew from her family to a place in the east﴾.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Ya'mur, as reported by Abu al-Fath, read (dhakara) as a past tense verb with a shadda, and (rahmata) in the accusative. According to al-Bahr, it is the second object of (dhakara), and the first object is omitted, and (ʿabdahu) is the object of (rahmah). The subject of (dhakara) is a pronoun referring to the Qur'an, known from the context, meaning: "The Qur'an mentioned to people that the Exalted One had shown mercy to His servant." It is also permitted that the subject of (dhakara) be a pronoun referring to Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad, on the basis that what is meant by it is the Qur'an, and then it is the subject and the sentence is its predicate. It is also possible that the subject is His pronoun, Mighty and Majestic, meaning: "God, Exalted is He, mentioned that to people." It is also permitted that ﴿rahmata rabbika﴾ is the second object, and the first object is (ʿabdahu), and the subject is His pronoun, Exalted is He, meaning: "God, Exalted is He, mentioned to His servant His mercy," i.e., He made the servant mention His mercy. The grammatical analysis of (Zakariyya) is as already mentioned. It is also permitted

[p. 59]

that it be the object of (rahmah), and what is meant by "His servant" is the category, as if it were said: "The mention of His servants of the mercy of Zakariyya." This is, as you see, far-fetched. It is also permitted on this reading that the subject be a pronoun referring to the Qur'an. It is also said that it is permitted that the subject be His pronoun, Exalted is He, and (rahmah) is the first object and (ʿabdahu) is the second object, and he uses a metaphor, meaning: "God, Exalted is He, made mercy a mention for His servant." It is also said that (rahmah) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning: "A mention with mercy." Al-Dani reported from Abu Ya'mur that he read (dhikru) in the imperative with the shadda, and (rahmata) in the accusative, meaning: "Mention mercy, or with the mercy of your Lord, to His servant Zakariyya," (addressed to the people).

Al-Kalbi read (dhakara) as a past tense verb without the shadda, and (rahmata rabbika) in the accusative as the object of (dhakara), and (ʿabduhu) in the nominative as its subject.

Zakariyya, peace be upon him, was from the descendants of Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them both. Al-Hakim transmitted, and authenticated, from Ibn Mas'ud that he was the last of the prophets of the Children of Israel. He was the son of Azar ibn Muslim, of the descendants of Ya'qub. Ishaq ibn Bishr and Ibn 'Asakir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he was the son of Dan, and he was one of the sons of the prophets who used to write down the revelation in Bayt al-Maqdis. Ahmad, Abu Ya'la, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that he, peace be upon him, was a carpenter.

Five dialects are reported for his name. The first is with a long vowel (al-madd), the second is al-Qarr, and both were read in the seven canonical readings. The third is Zakariyy with a shadda on the ya'. The fourth is Zakriyy without the shadda. The fifth is Zakar, like qalam. It is a non-Arabic name. Al-nida' (calling) originally means raising the voice and making it apparent, and it may be used for the mere voice, or even for everything that indicates something, even if it is not a voice, as al-Raghib has verified. What is meant here is that when he called upon his Lord, ﴿nida'an﴾ ("a call"), meaning a supplication, ﴿khafiyyan﴾ ("secret"), concealed from people, so that none of them heard it, since they were not present with him. This was, as is said, in the depth of the night. He, peace be upon him, concealed his supplication because it is more conducive to sincerity, further from ostentation, and closer to deliverance from the blame of people for seeking a child, since that depends on preliminary matters that it is not fitting for him to undertake in old age and advanced years, and from the danger from his guardians. According to what we have mentioned, there is no contradiction between calling and its being secret. Indeed, there is no contradiction between them even if calling is interpreted as raising the voice, because secrecy is not the same as softness of voice. Whoever raises his voice in a place that is neither in view nor in earshot of people has concealed it. It is also said that it is a metaphor for absence of ostentation, meaning sincerity, and the calling, in the sense of raising the voice, does not contradict this.

In al-Kashf it is stated that the more likely reading is that it is a kinaya (indirect expression) while the literal meaning is still intended, because secrecy in itself is also desired, but the primary aim is sincerity. It is also said that it means concealed from people by speaking in a low voice. There is no contradiction on the basis of the use of metaphor, or on the basis that calling does not necessarily entail raising the voice. For this reason it is said: "O you who call with the heart, and it hears." His, peace be upon him, call was like this for the reason mentioned just now, or because of the weakness of his voice due to his old age, as it is said: "The old man's voice is faint, and his hearing is intermittent." It is said that his age at that time was sixty years. It is said sixty-five, and it is said seventy, and it is said seventy-five, and it is said eighty, and it is said eighty-five, and it is said ninety-two, and it is said ninety-nine, and it is said one hundred and twenty, and this last is most in accord with the stated reasoning.

Some claimed that it was indicated that the calling was secret, without raising the voice, by the deletion of its particle in His saying, Exalted is He,

[p. 60]

**"He said, 'My Lord'"** The clause (al-jumla) explains the call (al-nida', the vocative) and specifies its manner, so it has no place in the grammatical analysis (i'rab).

**"Indeed my bones have weakened (wahana) within me."** That is, they have become weak. The attribution of this to the bones is because they are the pillar (ʿimad) of the body and the support (di'am) of the frame. When weakness and slackness afflict them, what lies behind them gives way and their strength falls away. So the speech contains a metonymy (kinaya) founded on an implicit comparison (tashbih) in the mind. Or, it is because the bone is the hardest of the body's parts and the most firm in structure, and the least affected by ailments. When it weakens, what is behind it is weaker still. So the speech contains a metonymy without an explicit comparison.

The noun is given in the singular, according to what al-'Allama al-Zamakhshari said and what many of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) approved. The singular is what indicates the sense of the genus (al-jinsiyya), and the intention is that this genus, which is the column and the structure, and the strongest of what the body is composed of, has been afflicted by weakness. Had it been put in the plural, the intention would have been another meaning: that only some of his bones had weakened, not all of them, as if the speaker had been met by a listener who doubted the totality and comprehensiveness, because the restriction in the speech looks to the negation of its opposite. This is not appropriate to the context. Al-Sakkaki said: he turned the plural (al-'a?am) into the singular in order to seek that the weakness encompass the bones one by one, and had it been plural, this would not have been specified, since it would be valid to say the bones weakened when weakness reached some of them and not every single one. This is another, less preferred path according to many, and the verification of this is in its place.

It is related from Qatada that he (peace be upon him) complained of the falling out of his molars. It should not be overlooked that this requires a report (khabar) indicating it, since understanding it from the verse is hardly to be accepted.

The phrase **"from me" (minni)** is attached to an omitted element which is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "the bone." He did not say "my bone" (ʿazmi), although that is more concise, because of the detail after the general statement that it contains, and because it is more explicit in indicating the intended genus here. The emphasis of the clause (ta'kid al-jumla) serves to show the full care given to establishing its content.

Al-A'mash read **"wahina"** with a kasra on the ha', and it was also read with a damma.

**"And the head has blazed (ishta'ala) with white hair (shayban)."** He likened the grey hair, in its whiteness and brightness, to the flame of fire, and its spreading through the hair, its pervasion of it, and its taking hold of it in every way, to the burning of that flame. Then he expressed it in the manner of a metaphor (isti'ara). So the speech contains two metaphors: an explicit metaphor of the verbal kind (tab'iyya) in "ishta'ala," and an implicit metaphor (makniyya) in "shayb." That they are separated from the imaginative (takhyiliyya) is what the verifiers among the scholars of rhetoric (ahl al-ma'ani) hold, although on a remote view it is possible that the imaginative metaphor exists here too. Some people, claiming that separation is not permissible and that the existence of the imaginative metaphor is not evident, put what is in the verse into the form of a representational metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya), but this is not so.

He attributed the blazing to the place and origin of the hair, and expressed it in the manner of a specification (tamyiz) for the sake of emphasis and to convey comprehensiveness. Attributing a meaning to a container, whether temporal or spatial, of which it is a property, conveys that its meaning is general to everything within it according to the usage of discourse. So your saying "his house blazed with fire" conveys the burning of everything in it, unlike "the fire of his house blazed."

Some people claimed that **"shayban"** is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), because the meaning of "the head blazed" is "turned grey." It was also said that it is a circumstantial qualifier (hal), meaning "greying." Neither of these two views is fully accepted by a complete scholar, as is not hidden. He dispensed with the definite article (al-lam) instead of an annexation (idafa), because the definiteness of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd) intended here conveys what the annexation conveys. Since the definiteness of "the bone" earlier was of the genus, as you know, he did not suffice with it and added "from me." In sum, how eloquent and forceful this clause is! From it Ibn Durayd took his verse:

*"The white hair blazed in its black, like the blazing of fire in the dry wood of the ghada."*

It is related from Abu 'Amr that he assimilated the sin into the shin (idgham).

**"And I have never been unsuccessful (shaqiyyan) in my supplication to You, my Lord."** That is: I have never been disappointed in my supplication to You at any time during this long life. Rather, every time I called upon You, You answered me. The clause is coordinated with what precedes it. It was also said that it is a circumstantial qualifier of the first person pronoun (ya' al-mutakallim), since the meaning would be "my head blazed," which is strange.

This is a means of supplication (tawassul) by him (peace be upon him) through what had preceded from Him, exalted is He, of answering at every supplication, following the groundwork that calls for mercy: old age and weakness of condition. For after He had accustomed His servant to answer for a long age, He would hardly disappoint him ever, especially at the time of his necessity and extreme need. In this means of supplication there is an indication of the immensity of the generosity of Allah, mighty and majestic, to the extent it contains.

It is related that Hatim al-Ta'i, or it was said Ma'n ibn Za'ida, was approached by a needy man who asked him, and the man said: "I am the one whom you did good to on such and such occasion." He said: "Welcome to one who has used us as a means to reach us," and fulfilled his need.

It was also said that the meaning is: "I have never been unsuccessful in Your calling me to obedience, but rather I was among those who obeyed You and worshipped You, singled out." The "kaf" (of "bidu'a'ika," your calling) in this case is the subject (fa'il). The first view is more evident and preferable. This was related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

The mention in both places of the attribute of lordship (rububiyya), which indicates the bestowal of what contains the good of the one who is nurtured (al-marbub), along with the attachment to his pronoun (peace be upon him), is especially so in the placing of the pronoun between "kana" and its predicate, to set the chain of answering in motion through exaggeration in humble supplication.

It has come in some reports that when the servant says in his supplication, "O Lord," Allah, exalted is He, says to him: "Here I am at your service, My servant" (labbayka 'abdi).

It is related that Musa (peace be upon him) once said in his supplication, "O Lord," and Allah, glorified and exalted is He, said to him: "Here I am at your service, O Musa." Musa said: "Is this for me alone?" Allah, blessed and exalted is He, said: "No, but for everyone who calls upon Me with lordship."

It was also said: when the servant wishes his supplication to be answered, let him call upon Allah, exalted is He, with what is suitable to Him of His names and attributes, mighty and majestic is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 5:

﴿And indeed I fear the mawali (the kinsmen/heirs) after me﴾ — they are the 'usbah (close paternal kin) of the man, according to what has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and Mujahid; and on the authority of al-Asamm, they are the paternal cousins (banu al-'amm), who are the ones nearest to him in lineage. It has also been said: those who take charge of his affairs from among his relatives in general. And they, according to all the other opinions, were the wicked among the Children of Israel, so he, peace be upon him, feared that they would not manage his succession over his community well. The clause is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon his saying ﴿Indeed my bones have weakened within me﴾, its content following from its content, for the weakening of strength and the advancing of age are among the beginnings of his fear, peace be upon him, of those who would take charge of his affairs after his death, as indicated by his saying ﴿from behind me﴾, for its meaning, by the consensus of those of the exegetes whom we have learned from, is "after my death". The prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element that the mind naturally infers, i.e., "I feared the conduct of the mawali from behind me" or "the tyranny of the mawla". It has been read thus, as in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim. It is also permitted to connect it to mawali, and that suffices for this that the meaning of the verb be present in it to some extent, for they have said: "The scent of the verb suffices for the connection of an adverbial phrase, and it is not required that it indicate occurrence, as with the active and passive participles, so that one would strain for it." It is said that the lam in mawali on this view is a relative element (mawsul) and the adverbial phrase is connected to its complement; and that mawla is a lightened form of muwallan, as has been said regarding its meaning that it is lightened in meaning — but that is an unwarranted strain with no need for it. Indeed, they have stated the sense of the meaning on this view as: "I feared those who would take charge of the matter from behind me." Al-Zamakhshari did not permit its connection to khiftu (I feared), because the meaning would be corrupt; and he explained this in al-Kashshaf: the prepositional phrase is not the complement of the verb, since the verb transitively reaches the object of fear without an intermediary, so it is necessarily an adverb of place, in the manner of "I feared the lion before you" or "from before you"; and then it would follow that the fear persists after his death, and its corruption is evident. Some have seen the permissibility of the connection on the basis that the object's being within a time/place that makes that adverb connected to its verb is sufficient, as in your saying: "I shot the game in the sacred precinct," when the game is within it but not your shooting. The apparent view is that it is not permissible, so understand. Ibn Jinni said: it is a presumed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah) from (al-mawali). And it is related from Ibn Kathir that he read (wa min waraya) with a short vowel and a fatha on the ya, like 'asaya.

Al-Zuhri read (al-mawali) with a sukun on the ya. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn Thabit, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn and his two sons Muhammad and Zayd, Sa'id ibn al-'As, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Ya'mur, Shubayl ibn 'Azrah, and al-Walid ibn Muslim read, for Ibn 'Amir: (khaffat) with a fatha on the kha and the fa, shadda-ed, and a kasra on the feminine ta, and (al-mawali) with a sukun on the ya, on the basis that (khaffat) is from lightness, the opposite of heaviness. The meaning of ﴿from behind me﴾, as previously stated, is: "and the mawali have become few and have become unable to carry out the affairs of religion after me," or it is from al-khufuf in the sense of swift travel; and the meaning of ﴿from behind me﴾ is "from before me and before me," and the intended sense is: "the mawali who were capable of establishing the rites of the religion and the welfare of the community have passed away before me, and none remains among them in whom there is strength and support, so he would be in need of a successor, because his kinsmen would be unable to undertake after him what he himself was undertaking, or because they died before him, so he remained in need of someone to lean upon." The connection of the prepositional phrase on the second aspect to the verb is evident; as for the first aspect, if it is considered that their incapacity and paucity will occur after him, not that it is actual at the time of his supplication, it is valid to connect it to the verb as well; and if it is not so, it is connected to something else.

﴿And my wife has been barren﴾ — that is, she has not borne children from her youth until her old age; al-'aqr, with a fatha or damma, means sterility, and 'aqir is said of both the male and the female. ﴿So grant me from Yourself﴾ — both prepositional phrases are connected to hab, and the lam is its complement; min denotes the starting point of the extent, metaphorically; the first is placed first because what it signifies is more important to him. It is also permitted that the second be connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause from the object that follows. The discussion of ladun has already preceded. The intended meaning is: give me from the pure bounty of Your vast favor and Your overwhelming power, by way of innovation and not through the intermediary of ordinary causes. It has been said the intended meaning is: give me from Your bounty however You wish, (a successor) — that is, a child from my loins, and this is the apparent meaning, and it is supported by the saying of the Exalted in the surah of Al 'Imran, relating about him, peace be upon him: ﴿He said: My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring﴾. It has also been said that he, peace be upon him, requested someone who would stand in his place and inherit from him, whether a son or otherwise; and it has been said that he, peace be upon him, despaired that a child would be born to him from his wife, so he requested someone who would inherit from him and stand in his place from among the rest of the people. Both of these views are not relied upon. Al-Zamakhshari claimed that ﴿from Yourself﴾ is an emphasis on his being a pleasing successor, and what is in this is not hidden. The placement of the object after the two prepositional phrases is to show full concern with the gift being granted to him in that wondrous manner, along with what is in it of suspense toward the delayed element, and because there is a kind of length with what follows of the descriptive clause; so placing them after everything and inserting them between the qualified and the qualifier is not fitting for the eloquence of the noble composition. The fa' indicates that what follows is consequent upon what precedes, for what he, peace be upon him, mentioned of old age, weakness of strength, and the barrenness of the woman necessitates the cutting off of his hope, peace be upon him, of the birth of a child through the intermediary of ordinary causes, and asking for it in the manner that breaks custom.

It has been said: because that necessitates the cutting off of his hope of a child from her while she is in that state, and asking for it in the manner that God, Exalted is He, wills; and this is based on the second view regarding the meaning of ﴿so grant me from Yourself a successor﴾; and the first is preferable.

What has been mentioned is not undermined by there being another motive for turning to supplication, namely his, peace be upon him, witnessing of the manifest wonders regarding Mary, as is indicated by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿There Zakariya called upon his Lord﴾ and the verse. Its not being mentioned here is for reliance on what was mentioned there, just as the non-mention of the preface to the supplication there is for the sufficiency of its mention here; and the sufficiency of what is mentioned in one place for what is omitted in another is among the revealed customs.

**[Page 62]**

His saying, ﴿who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾, is an attribute of *waliyyan* (a successor), as is apparent from the sentence that follows indefinite nouns. It is said that *warithahu* and *waritha minhu* are two dialects, as has been reported. It is also said that *min* here indicates partiality, not transitivity. *Al* (family) of a man means his close associates, those whose affairs return to him, whether through kinship, companionship, or agreement in religion. As for Ya'qub, according to what is narrated from al-Suddi, he is Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, for Zakariyya was from the descendants of Harun, who was from the descendants of Lawi ibn Ya'qub. Zakariyya was married to the sister of Maryam bint Imran, and she was from the descendants of Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them both, who was from the descendants of Yahudha ibn Ya'qub also. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: he is Ya'qub ibn Mathan, and his brother Imran ibn Mathan was the father of Maryam.

It is also said that he was the brother of Zakariyya, peace be upon him. The meaning of inheritance in both places is knowledge, according to what has been said.

Al-Kalbi said: the sons of Mathan were the chiefs and kings of the Children of Israel, and Zakariyya, peace be upon him, was at that time the chief of the rabbis (*ahbar*). So he wished that his son would inherit from him the office of *al-Hubura* (the rabbinical leadership), and would inherit from the sons of Mathan their kingship. Thus the inheritance would be of different kinds in the two places. This is supported by the fact that the conjunction (*'atf*) on the object pronoun was not chosen, and the first *yarithu* was sufficient. It is also said that the first inheritance is the inheritance of prophethood, and the second is the inheritance of kingship, so they would also be of different kinds. However, His saying ﴿and make him, O my Lord, one with whom You are pleased﴾, meaning one who is pleasing to You in word and deed, and it is said, *radiyan* (one who is pleased), and the first is more fitting. In this case it is an emphasis, because the prophet's condition is that he be like this. According to what we have said, it is a supplication for his being enabled to act, just as the first (request) includes a supplication for his being enabled to acquire knowledge. It is as if he asked that his son be a scholar who acts. It is also said that the meaning is: make him pleasing among Your servants, that is, one who is followed, so there is no emphasis at all. The placement of *Rabbi* between the two objects of *ja'ala* (make) in all the other views is for the sake of emphasizing care for the matter that it requires.

Al-Sakkaki chose that the two sentences are resumptive (*isti'naf*) of an explanatory kind (*isti'naf bayani*), because it could be objected that, on the attributive reading, Zakariyya would not have been given a son with such an attribute before the death of Yahya, peace be upon him, since Yahya was killed before Zakariyya was killed. This was challenged in *al-Kashf* on the ground that the objection is refuted because the reports conflict, and most say that Zakariyya died before him, peace be upon them both. Then he said: as for the answer that there is no objection to some of what a prophet asks being granted and not all, do you not see the supplication of our Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, regarding his community, when he said, peace be upon him: ("I asked Him that He would not let some of them suffer the violence of others, but He refused me").

And [also] the supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, regarding his father. That would only be complete if the prohibited matter were that, but the prohibited matter is the breaking of the promise in His statement, exalted is He, which concerns the prophets: ﴿So We answered him﴾, and this indicates that he, peace be upon him, was given what he asked without distinguishing between one part and another, and the context of the other verses is similar. You may use the apparent meaning of this verse as evidence against the weakness of the narration of those who claim that Yahya died before his father, peace be upon them both. As for the objection that what was chosen, namely reading it as resumption, does not remove the prohibited matter because it is a connection of meaning (*wasl ma'nawi*), it is not valid, because the connection exists, but it is not included in what is asked, since it is an explanation of the cause that prompted the request, and it does not follow that the cause of the request must be something requested. End of quotation.

Some have answered that since the meaning of inheritance here is inheritance of knowledge, his death before his father, peace be upon them both, does no harm, because the purpose is achieved, which is taking that knowledge and transmitting it to others in such a way that its effects remain long after Zakariyya, peace be upon him. It is not hidden, however, that what is known is the continued existence of the heir's person after the one from whom he inherits.

Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, al-Zuhri, al-A'mash, Talha, al-Yazidi, Ibn 'Isa al-Isfahani, Ibn Muhaysin, and Qatada read both verbs in the jussive (*yarithni* and *yarith*), on the basis that they are the answer to the supplication, and the meaning is: "Grant me that, and he will inherit me," and so on. The intention is that this is what he expects and hopes for. 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, Ibn 'Abbas, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with them, al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur, al-Jahdari, Abu Harb ibn Abi al-Aswad, and Abu Nahik read ﴿yarithni﴾ with *raf'* (nominative), and *wa-arith* as a verb in the imperfect from *waritha*. This is explained as meaning: "He will inherit from me the knowledge, and I will inherit from him, with it, the kingship of the family of Ya'qub." This is by treating the inheritance of the successor as kingship, an inheritance from Zakariyya, peace be upon him, because the elevation of a son is the elevation of the father. The *wa* is for general combination. Some said: the *wa* is for the circumstantial (*hal*), and the sentence is a circumstantial clause from one of the two pronouns. The author of *al-Lawami'* said: there is inversion (*taqdim*) in it, and its meaning is: "So grant me a successor from the family of Ya'qub, who will inherit from me prophethood if I die before him, and I will inherit from him his wealth if he dies before me." There is something in this that you will know shortly, if Allah wills. It is also reported from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and a group, that they read ﴿yarithni wa-arithu﴾ with *raf'* of *arithu* in the pattern *fa'il* (agent noun), on the basis that it is the subject of *yarithni*, according to the manner of *tajrid* (abstraction), as Abu al-Fath and others said. That is, a successor of that successor will inherit from me, or inherit by him. He has abstracted from the successor a successor, just as you say "I saw from him, or by him, a lion." It is reported from al-Jahdari that he read *wa-arith* with *imala* of the *waw*. Mujahid read ﴿Uwayrith﴾, the diminutive of *warith*, and its original form is *Wuwayrith*,

**[Page 63]**

with two *waws*: the first is the root letter of the word, and the second replaces the *alif* of the agent pattern, because in diminutive formation it reverts to *waw*, as in *duwayrib*. When a *waw* carrying a *damma* occurs before another *waw* at the beginning, it is changed to a *hamza*, as established in morphology. It is reported from him that he said: the diminutive is because of his youth. For when he asked for him in his old age, he knew, even by conjecture, that he would inherit from him in his young age. It is also said that the diminutive is for praise, but this is not the correct view.

The Shi'a have cited this verse as evidence that the prophets, peace be upon them, have their wealth inherited from them, because inheritance is literal in the case of inheriting wealth, and there is no reason to turn away from the literal meaning. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti, in *al-Durr al-Manthur*, has mentioned on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, and Abu Salih that they said regarding the verse: "He will inherit my wealth."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan that the Prophet (ﷺ) said regarding the verse: ("May Allah have mercy on my brother Zakariyya; what did he have to do with heirs?"). In another narration: ("What did he have to do with someone who would inherit his wealth?").

Some have said: inheritance is evident in that sense, and it is not permissible here to interpret it as inheritance of prophethood, lest His statement ﴿and make him, O my Lord, one with whom You are pleased﴾ be meaningless, nor as inheritance of knowledge, because knowledge is acquired, whereas what is inherited is obtained without acquisition. The position of the People of the Sunna is that the prophets, peace be upon them, do not inherit wealth nor pass it on, because the reports that are authentic to them say so. This has also come through the chain of the Shi'a.

Al-Kulayni reported in *al-Kafi*, from Abu al-Bakhtari, from Abu 'Abd Allah Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets," because the prophets did not bequeath a dirham or a dinar, but bequeathed hadiths from their hadiths. Whoever takes any of them has taken a full portion.

The word *innama* (only) is conclusively restrictive, by the acknowledgment of the Shi'a. The inheritance in the verse is to be understood as what you have heard, and we do not accept that it is literal in its linguistic sense in the case of inheriting wealth. Rather, it is literal for what encompasses inheritance of knowledge, office, and wealth. It has become restricted to wealth through the predominance of usage in the terminology of the jurists, like conventional transfers of meaning. Even if we grant that it is a metaphor in that sense, it is a well-known and established metaphor, especially in the usage of the Glorious Qur'an, to the extent that it equals the literal meaning. Among that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We gave the Book as an inheritance to those whom We chose from Our servants﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then after them there succeeded a generation who inherited the Book﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed those who were given the Book as an inheritance after them﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed the earth belongs to Allah; He gives it as an inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants﴾, and ﴿And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾.

As for their claim that there is no reason to turn away from the literal meaning, we say: the reason is established, which is preserving the word of the infallible from falsehood, and without interpreting it, one would be trying to uproot thorns with the hand (*kharṭ al-qatad*). The indications that they bequeath wealth are not relied upon by the critics. Some claimed that it is not permissible to interpret the inheritance here as inheritance of prophethood, lest His statement ﴿and make him, O my Lord, one with whom You are pleased﴾ be meaningless. We have already mentioned what can be known about that and its problems. It was claimed that the acquired nature of a thing prevents it from being inherited; this is not valid, for inheritance has been applied to what is not acquired in the words of al-Sadiq. Among that also is what al-Kulayni reported in *al-Kafi* from Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "Sulayman inherited Dawud, and Muhammad (ﷺ) inherited Sulayman, peace be upon him."

The inheritance of Sulayman by the Prophet (ﷺ), peace be upon him, cannot be conceived as anything other than knowledge, prophethood, and the like. Among what supports interpreting the inheritance here as knowledge and the like, rather than wealth, is that in the lofty views and exalted aspirations of the holy souls, which have severed their ties with this changing and perishing world and joined the enduring world, there is no inclination toward worldly goods even to the size of a mosquito's wing. This is especially so for Zakariyya, peace be upon him, who was well known for complete detachment and renunciation. It would be customarily impossible for him to fear the inheritance of wealth and goods, which in his lofty view had no value at all, or for such anxiety, sorrow, and fear to appear on his account, or for him to make that kind of request from the presence of the Truth, exalted is He. That would indicate complete love and attachment of the heart to this world. The Shi'a said: he, peace be upon him, feared that his cousins would spend his wealth after his death on what is not fitting, **[Page 64]** so he sought an heir for it who would be pleasing for that purpose. In response: this is not something to fear, for when a man dies and his wealth passes by inheritance to another, the wealth becomes that other person's wealth, so spending it, rightly or wrongly, is on his responsibility, and there is no blame on the deceased for that expenditure, nor even any reproach. Moreover, the removal of this fear was made easy for him, peace be upon him, by his spending it before his death, giving all of it in charity in the way of Allah, and leaving his wicked cousins disappointed because of their evil conditions and ugly deeds.

For the prophets, peace be upon them, according to the Shi'a, there is knowledge of the time of their death and a choice concerning it. Therefore, he had no fear of sudden death either. His purpose, peace be upon him, in asking for a child was nothing but carrying out the commands of Allah, spreading the Sharia, and the continuation of prophethood among his offspring, for that brings multiplied reward until such time in time as Allah wills. Whoever is fair does not hesitate in accepting this, and Allah, exalted is He, is the guide to the most upright paths.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 7:**

﴿O Zakariyya!﴾ [This is] according to the intention of speech, meaning: it was said to him, or Allah the Exalted said, "O Zakariyya!" ﴿Indeed, We give you good news of a boy whose name is Yahya.﴾ However, this does not mean that He, glorified and exalted, addressed him with this directly in His own essence; rather, it was through an angel (al-malak), as another verse indicates, and [it was] that he, peace be upon him, related the expression from Him, mighty and majestic, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves...﴾ and the rest of the verse. This is a response to his call, peace be upon him, and a promise of answering his supplication, as is understood from the expression "good news" (bishara) rather than "giving" (i'ta') or something similar. The delay inherent in the promise does not contradict the immediacy (ta'qib) in His saying: ﴿So We answered him...﴾ and the rest of the verse, because it is an immediacy by custom, as in the expression "he married, and a child was born to him." Moreover, the meaning of "answering" (istijaba) here is also the promise, because the promise of the Generous is [as good as] cash. It is well known that this statement came immediately after the supplication, and there were only a few months between the good news and the birth. It was also said that the child was granted after forty years of his supplication, and it was said: after sixty.

The ghulam (ghulam, a boy) is a male offspring, and it may be said of a female: ghulama, as the poet said:

*"The ghulama is despised by her, and the ghulam [too]."*

In specifying his name, peace be upon him, there is an emphasis on the promise and an honoring of him, peace be upon him. In singling him out with it, as is known from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We have not made for him before any namesake﴾, meaning: no one as his equal (sharik) in the name, since no one before him had been named Yahya, as is reported from Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Aslam. This is an additional honor and exaltation for him, peace be upon him. This, as al-Zamakhshari said, is evidence that rare names, which people hardly use, are worthy of preference, and it was for these that the Arabs would seek out [names] in naming, because they are more distinguished, more elevated, and further removed from disparagement (nabz). Thus, the poet said in praising a people:

*"Strange of names, trailing their waistwraps, red, [their garments] brushing the earth with their hems."*

It was said to al-Salt ibn Ata: "How did you come to advance among the Barmakids, when among them is one more refined than you?" He said: "I was a stranger in the land, a stranger in name, light in weight, and stingy with my reputation." So among what he advanced was his being strange in name.

Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from Mujahid that (samiyyan) means "similar" (shabihan), and it is reported from Ata and Ibn Jubayr something similar, meaning: We have not made for him a like, since he did not disobey and did not intend any disobedience. Ahmad, al-Hakim, al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no one among the children of Adam but that he has erred or intended a sin, except Yahya ibn Zakariyya, peace be upon them both; he did not intend a sin and did not commit it."

The reports on this are mutually corroborating (mutaZaharah). It was also said: he had no like in that respect, and because he was born between an aged old man and a barren old woman.

It was also said: because he was, as Allah the Exalted described, "confirming a word from Allah, and a master, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous," so this would be a summary of that. The reason a similar one is called samiyy is that two similar things share the name, and from this usage is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Do you know of any namesake for him?﴾ because this is what the sequence of the statement requires.

The more apparent view is that the name is non-Arabic (a'jami), because their custom was not to name with Arabic words; so its being diptote (mamnu' al-sarf), according to the well-known opinion regarding such [names], is due to proper-name status (ʻalamiyya) and foreignness (ʻujma). It was also said that it is Arabic, and that custom has a role in its strangeness. On this view, it is derived from a verb, like Ya'mur and Ya'ish, and [names derived from verbs] have been used, such as Yamut, and Yamut ibn al-Muzarri' ibn Ukht al-Jahiz was [a person] with this name. The reason for naming him by this, on the view that it is Arabic, has been said to be an indication that he would live long (ya'muru), and this is in the sense of an omen (tafa'ul) of a long life. In this there is an indication that he, peace be upon him, would inherit, as Zakariyya, peace be upon him, had asked.

It was also said: he was named this because life (hayah) was [given] to the womb of his mother through him. It was said: because he was alive between an aged old man and a barren old woman. It was said: because he lives by wisdom and chastity. It was said: because he lives by guiding and directing people. It was said: because he was martyred, and martyrs are alive. Other views have also been said.

Then, it is not hidden that, whether it is Arabic or foreign, the [morphological] weight and diminutive form differ, as has been clarified in its proper place.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 19, verse 8:**

(Qala) is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question), as if it were said: "What did he (peace be upon him) say then?" It is answered: he said, (*Rabbi*, "My Lord"). God addressed him directly (*bi'l-dhat*), while His address also reached him through the angel, for the sake of intensifying his supplication, his intimate conversation (*munajat*), and his earnest devotion (*tabattul*) to Him, Mighty and Majestic. It has also been said that this was done to avoid what might suggest that His address to the angel implies that His knowledge of what proceeds from him depends on an intermediary, just as the knowledge of human beings of what proceeds from Him depends on that in most circumstances. It is not hidden that limiting oneself to the first explanation is better.

﴿Anna yakunu li ghulam﴾ ("How can I have a son?"): the word (*anna*) means "how" or "from where." (*Kana*) may be a complete verb (*tamma*), with (*anna*) and (*li*) both related to it. The prepositional phrase is placed before the subject, as explained more than once earlier; the meaning is: how or from where will a boy come into being for me? It is also permissible for (*li*) to be related to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of (*ghulam*), meaning: how will a boy come into being, existing for me? Or (*kana*) may be a defective verb (*naqisa*) whose subject is an explicit noun, and whose predicate is either (*anna*), with (*li*) related to an omitted element as above, or the predicate is (*li*) itself, with (*anna*) in the accusative as an adverb of place (*zarf*).

﴿Wa kanat imra'ati 'aqiran﴾ ("And my wife has been barren"): this is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun of the speaker, with an implied (*qad*). Likewise ﴿wa qad balaghtu mina'l-kibari 'itiyyan﴾ ("And I have indeed reached extreme old age") is a circumstantial clause from the same pronoun, emphasizing the sense of improbability after an emphasis. (*Min*) is for the starting point (*ibtida'*), the high (*'ali*) one. (*'Itiyy*) derives from (*'ata ya'tu*), meaning dryness, desiccation, and the stiffness of the joints and bones.

Al-Raghib said: it is a state for which there is no way to repair or cure it. It has also been said: a way to train it, which is the state alluded to by the poet's verse:

"And from hardship is the training of old age."

Its original form is (*'utuwwun*), like (*qu'udun*). The succession of the two *damma*s and the two *waw*s was felt to be heavy, so the *ta'* was given a *kasra*, the first (*waw*) became a *ya'* because it was quiescent and preceded by a *kasra*, then the second also changed into a *ya'*, because of the meeting of a *waw* and a *ya'*, with one of them preceded by a quiescent letter. The *'ayn* was given a *kasra* to match what follows it. That is: my wife has been barren, not having borne children in her youth and mine; how much more so now, when she is an old woman and I have reached, because of advanced age, dryness and desiccation. Or it is a state for which there is no way of repair. The views on his age at that time have already been presented to you. As for the age of his wife, it has been said that she was ninety-eight.

It is also permissible for (*min*) to be partitive (*tab'idh*), meaning: she has reached, of the stages and levels of old age, what is called (*'itiyyan*). Some have made it explanatory (*bayaniyya tajridiyya*), but there is a discussion about this. The prepositional phrase is either related to what is before it, or to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause of (*'itiyyan*), which is in the accusative as an object. The basic meaning agrees with His words, Exalted is He, in Al 'Imran, quoting him: ﴿Balaghani al-kibaru﴾ ("Old age has reached me"). The difference in the grammatical subject does not harm this, for what reaches you of meanings has also reached her. There is a difference between the two statements from another aspect, which is not hidden, so the choice of each of them in its context requires a reason, so reflect upon this. Likewise is the reason for beginning here with mention of the state of his wife (peace be upon him), in reverse order to what is in that surah.

[Page 67]

In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim: "Perhaps that is because he had mentioned his own state within the course of his supplication, whereas what is mentioned here is his reaching the furthest stages of old age, as a completion of what was mentioned before. As for here, the mention of his state had not preceded in the supplication, so for that reason he placed it before the mention of his wife's state, because hastening to explain the deficiency of his condition is more fitting." End of quote.

Some have said: it is possible that the supplication and the dialogue were repeated, and that the variation in style is for variety, while each contains what the other does not, so reflect. God is the Granter of success. The apparent meaning is that he (peace be upon him) knew about himself that he was not barren; that is why he mentioned old age and did not mention barrenness. He said what he said, though his supplication for this had preceded, and his certainty in God's power was strong, especially after witnessing the signs mentioned in Surah Al 'Imran, glorifying the power of God, Exalted is He, and acknowledging His blessing upon him in this matter, by showing that it was purely from God's grace and kindness, even though in itself it was among things that are customarily impossible; and it was not an expression of disbelief. Thus it has been said.

It has also been said: it is an expression of disbelief, but it does not refer to the speaker. Rather, it is in relation to those who deny. He (peace be upon him) only sought what would remove the sharpness of their disbelief and deter them from their evil habits. This is not objectionable from a Prophet, contrary to the view of Ibn al-Munir. Indeed, an objection was raised to this: the supplication was secret from the deniers.

It is answered that it is possible that he made it public after that, to show God's blessing upon him and to seek what has been mentioned, so consider this. It has also been said: it is an expression of disbelief referring to the speaker, since there were sixty years between the supplication and the glad tidings, and he (peace be upon him) had forgotten his supplication. But this is very far-fetched.

In al-Intisaf: "The apparent meaning, and God knows best, is that Zakariyya (peace be upon him) asked for a child in general terms. The verse does not indicate that it would come from him while he was in decrepitude, nor that it would come from his wife while she was barren, nor that their strength and youth would be restored to them, as was done with others, or that the child would be from a wife other than his barren one. The child from the two of them was regarded as unlikely while they were in their present condition, so he asked whether it would be so while they were as they were. It was said to him: 'Thus,' that is, the child will be [born] and you will be as you are." This is critiqued: His words ﴿Fa hab li min ladunka﴾ ("So grant me from Yourself") are clear that he asked for a child, while they were in a state in which a child from them is customarily impossible.

My own view is that it is an expression of disbelief from the standpoint of custom, or that it is in relation to those who deny, and this, as in al-Kashshaf, is more appropriate.

Most of the seven readers read (*'itiyyan*) with a *damma* on the *'ayn*. Ibn Mas'ud read it with a *fatha* on the *'ayn*, and likewise with a *fatha* on the *sad* of (*siliyyan*). The origin of this, as Ibn Jinni said in reply to the statement of Ibn Mujahid, "I do not know of any origin for these two in Arabic," is that there are masdars in the pattern (*fa'il*), such as (*al-hawil*) and (*al-zawil*). It is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid that they both read (*'usiyyan*) with a *damma* on the *'ayn* and a *kasra* on the *sin*. Al-Dani transmitted this from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Zamakhshari from Ubayy, and Mujahid. It derives from (*'asa al-'udu ya'su*), meaning the stick became dry.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 9 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Said: "So it is; your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me.'"﴾ Al-Hasan (al-Hasan al-Basri) read "وهو عَلِيَّ هَيِّنٌ" with a *waw*, and it is also reported from him that he kasra-ed the *ya'* of the first person, as in the verse of al-Nabigha:

*"ʿalayya li-ʿAmrin niʿmatun baʿda niʿmatin / li-wālidihi laysat bi-dhāti ʿaqārib"*
("A favour is upon me for ʿAmr, after favour upon favour, to his father; it is not one with scorpion-stings.")

Similar to this is the reading of Hamza, "وما أنْتُمْ بِمُصْرِخِيِّ" with a kasra on the *ya'*. The *kaf* (in ذَلِكَ) may be in the nominative as a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "the matter is so." The pronoun in "قالَ" refers to the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, not to the angel who gave the good news, lest the composition be disrupted. "That" (ذَلِكَ) points to the words of Zakariyya, peace be upon him. The address in ﴿قالَ رَبُّكَ﴾ is to him, peace be upon him, and not to our Prophet ﷺ, as shown by what precedes and follows it. The clause ﴿هُوَ عَلَيَّ هَيِّنٌ﴾ is the second object of "قالَ," and the clause "the matter is so," together with the clause ﴿قالَ رَبُّكَ﴾ and so on, is the first object of "قالَ," even though no conjunction separates the two clauses, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وقالَ ارْكَبُوا فِيها بِسْمِ اللَّهِ مَجْراها ومُرْساها إنَّ رَبِّي لَغَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ and His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿قالُوا أإذا مِتْنا وكُنّا تُرابًا وعِظامًا أإنّا لَمَبْعُوثُونَ﴾ ﴿لَقَدْ وُعِدْنا﴾, the verse.

[p. 68]

"Kadhalika" and "kadhalika" (repeated). The first clause is given as confirmation from Him, exalted is He, of Zakariyya, peace be upon him, and the second as an answer to what might be suspected: that if that was (considered) remote in such a station, and it has been fulfilled in it, how could it be attained? So it is, in itself, a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a new sentence) answering that. A conjunction does not fittingly intervene between two such clauses when the one being quoted spoke them together without a conjunction, so as to indicate the first form of the saying itself. Likewise, it is not fitting to supply another verb of saying, because it would be a resumptive answer to the one addressed, and so it would not show that it is also a resumption in the first (clause) except by an explicit separator. But if he spoke them at two different times, or without that order, then the apparent reading is either conjunction or resumption with an implied verb of saying.

Then, if Zakariyya's answer had been limited to ﴿هُوَ عَلَيَّ هَيِّنٌ﴾ without inserting ﴿قالَ رَبُّكَ﴾, it would have been acceptable. But (the Qur'an) turned to the insertion only to indicate the confirmation of the promise and the complete removal of the remoteness, in the manner of a king who promises one of his intimates something which he does not find himself worthy of; so he begins to wonder, deeming it remote that it should come from the king in such a station. So he tries to affirm his intention and remove his astonishment. Then he may say, "Do not consider it remote; it is the easiest thing for Me," in the apparent sense; or he may say, "Do not consider it remote; I have said that it is the easiest thing for Me," indicating that it is a promise whose saying preceded and was decided, and that its exalted rank is such that its fulfilment for the one who seeks it does not appear as an event, whoever he may be. How much more so for one who deserved from Him, because of the truthfulness of his foot in His servanthood, honour and elevation. This is a saying in the language of allusion, which is confirmed even if it was not expressly uttered, because the purpose is that elevated standing, vastness of power and perfection of generosity require it. It was said: first. Then, when he wanted to reinforce this meaning, he turned away from the narrative saying: "The One whose blessings you are, has said that it is the easiest thing for Me." Then, when a king narrates the story to some of his select companions, he may say: "I said to my servant so-and-so such-and-such." He says: "I have certainly ..." and so on; and he may say instead: "The master of so-and-so said to him," and narrate the story. So this is the parallel of the verse in what happened to Zakariyya, peace be upon him, and it is narrated to our Prophet, may the best of prayers and the most complete peace be upon him.

It has become clear from this explanation that the loss of the nuance of insertion prevents making the nominative part of the second *qala* (verb "said") and the whole thing the complement of the first. The apparent direction of al-Hasan's reading on this basis is that the clause ﴿هُوَ عَلَيَّ هَيِّنٌ﴾ is coordinated with an omitted element of the type "I will do, and I am doing." It may be said, and perhaps the words of al-Zamakhshari suggest a preference for it, that it is coordinated with the preceding clause, considering the original form, since it has passed that "qala" is inserted for a nuance. So it is as if it were said: "The matter is so, and He is, by that, easy for Me." As for the accusative with the second "qala", the *kaf* is that which is used inserted in a wondrous, strange matter to affirm it. That refers to an ambiguous thing which is explained by what follows it, namely ﴿هُوَ عَلَيَّ هَيِّنٌ﴾. The pronoun in "qala" refers to the Lord, as already mentioned, and the address is also to our Prophet ﷺ; that is, the Lord of Zakariyya said to him: "Your Lord said the like of that wondrous, strange saying: 'It is easy for Me,'" with the second "qala" and what is in its complement being the quoted speech of the first saying, and the insertion of the second saying being for what has passed. The *kaf* is not made accusative by the first "qala", otherwise "qala" would be a second verbal emphasis, lest a foreign element intervene between the explainer and the explained; and that is impossible, since it cannot be properly said: "The Lord of Zakariyya said, 'Your Lord said,'" with the address being to Zakariyya while the addressee is someone else. How, when this kind of speech comes with the simile placed first, especially in the glorious revelation, as in ﴿وكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْناكم أُمَّةً﴾ ("Thus We have made you a community") and "Thus Allah does what He wills," and so on. This aspect does not work with al-Hasan's reading, because the explained element does not take the *waw*, and it is not permissible to omit it so that it becomes coordinated with it, since omission and explanation are contradictory.

It is also permitted, on the assumption of the accusative, that the reference be to what preceded of the promise of God, exalted is He, to him, peace be upon him, by His saying: ﴿إنّا نُبَشِّرُكَ﴾ ("We give you good news") and so on; that is: his Lord, glorified is He, said to him: "Your Lord said the like of that," that is, the like of that wondrous saying which He promised and made known to him, which is ﴿إنّا نُبَشِّرُكَ﴾ and so on, the particle of comparison being inserted as already mentioned. So the meaning is: He promised that, fulfilled it and finished with it; so be at ease concerning its attainment with the most secure ease. Then He said: "It is easy for Me," that is, your Lord said: "It is easy for Me." So He implies the saying in order that the two may correspond in eloquence, and because His saying "like that" is singular, so it is not fitting to attach the clause to it so that the same saying applies to it precisely. Rather, only its like is implied as a resumption, in fulfilment of the due of correspondence.

If you wish, you do not signal it, so that it becomes a quoted report aligned in the thread of ﴿قالَ رَبُّكَ﴾, with the first saying applying to it: that is, the Lord of Zakariyya said to him: "It is easy for Me," because God, exalted is He, is the one addressing Zakariyya, peace be upon him. So there is no obstacle to making it the quoted speech of the first saying without implication, because both sayings, namely "Your Lord said the like of that: 'It is easy for Me,'" are issued together and quoted in their state. But if it were assumed that the addressee were other than God, exalted is He, namely the king, the implication of the saying would be necessary, because it is impossible for "It is easy for Me" to be part of the speech, so the first does not apply to it.

As for al-Hasan's reading: if it is made coordinated with ﴿قالَ رَبُّكَ﴾, there is no need for implication, because the application is sound. If it is also intended to be emphasised, the saying is implied so that eloquence is not lost, and the correspondence is achieved. Making it coordinated with what follows the second "qala", without implication, loses the observance of correspondence in form, since what follows it is singular; and the agreement is in meaning, because of what you know, that "qul" (say) is literal. The meaning is: "His Lord said, the promised matter has been realised and completed," so it must be implied before ﴿هُوَ عَلَيَّ هَيِّنٌ﴾ in order to indicate its realisation too. If it were assumed that the addressee were other than God, exalted is He, the implication is necessary, because there is no application without it; so understand.

This is what the author of al-Kashf (Sahib al-Kashf) verified, and by means of it he set out the wording of al-Kashshaf with slight abridgement. Then he mentioned that the essence of what he found from the words of the scholars is that the implication, on the assumption that the allusion is to the promise that has passed, is: "The Lord of Zakariyya said to him: 'Your Lord said a saying like His saying, glorified and exalted is He, previously, in its strangeness and wonder.'" So it became proper for him, peace be upon him, to ask: "What did You say, my Lord?" when it is like it, and He says: "It is easy for Me," that is, "I said," or "your Lord said." The original on this implication is: "I said a saying like the promise in strangeness," so He turned to *iltifat* (shift of person) or *tajrid* (abstraction), whichever you wish to call it, for its known purpose. There is no departure from the apparent sense in bringing the original saying, since it is necessary for the speech to be coherent. This is because the meaning on this implication is: "Do not be amazed at that saying; look at its like and be amazed, for We have said it."

Likewise, the question may be directed to our Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and the answer is given that his Lord said to him: "It is easy for Me." The correctness of its being the answer to the question of our Prophet, may the prayers and peace be upon him, is the more apparent on this aspect, because the speech is with him. Since it is correct that it be made an answer to him, the implication of the saying is permissible, because it is an answer to him ﷺ, with what indicates that it was addressed to Zakariyya, peace be upon him, too. And it is also permissible that it not be implied, because the addressee of both is one, and the address is with our Prophet ﷺ. It is known from the necessity of the similarity that this statement was also said to Zakariyya. If the reporter and the first speaker differed in this form, there would be no escape from implying it. For if 'Amr says to Bakr, "What did Zayd say to Khalid of what resembles his earlier statement to him?" and he replies, "You are beloved and pleasing," it must be that the implication is: "Zayd said to Khalid this statement without doubt." There is no distance in applying the words of al-Zamakhshari to this, and this is what the author of al-Taqrib hinted at, and al-Imam al-Tibi preferred it; but in it the nuance mentioned in ﴿قالَ رَبُّكَ﴾ is lost. Furthermore, if the saying had not preceded, it would be a lie on the surface, since there is no saying in the language of allusion except that it be interpreted as future in meaning. This is so, and the speech is directed to what removes the remoteness and realises the promise sought; and in that implication there is a departure from it to another meaning, which may entail this meaning incidentally; and what the speech is directed to should be taken as the basis. End of quotation.

This is a speech of verification and precision, to which none is guided except by success. In the verse there is another aspect, which is what the author of al-Intisaf indicated: "(وهَيِّنٌ) is *fay'al*, from 'hāna al-shay'u yahūnu' when it is not difficult," and the meaning is: "I am fully capable of that, if I wish it, it is."

[p. 70]

﴿And I created you before, when you were nothing.﴾ This is an affirmation of what came before, and "a thing" (شَيْئًا) here means "existent"; that is, you were not existent but were non-existent. The apparent sense is that this refers to his creation through procreation and transition through stages, as the rest of human individuals are created. Some verifiers said: what is meant is the beginning of the creation of mankind, since it is what follows pure non-existence, not what came after that by the customary procreation. So it is as if it were said: "I created you before, among the creation of Adam, and you were not then anything at all, but were pure non-existence." He did not say, "I created your father or Adam before, and he was not anything," although that would have sufficed to remove the remoteness by comparing the state of what was given good news to his state, peace be upon him, in order to emphasise the argument and clarify the method of analogy: he was alerted to the fact that every individual of mankind has a share of his creation from non-existence, peace be upon him. For he, peace be upon him, originated a model containing all the individuals of the kind, so his origination in that manner was an origination of every one of his offspring in the same way. And since his creation, peace be upon him, was of this pattern, flowing to all his descendants, it was more eloquent than being restricted to himself, as is understood from the attribution of the mentioned creation to him; and more indicative of the greatness of His power, exalted is He, and the perfection of His knowledge and wisdom. And Zakariyya's non-existence at that time was more evident to him, and his state was more fitting to be the standard for the state of what was given good news; the attribution of the mentioned creation to him is like the attribution of creation and formation to the addressees in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ولَقَدْ خَلَقْناكم ثُمَّ صَوَّرْناكُمْ﴾ ("We created you, then We formed you"), to fulfil the station of blessing its due. End of quotation. It is not free of artificiality.

It is also permitted that "thing" (شَيْئًا) means "that which is considered significant," which is a common metaphor; from it is the saying of al-Mutanabbi:

*"The earth became so narrow that their fleeing man / when he sees other than a thing, thinks it a man."*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 9 (part 2 of 2):

And their saying, "I am amazed at what is nothing, and is not a thing," is rejected, since the context (al-maqam) refuses it and the arrangement of the speech (nazm al-kalam) repudiates it. And al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Wathhab, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "خَلَقْناكَ" (khalaqnaka, "We created you").

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 10:

﴿He said: "My Lord, appoint for me a sign."﴾ That is, a sign that will show me the realization of what was asked and the occurrence of the news. This request, as al-Zajjaj said, was for identifying the time of conception, since the glad tidings were unrestricted as to its timing, and that is a hidden matter which cannot be ascertained, especially if his wife was one whose menstruation had ceased due to her old age. He wished that Allah, exalted is He, would inform him so that he might receive that great blessing with gratitude from the moment it came about, and not delay it until it became apparent in the usual way. It was also said: he asked for this so that he might increase in certainty and tranquility, just as Abraham, peace be upon him, asked about the manner of giving life to the dead for that reason. The first view is preferable. In sum, he did not ask for it out of doubt about the truthfulness of the promise, nor out of supposing that this came from other than Allah, exalted is He. The report of this from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, does not hold, given the infallibility of the prophets, peace be upon them, from such things.

It has been mentioned that this request should have come some time after the glad tidings, because it is reported that Yahya was older than 'Isa, peace be upon them both, by six months or by three years. There is no doubt that his supplication, peace be upon him, was during Maryam's youth, given the words of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿There Zakariyya called upon his Lord﴾, and she only bore 'Isa, peace be upon him, when she was ten or thirteen years old.

The "appointing" (ja'l) is creative (ibda'i), and the lam is connected to it. The fronting of the phrase before "sign" (ayah), which is the object, is due to what has been mentioned many times, or it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial state (hal) of "sign." It was also said: it means "making" (tasyir), which requires two objects, the first being "sign" and the second the adverbial phrase, and its fronting is because there is no justification for "sign" to be a subject when the sentence is resolved into subject and predicate, other than fronting the adverbial phrase; so their states do not change after the particle of abrogation (al-nasikh) appears.

﴿He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people"﴾ — that is, you will not be able to speak to them in their familiar speech in their dealings.

It is reported from Abu Zayd that when his wife, peace be upon him, became pregnant, he was unable to speak to anyone, yet he was still reciting the Torah; when he wished to call out to someone, he could not manage it. ﴿for three nights﴾ together with their days, for the explicit mention of days in the surah of Al 'Imran; the story is one, and the Arabs use metonymy or are content with one of the two for the other, as al-Sirafi mentioned. The reason for mentioning only nights here, and days there, is said to be that this surah is Meccan and earlier in revelation, while that one is Medinan; and the nights are, in their reckoning, prior to the days, because their months and years are lunar, known by the crescents, and for this reason they reckoned by them in dating, as the grammarians mentioned; so the earlier was given to the earlier. "Nights" (layali) is the plural of "layl" in an irregular pattern, like ahl and ahali, or the plural of "laylah"; it is also pluralized as "layali."

(sawiyyan) is a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of (tukallima), indicating that the absence of speech is by way of a miracle and a breaking of custom, not from a tongue being tied by illness; that is, it will be impossible for you to speak to them, and you will be unable to do so, while you are of sound creation, with healthy limbs, having no trace of muteness or dumbness. This is the view of the majority. From Ibn 'Abbas, however, it is reported that "sawiyyan" refers to the nights, meaning complete and level, so it would be an adjective of "three." Ibn Abi 'Ablah and Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them, read (an la tukallima) with a nominative verb, on the basis that "an" is the light form of the heavy "anna," and its subject is the pronoun of the matter, meaning: indeed, you shall not speak.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 11:

﴿So he came out to his people from the prayer niche (al-mihrab)﴾ That is, from the place of prayer (al-musalla), as related from Ibn Zayd; or from the upper chamber (al-ghurfa), as has been said. The original meaning of al-mihrab, as al-Tabarsi said, is the noble assembly place which is defended against attack in order to protect its people.
