The place of worship is called a mihrab because the worshipper is like one who fights against Satan within it. The application of the term mihrab to what is known today in mosques (as the niche indicating the qibla) is for this reason, and it is an innovation that did not exist in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Al-Jalal al-Suyuti wrote a short treatise on this subject, which he named "Informing the Discerning of the Innovation of Prayer Niches" (I'lam al-Arib bi-Huduth Bid'at al-Maharib). It is related that his people were behind the mihrab, waiting for the door to be opened for them so that they might enter and pray. While they were like that, he came out to them with his color changed, and they disapproved of him and said: "What is wrong with you?" ﴿Then he signaled to them﴾, that is, he gestured to them and indicated, as related from Qatadah, Ibn Munabbih, al-Kalbi and al-Qurtubi, and it is one of the two reports from Mujahid. Supporting this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except by gesture﴾. It is also related from Ibn Abbas that he "wrote for them on the ground."

﴿that glorify (Him) morning and evening﴾. This is the other report from Mujahid, but with the wording "on the dust" instead of "on the ground." Ikrimah said: he wrote on a tablet. The use of "wahy" (revelation) for writing occurs in the speech of the Arabs, and among its examples is the saying of Antarah:

"Like the revelation of pages from the time of Khosrow, which he gave to a non-Arab, a stammerer."

And the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"Apart from the four dark (horses) which are as if they were the remnant of revelation within the bellies of the pages."

("An") is either explanatory (mufassira) or verbal-infinitive (masdariyya), in which case the preposition "bi" (with) is presumed before it. By "glorification" (tasbih) is meant prayer, metaphorically, through the relation of inclusion (ʿalaqat al-ishtimal), and this is what is related from Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and a group. "Morning and evening" are adverbs of time for it. By this, as Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-Aliyah, is meant the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer. Some said: glorification is in its literal sense, which is declaring Allah free of imperfection; that is, glorify your Lord at the two ends of the day. Perhaps he (peace be upon him) was commanded to glorify in gratitude and to command his people to do likewise.

The author of al-Tahrir wa-al-Tahbir said: "In my view there is a subtle meaning in this, namely that he specified glorification by mention only because it is the custom that whoever sees a matter and marvels at it, or sees in it a wondrous craftsmanship or a strange wisdom, says: 'Glory be to Allah, glory be to the Creator, may His majesty be exalted.' So when he saw the birth of a child from an old man and a barren woman, he marvelled at that, glorified, and commanded glorification." End of quote.

So he commanded them to glorify, as a sign that a wondrous matter was about to occur. It was also said: he had already informed his people of what he had been given glad tidings of before the sign was set, so when speech became impossible for him he indicated to them the occurrence of the wondrous matter he had been given glad tidings of, and they rejoiced at that.

Talhah read ﴿that glorify Him﴾ (anna sabbihuhu) with a pronoun ha' referring to Allah, exalted is He. Ibn Ghazwan related from Talhah ﴿that glorify﴾ (anna sabbihunna) with a doubled nun.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 12:

﴿O Yahya﴾: this is according to the assumption of a saying (qawl) and another statement that has been omitted, in haste to report the fulfilment of the noble promise. That is, when he was born and reached an age at which one like him is commanded, We said: "O Yahya, ﴿take the Book﴾." That is, the Tawrah (the Torah). Ibn 'Atiyyah claimed a consensus (ijma') on this, on the basis that the definite article (al) is for a known referent (al-'ahd), and that there was no known book at that time other than it, since the Injil (the Gospel) did not yet exist. This is not as he said. Rather, it was said that he was told: "A book, specially given to him, just as many of the Prophets, peace be upon them, were given something similar." It was also said that the intended "Book" is the scrolls of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. And it was said that the intended meaning is the genus, that is, the books of Allah, Exalted is He. ﴿With strength﴾: with earnestness, with memorisation, and with acting upon what is in it. The one who says this is Allah, Exalted is He, through the tongue of the angel, as is most common in speech addressed to the Prophets, peace be upon them. Al-Tibrizi was far off the mark when he assumed the saying to be: "His father said to him when he had grown and matured: 'O Yahya...'" and so on. What adds to its distance is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him judgment while still a boy﴾.

Abu Nu'aym, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said regarding this: "He was given understanding and worship while he was seven years old."

Another narration from him, also traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), has come: "Let us go and pray. The boys said to Yahya ibn Zakariyya, peace be upon them both: 'Come, let us go and play.' He said: 'Were we created for play?!' Let us go and pray."

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We gave him judgment while still a boy﴾: the apparent meaning, according to this, is that "judgment" (al-hukm) means wisdom (al-hikmah). It was also said that it means reason (al-'aql), that it means knowledge of the etiquette of service, that it means true insight (al-firasah al-sadiqah), and that it means prophethood, which is the view of many. They said: he was given it when he was seven years old, or three, or two, and most of the Prophets, peace be upon them, were not granted prophethood before the age of forty. The clause is a conjunction (ataf) upon the implied "We said" (qulna al-muqaddar).

[Hanan] (tenderness) is coordinated with [al-hukm] (wisdom). Its [tanwin] (nunation, the indefinite ending) is for magnification. Originally it derives from [hanna], meaning he felt at ease and longed, and then it came to be used for mercy and compassion. From this comes [al-Hanan] as a divine attribute of God, Exalted, contrary to those who forbade applying it to Him, Mighty and Majestic. Al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Ikrimah, al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah, and a narration from Ibn 'Abbas, interpreted it here as mercy. It is related that he recited to this effect a line by Ibn al-Azraq, the verse of Tarafah:

*O Abu Mundhir, you have spent us; so spare some of us.*
*Hanaanayka: some evil is less severe than some other evil.*

Sibawayh also recited the verse of al-Mundhir ibn Dirham al-Kalbi:

*The most recent of my meetings with Umayna was a glance,*
*As I stood on the edge of al-'Ulya.*
*She said: "Hanaanan, what brought you here?*
*Are you a man of lineage, or do you know the tribe?"*

The prepositional phrase [min ladunna] (from Us) is connected to an omitted element that stands as a descriptive qualifier, emphasizing what the [tanwin] conveyed of intrinsic magnificence through the magnificence of annexation [idafa] (annexation). The meaning is: We gave him great mercy, coming from Our presence. This is more eloquent than "We had mercy on him." This interpretation is also reported from Mujahid. It was also said that the meaning is: We gave him mercy in his heart and compassion for his parents and others. On this view, the purpose of the qualifier is to indicate that this was pleasing to God, Mighty and Majestic, since some mercy and compassion is unacceptable, such as that which leads to abandoning some of God's rights, Glorified is He, such as the prescribed punishments, for example. Or it indicates that this mercy exceeded what was in the natural disposition of others, peace be upon him, because what the Mighty gives is mighty.

It was objected to this that excess is blameworthy, like deficiency, and the best of matters is the moderate. It was answered that the context of praise requires this. Often an excess is praised in one person and blamed in another: a sultan gives thousands, and if someone else gave them, it would be blameworthy extravagance.

It is related from Ibn Zayd that [hanan] here means love, and this is also a narration from Ikrimah. The meaning is: We gave him love from Us. It was said that the meaning is that He made him beloved among people, so that everyone who saw him loved him, like the Exalted's saying: *"And I cast upon you love from Me."* Some have allowed that the meaning may be similar to what preceded, according to the earlier view. It was also said that it is in the accusative as a [masdar] (verbal noun), and thus it belongs to the category of *"And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and as a protection."*

It is permitted to make it an object of purpose [maf'ul li-ajlihi], and to make it coordinated with [sabiyyan] (as a child). That is evident if the meaning is mercy for his parents and others. If it is taken as "and tenderness from God, Exalted, upon him," then it cannot be a circumstantial clause [hal], while the remaining aspects stand as they are. The attentive reader will not miss the circumstantial clause according to what is reported from Ibn Zayd.

[Wa-zakatan] (and purity), that is, blessing, as Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas. It is coordinated with the object. The giving of blessing, according to what was said, means making him blessed, beneficial, and a teacher of good. It was also said: [zakah] here means charity, and what is meant is what he gave in charity to people. It is coordinated with the circumstance, meaning: We gave him what he gave in charity to people. This is, as you see, far-fetched.

It was also said: it means charity, and the coordination is with the circumstance, and the meaning is: We gave him the wisdom while he was giving charity to his parents. This is related from al-Kalbi and Ibn al-Sa'ib. It was also permitted to coordinate it with [hananan] under the assumption of causality. It was said that the coordination is with the object, and the giving of charity means that he, peace be upon him, was a charity to them both. From al-Zajjaj it is reported that it is purity from sins. Using expressions some of which may be substituted for others does not harm the context of praise.

*And he was pious* [taqiyyan]: obedient, avoiding sins. It has come in more than one hadith that he, peace be upon him, never committed a sin nor intended one.

Malik, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn al-Mubarak and Abu Nu'aym related from Mujahid that he said: the food of Yahya ibn Zakariyya, peace be upon them both, was grass, and he would weep from the fear of God, Exalted, so much that if pitch were on his eye it would have pierced it, and the tears had carved a channel in his face.

[Page 73]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 14:

﴿And dutiful to his parents﴾, greatly dutiful to them and kind to them. The apparent reading is that it is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the predicate of kāna (khabar kāna, the predicate of the verb "kāna"). It has also been said that it is of the type of "ʿalaftuhā tibnan wa māan bāridan" (I fed it straw and cold water), where one word serves two functions. The meaning is "and We made him dutiful," which fits its counterpart in the report about ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Jaʿfar in one narration, Ibn Nahīk, and Abū Mijlaz read "wa barran" in both places with a kasra on the bāʾ, meaning "wa dhā barrin" (and possessing dutifulness).

﴿and he was not tyrannical﴾, arrogant, exalting himself above accepting the truth and submitting to it, or domineering over creation. It has been said that al-jabbār is one who does not see that anyone has a right over him. From Ibn ʿAbbās it is narrated that it is one who kills and beats in anger.

Al-Rāghib said: It is used of a human being to describe one who compensates for his deficiency by claiming a rank of loftiness that he does not deserve.

(ʿaṣiyyan) disobeying the command of his Master, Mighty and Majestic. It has also been said: disobedient to his parents. It is on the pattern faʿūl, and it has been said to be faʿīl. The intent is emphasis in the negation, not the negation of emphasis.

Page 74

﴿And peace be upon him﴾. Al-Tabari said: It is a security from God Most High upon him, ﴿the day he was born﴾, from Satan touching him in the way he touches the children of Adam, ﴿and the day he dies﴾, from the terror of parting from the world, and he is the one who witnesses it, and from the punishment of the grave. In this there is evidence that the one who is killed is called dead, on the basis that he, peace be upon him, was killed by one of the adulteresses of the Children of Israel. ﴿And the day he is raised alive﴾, from the terror of the Resurrection and the punishment of the Fire. The circumstantial clause (al-ḥāl) was used for emphasis. It was also said that it indicates that the resurrection is bodily, not spiritual. It was also said that it serves as an alert that he, peace be upon him, is among the martyrs.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The more apparent view is that what is meant by peace (al-salām) is the customary greeting, and the honouring of him by it, because it comes from God Most High in the situations in which the servant is in the utmost weakness, need, lack of resources and poverty before God, Mighty and Majestic. A report has come, narrated by Aḥmad in al-Zuhd (Book of Asceticism) and others, from al-Ḥasan, that Jesus and John, peace be upon them both, met, and they were cousins on the mother's side. John said to Jesus: "Pray to God Most High for me, for you are better than me." Jesus said to him: "Rather, you pray for me, for you are better than me. May God Most High's peace be upon you," and I only greeted myself.

This sentence, as al-Ṭībī said, is coordinated in meaning (ʿaṭf) with ﴿(We gave him the wisdom)﴾, as if it were said: "And We gave him wisdom as a child, and so-and-so, and We granted him peace, or We granted peace upon him in those situations." So it turned to the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya) to indicate continuity and permanence, and it is like a conclusion to the preceding discourse.

Thus he (al-Alusi) moved on to another story, and this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And mention in the Book﴾, and so on. It is a resumptive statement (isti'naf, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic), addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he (ﷺ) was commanded to mention the story of Maryam (Mary) right after the story of Zakariyya (peace be upon him), because of the complete connection and relevance between them.

Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) hold that the "Book" here means the surah itself, not the whole Qur'an as most scholars maintain. This is because it is the surah that opens with the story of Zakariyya (peace be upon him), which is followed by her story and the stories of the prophets (peace be upon them) mentioned in it. The meaning is: mention to the people in it (Maryam), that is, her account, since remembrance (dhikr) does not attach to physical entities.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when she withdrew﴾ is an adverbial complement of time (zarf) for that genitive construction (the implied "account of"), but not in the sense that the command is to mention her account only at the moment of her withdrawal. Rather, everything that is conjoined to it and narrated after it by way of resumption falls within the scope of this time complement and completes the structure. Abu Hayyan made it a time complement for a deleted verb, meaning: "mention Maryam and what happened to her when she withdrew." What we have mentioned is preferable.

It was said that it is a time complement for a deleted element that functions as a circumstantial state (hal) of that genitive construction. It was also said that it is a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) for Maryam, because times include what occurs within them, and this gives grandeur to her wondrous story.

Abu al-Baqa' objected that if the time (idh) does not function as a circumstantial state of the body (al-jutha), nor as a predicate about it, nor as a descriptive attribute of it, then it cannot be a substitution from it. It was answered that failure of the stated conditions does not necessarily mean the substitution is invalid. Consider "salaba Zayd thawbuhu" (Zayd was stripped of his garment): the substitution is valid there even though the conditions mentioned for substitution do not hold. And the claim that this is only a circumstance of time is neither clear nor evident. It was said that it is a substitution of the whole from the whole (badal kull min kull), with Maryam meaning her story and the time in which it occurred, but this is remote.

It was said that (idh) here has the meaning of the verbal particle (an al-masdariyya), as in the saying "la akramtuka idh lam tukrimni," meaning "I will not honor you because you did not honor me," that is, due to your not honoring me. This is a weak view held by the grammarians. The apparent reading is that it is a temporal (zarfiyya) or causal (ta'liliyya) particle, if we take it as causal, and in that case substitution of inclusion is the only possibility.

The word al-intibadh means withdrawal and seclusion.

Al-Raghib said: it is said "intabadha fulan," meaning he withdrew in the manner of one who pays little attention to himself among people. And al-nabdh means throwing down a thing and casting it away because of little regard for it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from her family﴾ is connected to ﴿withdrew﴾. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿a place in the east﴾ (makanan sharqiyyan) was said to be in the accusative as an adverbial complement of place. It was also said to be a direct object of ﴿withdrew﴾, taking into account the sense of arrival (al-ityan) implicit in it, which follows it both in existence and in logical sequence, based on its original meaning, the verb that governs the prepositional phrase. This is the reason for placing it after the prepositional phrase. Some verifiers preferred this view, meaning: she secluded herself and separated from her family and came to a place in the east of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) or of her house, in order to be alone there for worship. It was said that she sat in a raised place to bathe from menstruation, screened by a wall or by a cord, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas, or by a garment, as was also said. This is what His saying, exalted is He, refers to:

Page 75

Her taking a screen apart from them (﴿So she took a screen from them﴾) happened to be east-facing; that was a coincidental matter.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that the People of the Book were commanded to pray toward the House (the Ka'bah) and to make the pilgrimage to it, and that nothing turned them away from it except the words of your Lord (﴿So she withdrew from her family to a place in the east﴾). Therefore they prayed toward the direction of the sunrise. In another narration: "The Christians only took the east as their qiblah (direction of prayer) because Maryam withdrew from her family to a place in the east." We have already mentioned, from some scholars, that during the time of 'Isa (peace be upon him) they faced Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and that they did not face the east until after he was raised (peace be upon him), claiming that he appeared to one of their elders and commanded them to do so. It is also permissible that God, exalted is He, chose it for her because it is the place where lights rise. God, glorified is He, knew that the moment of the manifestation of the light of 'Isa was near from her, so it was fitting that the manifestation of the spiritual light should be in the direction of the manifestation of the physical light. And this, as you see, is [weak].

It is narrated that her place was in the mosque; when she menstruated she moved to the house of her maternal aunt, and when she became pure she returned to the mosque. While she was in her place of bathing, the angel (peace be upon him) came to her in the form of a beardless young man of fair face and curly hair. This is the meaning of His words, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Then We sent to her Our Spirit﴾, that is, Jibril (peace be upon him), as most scholars have said. He was described thus because religion lives through him and through his revelation, so it is a figurative usage (majaz, a word used in a non-literal sense). The attribution (of "Spirit" to God) is for honour, like the House of God, exalted is He.

It is also permissible that this is like when you say to your beloved, "You are my soul," out of love for him and closeness to him; this too is figurative, except that it differs from the first in aspect, and the honour in the first lies in calling him a spirit. Abu Muslim said: the intended meaning of "the Spirit" is 'Isa (peace be upon him), based on His words: ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾; and the pronoun in the following "appeared" (﴿So she took a screen…appeared﴾) refers to the angel. But this is not correct.

Abu Haywa and Sahl read (rawhana) with a fatha on the ra, and the intended meaning of it is also Jibril (peace be upon him), because he is the cause of what gives rest (rawh) to the servants, and attaining rest (rawh) with God, exalted is He, which is the reward of those brought near, in His words: ﴿And as for if he is one of those brought near, then rest and fragrance﴾ [56:88-89]. Or because he (peace be upon him) is one of those brought near, and they are those promised rest; that is, [one who brings] nearness to Us, or possessor of Our rest.

al-Naqqash mentioned that it was also read (Ruhanna) with a shadda on the nun, as the name of one of the angels (peace be upon him). ﴿So he appeared before her﴾: the verb is derived from mithal (likeness), and its original sense is that one makes an effort to be the likeness of a thing; the intended meaning is that he (the angel) formed an image for her. ﴿A man in complete form﴾: well-formed in creation, perfect in structure, lacking none of the fine attributes of a human being. It was also said that he appeared in the form of a relative of hers named Yusuf, one of the servants of Bayt al-Maqdis, so that she would be at ease with his speech and receive from him what was conveyed to her of his words; for if he had appeared to her in the angelic form, she would have fled from him and been unable to converse with him. As for what has been said, that this was so that her desire would be stirred and her seed would descend into her womb, then, along with the vileness it contains, from which Maryam should be kept pure, this is refuted by His words, exalted is He:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 18:**

﴿She said, "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you."﴾ For this is a just witness that she had not entertained even a trace of inclination toward him, let alone the state that results from the utmost degrees of inclination and desire. Indeed, his taking that surpassing beauty and exquisite attractiveness was because it is the custom of an angel, when he takes a form, to take the form of a handsome human, as he used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the form of Dihyah (may Allah be pleased with him). Or it was for testing her and examining her chastity. And there appeared from her such scrupulousness and chastity that there is no beyond it. The intention of the speaker, that it occurred thus so that it would be a presumption of what was mentioned, whereupon its opposite is manifest, so that it would be stronger in her purity, is very far from his words.

Some later scholars said: Her seeking refuge in Allah the Exalted indicates the stirring of her desire and her natural inclination toward him, as the Exalted said, relating of Yusuf (peace be upon him): ﴿And unless You turn away from me their plot, I shall incline toward them﴾. It has been said: what is meant by the "inclination" (al-ṣabwah) there is the natural inclination according to the requirement of nature and the ruling of the appetitive faculty. Then it does not contradict her chastity; rather it confirms it, since it is natural and compulsory, not falling under obligation, as was said regarding His saying: ﴿And he certainly desired her﴾. And despite this, Yusuf (peace be upon him) sought refuge with what Allah the Exalted related of him, His saying: ﴿He said, "God forbid! Indeed, He is my Lord; He has made my residence excellent."﴾ So the claim that seeking refuge refutes stirring and natural inclination is a falsehood. And the statement that it [the form] refuses that, being a place for showing the effects of power that breaks custom, is nothing, because the creation of man from a single water is also one of the effects of power that breaks custom.

Causes in this context are not wholly rejected, as the story of Yahya (peace be upon him) guides to this. Moreover, one may claim that creating a thing from nothing at all is impossible, so it is not among the degrees of power, and the material of the creative making is the fixed entities (al-a'yan al-thabitah), which are eternal. End of quotation. But it is not free of discussion, and what we have mentioned in the explanation is safer from talk and dispute, so reflect.

"Basharan" (بَشَرًا) is in the accusative as a presumed circumstantial (ḥāl) or as a specification (tamyīz). It has been said that it is an object by implicit meaning, the verb "tamaththala" (took a form) being understood as "ittakhadha" (took).

The matter of this taking of form has been questioned: Gabriel (peace be upon him) is a person of great body, as the reports state. So when he becomes the size of a human body, it entails that Gabriel would not remain if the excess parts fell away, and that parts would interpenetrate if nothing went away, and this is impossible. Also, if taking form were permissible, reliance would be lifted and it would be impossible to be certain that this person seen now is Zayd who was seen yesterday, due to the possibility of taking form. Also, if taking the form of a human is permissible, why is taking a form other than a human's not permissible, such as that of a gnat or the like? It is known that every doctrine that leads to that is false. Also, if that were permissible, reliance on the mass-transmitted report (khabar al-mutawatir) would be lifted, like the report of the Prophet's (ﷺ) fighting at Badr, since the fighter might have been one in an assumed form.

I answer the first: it is not impossible that Gabriel (peace be upon him) has original parts, few in number, and excess parts. By the original parts he is able to take the form of a human. This is according to those who hold that he is a body. As for those who hold that he is spiritual, there is no improbability in his clothing himself at times with the great frame and at other times with the small frame.

As for the second: it is a common obligation for all. For whoever acknowledges the Creator, the Able, is bound by that too, since He, glory be to Him, may create the likeness of Zayd, for example, and with this possibility, certainty is lifted and certainty is impossible in the manner previously stated. Likewise whoever does not acknowledge [the Creator] and ascribes events to celestial conjunctions and configurations is bound by that, since a conjunction may occur that requires the occurrence of such a thing, and then certainty is also impossible. Perhaps, since such a thing is rare, it does not entail a flaw in ordinary knowledge based on sense perception, so there is no doubt that Zayd whom we now see is the one we saw yesterday.

I answer the third: the basic permissibility subsists in the intellect, and its corruption is known only through the proofs of revelation (al-sam'). This is the answer to the fourth as well; so said Imam al-Razi. But in my view, the question of taking form on the view of corporeality is among the matters where one should commit the affair to the Knower of the unseen, and there is no path for the intellect to a definite judgment in it on anything that would open hearts.

He, the Exalted, mentioned Him under the title of al-Rahmaniyyah only as a reminder to the one she saw, that he should show mercy to her weakness and her inability to repel him, or as an intensification of seeking refuge in Allah the Exalted, and seeking to attract the effects of the special mercy, which is protection from what has overwhelmed her. As for what is said, that this is a reminder to the one she saw of the recompense, so that he would desist, it is said: "O Merciful of the Hereafter" is nothing, because the Merciful of this world and the Hereafter, and their Merciful, is what has come [in the reports].

﴿If you are pious﴾: the conditional clause (sharṭ) whose answer is omitted, relying on the indication of context. That is: if it is hoped from you that you fear Allah the Exalted, dread Him, and take seriously seeking refuge in Him, then I seek refuge in Him from you. Thus al-Zamakhshari estimated it.

In al-Kashf, he pointed out that the reason for this condition, even though seeking refuge in the Merciful would be more appropriate if he were not pious, is that if one prefers seeking protection in Allah the Exalted (I mean its restraint from him and safety from him), that is only complete and manifest with regard to the pious one. In it is an indication that piety requires for the one seeking refuge in Allah the Exalted the right of protection and safeguarding, and of the great station of piety, in that it is made a condition of seeking refuge, which is not complete without it. He said: "If it is hoped" (in kāna yurjā) to show the meaning of "an" (if) and that it was preferred to indicate that the hope of piety was beyond knowledge of it.

The summary: piety was not made a condition of seeking refuge, but a condition of its restraining him and safety from him. She expressed by seeking refuge in Allah the Exalted an urging to him to restrain himself in the gentlest and most eloquent manner, and that whoever confronts one who seeks refuge in Him has confronted His great wrath. End.

Al-Zajjaj estimated: "If you are pious, then take heed by my seeking refuge." The better reading on this is "tatta'iẓ" (you will take heed) with the dropping of the fa', because the present-tense verb occurring as an answer does not take the fa', so it needs to be marfu' (in the nominative) by estimating a subject. Some estimated: "then go away from me," and some: "then do not approach me." It has been said: she meant, "If you are pious and scrupulous, then I seek refuge from you"; how much more so when you are not such. It seems she meant that she sought refuge with this condition so that he would know her seeking refuge by what is opposite to it, a fortiori.

Al-Shihab said: The apparent is that "in" (إنْ), on this view, is waṣliyyah (connective), and regarding its coming without the waw there is discussion. It was mentioned that the clause, on this view, is circumstantial, and the intended meaning is seeking refuge in Allah from his evil, not urging him to desist. It was said it is negative (nāfiyah), and the clause is a new sentence in place of a causal reason, i.e., "you were not pious and scrupulous, by your presence with me and your being alone with me." This is against the apparent. Whatever the case, al-taqiyy is a descriptive from piety. The saying of whoever said that it is the name of a righteous or wicked man is not correct.

He said, "I am only a messenger of your Lord," the One who owns your affair and watches over your welfare, the One you sought refuge in. I am not one from whom the evil you imagined could be expected.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that when she said, "(Indeed I seek refuge) etc.," Jibril (peace be upon him) smiled and said, "(I am only a messenger of your Lord), (to bestow upon you a boy)." That is, I will be the means of his being granted, by breathing into the shirt (of Maryam). It is also possible that this is a quotation of the words of God Most High, with the verb "said" understood, meaning: "your Lord, who said: I have sent this angel to bestow upon you..." This is supported by the qira'a (recitation variant) of Shayba, Abu al-Hasan, Abu Bahriyya, al-Zuhri, Ibn Manadhir, Ya'qub, al-Yazidi, Abu 'Amr, and Nafi' in one narration, reading "liyahaba" with the yaa', since its subject is the pronoun referring to the Lord, Exalted is He. As for what has been said, that the original form of "liyahaba" was "li-ahaba," with the hamza converted into a yaa' because of the kasra before it, this is a forced view without any need for it.

In some mushafs (codices of the Qur'an), the reading is: "He commanded me that I bestow upon you a boy (zakiyyan)," meaning pure, free from sins. It has also been said: a prophet. It has been said: growing in goodness, that is, advancing from one stage of life to another in goodness and righteousness, so that zakat (purity/growth) includes both moral and physical increase. Some have cited the sending of the angel to her as evidence of her prophethood.

It is answered: the sending of a messenger for such a matter does not require prophethood.

[p. 78]

**"She said, 'How can I have a son when no human has touched me?'"** That is, while the situation is that no man has had lawful contact with me. It was said "human" (*basharun*) to emphasize her purity from the beginnings of childbearing.

**"And I have not been unchaste."** That is, I have not been an adulteress (*zaniyah*). This sentence is coordinated (*'atf*) with "no human has touched me," and it falls under the same grammatical category of circumstantial clause (*hāliyyah*). It makes clear that *al-massu* (touching) is a metaphor (*kinayah*) for lawful intercourse. Such euphemism appears in His words, "before you have touched them" (2:236), and "or you have touched women" (4:43; 5:6), and in the line of poetry:

*"You had entered upon them and consummated the marriage."*

As for fornication (*al-zina*), it is not fitting to be expressed by a euphemism, because its context is either the purification of speech, in which case there is neither euphemism nor explicit statement, or reproach and censure, in which case it deserves more than plain statement. The expressions that are thought to be euphemisms for it have become so common that they have become explicit literal terms for it, and among them is what appears in this noble text. The verse in Surat Al 'Imran, where she says, "no human has touched me," and restricts herself to that, is not an objection to this, for the most that has been said about it is that it is a euphemism for marriage and fornication together by way of predominance (*taghlib*). It was not made a euphemism for fornication alone. Someone may say that it is a euphemism for marriage alone there, as it is here, and that the categories were exhausted here because this is a context of elaboration. She limited herself to denying marriage, then, because of the absence of suspicion, since she knew that they were angels who were calling out, and such a suspicion would not occur to her. This is unlike the present situation, since Gabriel, peace be upon him, had come to her in the form of a beardless young man. For this reason she sought refuge from him, and her fear had not been fully calmed until he said, **"I am only the messenger of your Lord."** It has also been said that in Al 'Imran there is both sufficiency and the omission of sufficiency in this matter, and that here it is the place of detail, because that surah was revealed earlier, so the knowledge had already been established there. It has also been said that *al-massu* here is a euphemism for both matters by way of predominance, as in that surah.

**"And I have not been unchaste"** is a specification after a generalization, for greater care in declaring her innocence of indecency. For this reason she chose *kana* (was) in the second negation, because that indicates that the absence of immorality is a necessary attribute of hers.

It seems that she, peace be upon her, because of her extreme astonishment and her utmost sense of the improbability of the matter, did not pay attention to the attribute in the angel's words, peace be upon him, **"that I may give you a pure boy"** (19:19), which negates every doubt and accusation. She cast it behind her back, mentioned only the qualified thing, and set about asserting its negation in the most emphatic way. That is, how far removed is the existence of this qualified thing, with these impediments, let alone the attribute. This is close to the wise indirect style (*al-uslub al-hakim*).

*Baghiyy* is of the pattern *fa'ul* according to al-Mubarrad. Its origin is *baghwiyy*. When the *waw* and the *ya'* came together and one of them was preceded by a sukun, the *waw* was changed into a *ya'* and assimilated into the *ya'*, and the *ghayn* was given a kasrah in accordance with it. For this reason the feminine *ta'* marker (*ha' al-ta'nith*) does not attach to it, because *fa'ul* is used equally for masculine and feminine, even when it has the meaning of *fa'il*, as in *sabur*. Ibn Jinni objected to this in his *Kitab al-Tamam* that if it were *fa'ul* it would be said *baghaw*, as one says *nahaw* ('an al-munkar). This was answered by saying that one does not analogize from an anomalous form, and the grammarians have explicitly stated that it is anomalous. It therefore departs from the rule of the coming together of *waw* and *ya'* with one of them preceded by a sukun. He preferred that it is *fa'il*, and according to Abu al-Baqa', it has the meaning of *fa'il*. The analogy would be that the feminine marker should attach to it, because in that case it is not among the forms used equally for masculine and feminine, like *fa'ul*. The reason it does not take the marker is that, because of the intensification (*mubalaghah*) inherent in it, it is treated as *fa'ul*, so the *ha'* does not attach to it. Some said that it is from the class of *nisbah* (relative adjectives), like *tali'* (having a menstrual cycle), and such a form is used equally for masculine and feminine. It has also been said that its feminine is left unmarked because in usage it is specific to women. It is said of a man *baghin*. It has also been said that *fa'il* here has the meaning of *maf'ul*, as in *'ayn* (having large eyes) *kahil* (collyrium-darkened), and on this view the meaning of *baghiyy* is one whom men desire for fornication with her. On the view that it has the meaning of *fa'il*, it means a sinful woman who desires men. Whichever it is, it has become, through its common use for the adulteress, an explicit literal term for her. So it is not objected that considering intensification in it is not appropriate to the context, because the negation of the more intense does not entail the negation of the basic act. Nor does it need an answer by committing to the view that this is from the class of *nisbah*, or by saying that the intended meaning is the negation of the attribute and the qualified thing together, or that the intensification is in the negation and not the negation of intensification.

[Page 79]

Commentators have spoken broadly that this is similar to what preceded in the story of Zakariya, peace be upon him. In al-Kashshaf, it is said that the full range of possibilities that al-Zamakhshari mentioned there does not apply here, because the first (*qala*, "he said") contains a pronoun referring to the Messenger. So if it is linked to the second, the meaning would be: "The Messenger said, 'Thus,' your Lord said [it]," and then he explained it with His words ﴿He is easy for Me﴾. Or the meaning is: "Like that statement, the wondrous one you heard and I promised you, your Lord said," with the particle *al-kaf* ("like") being used as an intensifier, and then he resumed with ﴿He is easy for Me﴾. It is necessary to posit an implied *qawl* ("saying"), because the one addressing her was Jibril, peace be upon him. His words ﴿He is easy for Me﴾ are the speech of the Exalted Truth, which He related to her. If it is linked to the first, the meaning would be: "The matter is thus," as confirmation of her, or "as I promised," as affirmation of it. Then he resumed: ﴿Your Lord said, "He is easy for Me"﴾ to remove the sense of improbability, or to establish the affirmation. It is not far-fetched to make ﴿Your Lord said﴾ in this case an explanatory and parenthetical statement. (End of quotation.)

I do not see what Ibn al-Munir reported there as a valid interpretation here. (*Wa-li-najʿalahu*, "and that We may make him") is a causal clause (*taʿlīl*) for an omitted element being explained, meaning: "so that We may make the gift of the boy" (*wahb al-ghulam*) "a sign" (*āyah*) "and a proof" (*burhān*) "for mankind" (*lin-nās*), all of them, or for the believers, according to what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, by which they may infer the perfection of Our power. ("And a mercy") great, existing (*kāʾinah*) "from Us" (*minnā*) toward them, by which they are guided through his guidance and find right direction through his instruction, by Our doing that.

It is also permissible that it be coordinated (*maʿtūf*) with another implied cause, meaning: "so that We may demonstrate through it the magnitude of Our power, and so that We may make him a sign," etc. Al-Kashshaf said: Such constructions allow both possibilities, and each one is preferred according to the context. Omitting the explained element here is more preferable, since if another cause were assumed, there would still be need for an omitted explained element; there was nothing before that suits it, so it would be an unnecessary lengthening of the distance. This clause, meaning the cause together with what it explains, is coordinated with His words ﴿He is easy for Me﴾. In choosing the first in the nominal form, it indicates the permanence of ease and removes improbability; the second in the verbal form indicates that He, the Exalted, brought him into being because he is a special sign and mercy, not for another matter that would contradict it, with the intention that the renewal is for the renewal of existence, so that one moves from astonishment to praise, with what grandeur is not hidden. (End of quotation.)

It is not objected that when a cause such as *li-nubayyina* ("so that We may clarify") is assumed, it may be related to what ﴿He is easy for Me﴾ indicates without omitting anything, so his statement that there is no alternative to an omitted explained element is not valid, given what is evident in it. As for his mention of coordination, some scholars disagreed with it, making the *waw* on the first reading parenthetical (*iʿtirāḍiyyah*). Some people said that (*wa-li-najʿalahu*), on the reading (*li-yahaba*, "that He may give"), is coordinated with it by way of *iltifāt* (a shift from third person to first person). It was also permitted to coordinate it with (*li-ahaba*, "that I may give"), according to the reading of most of the seven readers. After this coordination on both readings, it is not hidden that (and it was) that matter ﴿a decreed matter﴾, settled, to which Our eternal decree relates, or it was determined and inscribed in the Preserved Tablet, something you must have; or it was a matter truly fitting by the requirement of wisdom and bounty that He should do it, since it includes profound wisdoms. This sentence is a concluding statement (*tadhyīl*), either for the whole discourse or for the last part of it.

﴿فَحَمَلَتْهُ﴾ The *fa* here is *fa-faṣīḥa* (the explanatory *fa*, which signals an unstated intermediate step). The meaning is: she was reassured by his words, so he approached her and blew into her collar, the breath entered her body, and so she conceived him. This was reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. It is also said that he (peace be upon him) did not draw near to her but blew from a distance, and the wind reached her and she conceived. It is also said that the breath was in her sleeve, a report from Ibn Jurayj. It is said it was in her hem, and it is said it was in her mouth.

They differed about her age at that time. It is said she was thirteen years old. It is reported from Wahb and Mujahid that she was fifteen. It is said she was fourteen, and it is said she was twelve, and it is said she was ten, and that she had menstruated twice before she conceived. Muhammad ibn al-Haysam, the leader of the Haysamiyya sect of the Karramiyya, related that she had not yet menstruated at all. It is also said that she (peace be upon her) never menstruated at all, but was pure of menstruation.

Likewise they differed about the length of her pregnancy. In one report from Ibn ʿAbbas, it lasted nine months, as with all other women, and this is what is related from al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him, because if she had differed from other women in this custom, it would have been fitting to mention it in the course of this strange story. In another report from him, it lasted only one hour: just as she conceived him, she gave birth to him. He supported this with the subsequent verse of sequence, and with the fact that Allah, glorified is He, said in describing him: ﴿Indeed, the example of Jesus with Allah is like that of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was.﴾ This clearly indicates that He, mighty and majestic, said to him "Be" and he was, so no duration of pregnancy can be imagined in it.

From ʿAtaʾ, Abu al-ʿAliya and al-Dahhak it is reported that it lasted seven months. It is said it lasted six months. It is said she conceived him in an hour, he was formed in an hour, and she gave birth to him in an hour, when the sun had passed its zenith on that day. The well-known view is that it lasted eight months. It is said that no child born at eight months has lived except him, peace be upon him.

Al-Nisaburi transmitted from the astrologers that this is because the fetus is returned to the nurturing of the moon, so cold and moisture overcome it. This indicates that the nurturer of the fetus in the first months of pregnancy is the moon, and in the eighth month the matter returns to it according to the astrologers. This contradicts what is found in *Kifayat al-Taʿlim* from them: that the first month is attributed to Saturn (*Zuhal*), the second to Jupiter (*al-Mushtari*), and so on up to the seventh, which is attributed to the moon, after which the attribution returns to Saturn, then to Jupiter. It also says there that the ignorant astrologers claim: in the first month the drop of semen receives coldness from Saturn and so is solidified; in the second it receives the growth-power from Jupiter and begins to grow; in the third it receives the irascible power from Mars (*al-Mirrikh*); in the fourth the power of life from the sun; in the fifth the power of desire from Venus (*al-Zuhra*); in the sixth the power of speech from Mercury (*ʿUtarid*); and in the seventh the power of motion from the moon, and thus the fetus's creation is completed. If he is born at that time, he lives; otherwise, if he is born in the eighth month, he does not live, because he has received the power of death from Saturn; and if he is born in the ninth month, he lives, because it comes before the power of Jupiter. Such statements are superstitions. Every woman knows that when three months pass over the drop of semen, it moves. The natural philosophers have mentioned that the minimum period of gestation is six months, and the period of movement is a third of the period of gestation, so its minimum is two months. Whoever has tested miscarriage knows that the formation is completed in less than fifty days. End of quotation.

The statements of the religious scholars (*mutasharriʿīn*) on this subject are not hidden from you. It may happen that a child born at eight months lives, but this is rare, so that is not one of his special features, peace be upon him, if it is authentic. None of these conflicting, disordered statements has been established as sound in my view, though I lean toward the first of them. The argument for the second, from what you have heard, is not free from scrutiny.

﴿فانْتَبَذَتْ بِهِ﴾ That is: she withdrew, while he was in her womb. The *bāʾ* here is *bāʾ al-mulābasa wa-l-muṣāḥaba* (the *bāʾ* of accompaniment and association), like its use in His saying, ﴿grows with oil﴾ and in the verse of al-Mutanabbi describing horses:

*"They passed over them, not startled, trampling us over skulls and heads."*

The prepositional phrase is an adverbial complement fixed in place (*ẓarf mustaqarr*), occurring as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from her concealed pronoun, meaning: she withdrew, being joined with him. ﴿مَكانًا قَصِيًّا﴾ means a remote place, far from her family, beyond the mountain.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Aḥmad related in *Zawaʾid al-Zuhd* from Nawf that Gabriel (peace be upon him) blew into her collar, and she conceived, and when she grew heavy she felt the pains that women feel. She was in the house of prophethood, so she was shy and fled out of shame before her people. She headed toward the east, and her people went out seeking her, asking, "Have you seen a girl like such-and-such?" but no one informed them. So what Allah, exalted is He, has told us came to pass.

Al-Thaʿlabi related in *al-ʿArāʾis* from Wahb that when Mary conceived, a paternal cousin of hers named Yusuf the carpenter was with her. They were going together to the mosque near Mount Zion, and they used to serve that mosque together. No one of their time was more diligent or devoted in worship than the two of them. The first to learn of her matter was Yusuf, and he was perplexed about it, because he knew of her perfect righteousness and chastity, and that he had never been absent from her for an hour. He said to her, "Something has entered my mind about your affair which I could not keep hidden, and I see that speaking of it would ease my heart." She said, "Say a good word." He said, "O Mary, tell me: does seed grow without a sower? Does a tree grow without rain? Can a child be born without a male?"

She said, "Yes. Do you not know that Allah, exalted is He, made the crop grow on the day He created it without a seed? Do you not know that Allah, exalted is He, made the tree grow without rain? And by His power He made rain the life of the tree after He had created each of them separately. Do you say that Allah, glorified is He, is not able to make the tree grow until it seeks help from water?" He said, "I do not say this, but I say: Allah, exalted is He, is able to do whatever He wills by the word 'Be, and it is.'" She said, "Do you not know that Allah, exalted is He, created Adam and his wife without a male or a female?" At that, what he was feeling ceased. He had been serving in the mosque in her place, because weakness had overcome her due to the pregnancy and constriction of the heart. When her time of childbirth drew near, Allah, exalted is He, revealed to her: "Leave the land of your people, lest they kill your child." So Yusuf carried her on his donkey to the land of Egypt. When they reached that land, the pains of childbirth seized her, and so occurred what He, glorified is He, related.

It is also said: she withdrew to the farthest part of the house, and this is the most fitting view, given the brevity of the period of pregnancy.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 23:

﴿So the pains of childbirth drove her﴾ i.e., drove her (ألجأها), as al-Zamakhshari and a group said. In al-Sihah: "ajƎtuhu ila kadha" means "alja'tuhu" and "idtarartuhu ilayhi" (I compelled him to it and forced him to it). Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma said:

"And a neighbour who went, relying upon you, was driven by fear and hope."

Al-Farra' said: its origin is from "ji'tu" (I came), but the Arabs have made it "ilja'" (driving). In the proverb: "The worst of what comes to you is what drives you to the marrow of Uqayba (the hamstring)." End of quotation. Abu Hayyan chose that the meaning is "jā'a bihā" (brought her). He was objected to against al-Zamakhshari and extended the discussion in a manner whose refutation is not hidden.

(al-Makhad) with a fatha on the mim, as in the reading of the majority, and with a kasra as in a report from Ibn Kathir, is the verbal noun of "makhadat al-mar'a" (with a fatha or kasra on the kha') when the labour pains seized her and the child moved in her womb to come out. Al-A'mash and Talha read "fa-ja'aha" with imala of the fatha of the jim. Hammad ibn Salama, from Asim, read "fa-ja'aha" (from al-mufaja'a, sudden occurrence), and this was reported from Mujahid; Ibn Atiyya also transmitted it from Shubayl ibn 'Azra. The author of al-Lawami said: its reading may allow that the hamza in it has been changed to an alif, and it may also allow that it is between-between (bayna bayn) without being changed.

﴿to the trunk of the palm tree﴾ so that she might lean on it at the time of delivery, as was related from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi; or for that purpose. (And so that she might be screened by it, as it was said.) The jidh (trunk) is what lies between the root and the branching of the branches of a tree, and it may also be said of a branch: jidh. The palm tree is well known. The definiteness is either generic, so the meaning is one palm tree, not a specific one, or it is for a known referent, so the meaning is a specific palm tree, and its being specific in itself suffices for its determination, even if the addressee of the Qur'an, upon him be blessings and peace, did not know it, as when you say: "The sultan ate what the cook brought," meaning his cook, for he is the known one. It may also be said that it was specific to him, upon him be blessings and peace, in that God Most High showed it to him on the night of the Ascension (mi'raj). Some claimed that it still exists to this day. The apparent view is that it was existing before Mary came to it, and this is what the reports indicate. Thus, from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, when the labour pains became severe upon her, peace be upon her, she looked at a mound, climbed it quickly, and there was on it the trunk of a palm tree, withered, having no fronds.

It was said that God Most High created it for her on that day, but this is not correct. The time was winter. Perhaps God Most High guided her to it so that He might show her, among the trees most resembling a human being, among His signs, what would calm her fear: such as its fruits without a head (a stalk), at the winter season, in which this is not customary, and without pollination as is usual. In that there is also an indication that its root is firm and its branch is in the sky, and that its offspring is beneficial like the sweet fruit, and that he, peace be upon him, will give life to the dead just as God Most High through him gave life to the dead, together with the kindness in making its fruit a consolation for her. The prepositional phrase is connected to "ja'aha." On the other reading it is connected to an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: leaning upon the trunk of the palm tree.

﴿She said: "Would that I had died"﴾ with a kasra on the mim, from "mata yamatu" like "khafa yakhafu," or from "mata yumitu" like "ja'a yaji'u."

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr and Ya'qub read it with a damma, from "mata yamutu" like "qala yaqulu," "(before)" this time in which I have met what I have met, or before this matter. She, peace be upon her, said this although she knew what had passed between her and Gabriel, peace be upon him, of the gracious promise, out of shyness before people and fear of their blame, or out of caution against people falling into sin through what they would say about it.

It is related that she heard a call: "Come out, O you who are worshipped besides God Most High," so she grieved over that and wished for death. The wishing for death for such a matter is not disliked. Yes, wishing for it is disliked on account of a harm that has befallen one, from illness or poverty or affliction from an enemy or the like of the hardships of this world.

In Sahih Muslim and others, the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "None of you should wish for death because of a harm that has befallen him. If he must wish, let him say: 'O God, keep me alive as long as life is better for me, and cause me to die when death is better for me.'"

Whoever thinks that her, peace be upon her, wishing for that was due to the severity of the pain has assumed wrongly, and we seek refuge in God Most High.

﴿and I was a thing forgotten﴾ i.e., a trifling thing whose nature is to be forgotten and not regarded at all, like a menstrual rag.

The majority read "nisyan" with a kasra. Al-Farra' said: they are two dialects in this, like "al-watr" and "al-widr," and the fatha is more beloved to me. Al-Farisi said: the kasra is the higher of the two dialects. Ibn al-Anbari said: with a kasra it is a noun for what is forgotten, like "naqd" is a noun for what is broken; with a fatha it is a verbal noun standing in for the noun. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi read "nisy'an" with a kasra on the nun and a hamza in place of the ya', and this is the reading of Nawf al-A'rabi. Bakr ibn Habib al-Sahmi and Muhammad ibn Ka'b also read, in one report, "nas'an" with a fatha on the nun and hamza, on the basis that it derives from "nasa'tu al-laban" when you pour water on milk and the milk is destroyed in it due to its small quantity; so she wished to be like that milk which is not seen and is not distinguished from the water. Ibn Atiyya transmitted from Bakr ibn Habib that he read "nassan" with a fatha on the nun and sin, without hamza, like "asan" (sticks), "(forgotten)" which does not come to the mind of anyone of the people. He described the "nasy" with that because it is a conventional usage for what is little regarded, even if it is not forgotten. Al-A'mash and Abu Ja'far, in one report, read it with a kasra on the mim, following the vowel of the sin, as they say "mintin" following the vowel of the mim to the vowel of the ta'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 24:

(فَناداها) That is, Jibril (peace be upon him), as is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Nawf.

'Alqama recited "fakhatabaha" (and he addressed her). Abu Hayyan said: It should be taken as an explanation, since it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf (sawad al-mushaf). The Habr (scholar of the Qur'an, Ibn 'Abbas) recited "fanadaha malakun" (then a angel called to her) ﴿min tahtiha﴾ (from beneath her). It should be that the one meant by it is Jibril (peace be upon him), so that it agrees with what was related from him earlier. The meaning of ﴿min tahtiha﴾ is from a place lower than her, and he was standing beneath the mound which she had climbed hastily, as you heard a moment ago. In al-Bahr it is related from al-Hasan that he said:

Jibril (peace be upon him) called to her, and he was in a spot of the earth lower than the spot where she was, and he swore to that. Perhaps his standing there (peace be upon him) was out of reverence for her and out of modesty to be in her presence in that state. As for the view that he (peace be upon him) was beneath her, receiving the child, it should not be said, because it attributes to the trustworthy bearer of revelation of the Exalted King something that is not fitting to his station. It was said: the pronoun in (tahtiha) refers to the palm tree. Abu Hayyan preferred that the one calling was 'Isa (peace be upon him), and the pronoun refers to Maryam, and the fa' is a fa' of explanation (fasiha), meaning: she gave birth to a boy, and God Most High made him speak at the time of birth, so the newborn called to her from beneath her.

This is related from Mujahid, Wahb, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Zayd and al-Jubba'i, and al-Tabarsi transmitted it from al-Hasan as well. The two Ibns (Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir), Abu 'Amr, Hafs (from 'Asim), 'Asim, al-Jahdari, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan in one narration from them both recited "man" with a fatha on the mim, meaning "the one who" (alladhi) as the subject of nada, and "tahtaha" is an accusative adverbial phrase serving as the relative clause of "man". What is meant by it is either 'Isa or Jibril, peace be upon them both.
Page 83
﴿ala tahzani﴾ That is: do not grieve. Here "an" is explanatory (mufassira), or it is "bi-an la tahzani", where "an" is verbal (masdariyya) with the preposition removed. ﴿qad ja'ala rabbuki tahtaki﴾ (your Lord has placed beneath you) in a place lower than you. It was also said: "beneath your command": if you command it to flow, it flows, and if you command it to stop, it stops; but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. (sariyyan) That is, a stream, as al-Hakim recorded in his Mustadrak from al-Bara', and he said: it is authentic according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim). Al-Bukhari also mentioned it as a suspended (mu'allaq) report attributed to him as a companion's statement, and 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh in their tafsirs transmitted it from him likewise as a statement of his, but the elevated (marfu') form is not authenticated, as al-Jalal al-Suyuti made clear. On this meaning comes the verse of Labid describing a wild ass and a she-ass:

So they both crossed the breadth of the stream and split it, flowing past its tips in a flood.

Ibn 'Abbas also recited the verse of the poet:

Easy of disposition, noble, possessing bounty, like a stream that rivers feed.

This, according to what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, was a stream from the Jordan which God Most High caused to flow for her when thirst afflicted her. It is related that Jibril (peace be upon him) struck the earth with his foot, and a spring of sweet water appeared and flowed as a stream. It was also said that 'Isa (peace be upon him) did this, and this is what is related from Abu Ja'far (may God be pleased with him).

It was also said that this was already present earlier, but God Most High drew her attention to it. What came before is the one that accords with the context of showing the manifestation of extraordinary signs and what is immediately understood from the noble wording. The stream was called sariyy because water flows (yasri) in it, so its lam is a ya' on this meaning. But from al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and al-Jubba'i it is related that what is meant by sariyy is 'Isa (peace be upon him), and it is from sirr (nobility) and in the sense of elevation, as al-Raghib said, meaning: your Lord has placed beneath you a boy of lofty rank and exalted worth. In al-Sihah it is said: it is generosity in nobility, and desire for elevation, more exalted in rank; and its lam on this meaning is a waw. The sentence is a reason for the removal of the grief implied by the prohibition against it. The mention of the title of Lordship together with its attachment to her pronoun is for her honor, for the emphasis of the reason, and for the completeness of consolation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 19, verse 25:

﴿And shake towards you﴾, i.e., towards your direction. *Al-hazz* (shaking) is moving to the right and left, whether violently or not, or moving by pulling and pushing. It implies the meaning of *al-mayl* (inclining), which is why it is followed by *ila* (towards). Alternatively, it is a metaphor for that, or the transitivity with *ila* is considered because inclining is part of its meaning. This is what has been said.

Abu Hayyan prohibited connecting *ila* to *hzzi* (shake). He justified this by saying that it is established in grammar that a verb does not take an attached pronoun as its object. The attached pronoun has here been made the subject, and this is not one of the verbs of *zann* (thinking), *faqd* (losing) or *'adam* (lacking), whose two objects refer to one referent. So one does not say "I struck you" with the meaning of "Zayd struck him" in the sense of "you struck yourself and he struck himself." In their view, the pronoun in the genitive case is like the pronoun in the accusative case, so one does not say "I looked at you" and "Zayd looked" with the meaning of "I looked at yourself" and "he looked at himself." Because of this, they made *'ala* in the saying of the poet:

*Be at ease upon yourself, for affairs are in the hand of God, and their measures are His.*

a noun, as in the saying of the poet:

*She departed from upon him after her thirst had been fully quenched.*

He also made the prepositional phrase here dependent on a deleted verb, meaning "I mean to you," as they said in *saqyan laka* (may you have a drink) and similar expressions, which were brought for *al-tabyin* (specification).

You know that they have said that *ila* comes for specification. However, Ibn Malik said, and likewise the author of *al-Qamus*, that it specifies the subject of its genitive complement after something that expresses love or hatred, from a verb of wonder or an elative noun (*ism tafdil*), and what is here is not like that. In *al-Itqan*, it is related that Ibn 'Usfur, in his commentary on the verses of *al-Idah*, transmitted from Ibn al-Anbari that *ila* is used as a noun, so one says "I turned away from *ilayka*," just as one says "I departed from *'alayhi*," and "he came out from *'alayhi*" in the Qur'an: ﴿And shake towards you﴾. With this, Abu Hayyan's objection is dispelled. End of quotation.

It would have been necessary for him to explain its meaning on the view that it is a noun. Perhaps it then means *'inda* (at, with), since it is explicitly stated in *al-Qamus* that it comes with this meaning, and he recited:

*Or is there no path to youth, whose remembrance is dearer to me than the flowing, pure wine?*

However, this meaning does not suit the verse. Similar to this is the claim that it is an *ism fi'l* (verb-noun) in this sense. Furthermore, the report that it is used as a noun, if authentic, undermines Abu Hayyan's statement: "It is not possible to claim that *ila* is a noun, given the consensus of the grammarians on its being a particle." Perhaps he meant the consensus of those among them who are considered reliable in his view. What I incline to, in resolving the objection, is that the verb is implicitly (*mudammana*) given the meaning of inclining, and the prepositional phrase depends on it, not on the verb that takes the pronoun. This is a remote interpretation that should not be rushed into as an objection. Still, there is some doubt about the soundness of such a construction in light of the stated rule, because such expressions are very frequent in their speech. Among them is the Almighty's saying: ﴿Keep your wife to yourself﴾, and the verse just mentioned. Also the poet's saying:

*Leave aside the plunder whose cry was raised in its enclosures, but rather the talk of the cries*

and their saying: "Go yourself" and "Depart from yourself," and other examples that are not hidden from one who surveys them. The interpretation of all that has come is not free from artificiality, so reflect and be fair.

Then, the verb here is treated as intransitive, as in the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

*If he excuses himself with the barrenness of her udders, towards the guest, my sword will wound the tendons of his legs.*

Therefore it is made transitive by *bi* (with), meaning "do the shaking" ﴿with the trunk of the palm tree﴾. The *ba'* here is for the instrument, as in: "I wrote with the pen." It was also said that the verb is transitive and its object is deleted, and the sentence is according to a deleted modifier, meaning: "Shake the dates by shaking the trunk of the palm tree." The artificiality of this is not hidden, and shaking the dates is not free from vulgarity. From al-Mubarrad, it is related that its object is *rutaban* (fresh dates), which comes later, and the sentence is of the type of *tanazu'* (grammatical contention over a shared complement). It is objected that shaking applies to dates only incidentally. So he made it the principal and made the principal secondary, where he introduced *ba'* for assistance upon it, which is not appropriate, along with the separation between the response of the imperative and its object, and there would be the operation of the first (verb), which is weak, especially in this context.

What was mentioned about the reversal is directed at the view that contains artificiality, and this is evident. As for what has been said, that although shaking falls primarily on the trunk, the intended thing from it is the dates, and therefore for this suitable point it was made primary, because shaking the dates, the fruit of shaking, does not remove the vulgarity we mentioned, especially since what conveys that is what is mentioned in the response of the imperative. Some have made ﴿with the trunk of the palm tree﴾ a circumstantial (*hal*) phrase, on the assumption that the object is *rutaban* or *al-thamarah* (the fruit), meaning "being with the trunk of the palm tree." In this there is the fruit of what neither fattens nor satisfies. It was also said that the *ba'* is extra for emphasis, similar to it in the Almighty's saying: ﴿And do not cast yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾, and the poet's saying:

*They are free women, not mistresses of veils, black-eyed, who do not recite with the surahs.*

The correct view that is suitable for the revealed text's strangeness of composition, as in *al-Kashf*, is the first. As for al-Farra's saying: "It is said *hazzahu* and *hazza bihi*," if he means that both are with the same meaning, as is apparent, it is not to be paid attention to, as one of those relied upon has stated.

﴿Will drop﴾ is from *saqqata* in the sense of *asqata* (cause to fall). The feminine pronoun refers to the palm tree. The return of a pronoun to the genitive complement (*mudaf ilayhi*) is common, and whoever denies it is like the donkey carrying books.

Abu Hayyan permitted that the pronoun refers to the trunk, since it acquires the feminine gender from its genitive complement, as in the Almighty's saying: ﴿some of the travelers will pick him up﴾ according to the reading of one who reads with a *ta'* above, and the saying of the poet:

*As the spear's chest was stained with blood.*

It is objected that this is contrary to the apparent meaning, even if it is valid. Masruq and Abu Haywa read in one transmission ﴿will drop﴾ with a *ta'* above, *damma* (vowelled), and a *kasra* on the *qaf*. In another transmission from Abu Haywa, he read likewise except with a *ya'* below. The Almighty's saying ﴿upon you fresh dates﴾ is in all of this in the accusative case as an object, and it is the ripe stage of *al-busr* (unripe dates), its singular with a *ha'* (*rutabah*), and its plural irregularly is *artab*, like *rub'* and *arba'*. Also from Abu Haywa, he read ﴿will fall﴾ with a *ta'* above, *fatha* (vowelled), and *damma* on the *qaf*, and likewise from him, except with a *ya'* below, so *rutaban* is accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*). It is related from him that he read it in the last reading in the nominative as the subject.

Abu al-Sammal read ﴿will keep falling﴾ with two *ta'*s. Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib read *yassaqtu* with a *ya'* below, the present tense of *assaqata*. The majority read ﴿will drop﴾ with a *ta'* above, *fatha*, a doubled *sin* followed by an *alif*, and a *fatha* on the *qaf*. The accusative in these three is also a specification.

In some readings it was permitted that it be a *hal muwatti'ah* (preparatory circumstantial). When a masculine pronoun is implied according to one of the readings, it refers to the trunk; when a feminine pronoun is implied, it refers to the palm tree. The first thing you have heard is ﴿fresh﴾ (*janiyyan*), meaning picked, so it is *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul*, i.e., suitable for being picked. In *al-Qamus*: "*thamarun janiyyun*: picked at that time." Accordingly it has been said the meaning is: "Fresh dates, whoever sees them says, 'It is picked,'" and this is a praise description, since what is picked is better than what falls by shaking, and what has recently ripened is better than what is old. It was also said *fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il* (active), i.e., fresh dates, and what was meant, as it was said, is that its ripening had been completed.

Talha ibn Sulayman read *jinyyan* with a *kasra* on the *jim* for harmony. The reason for the masculine form is apparent. From Ibn al-Sayyid, in his commentary on *Adab al-Katib*, it is related that he said: "It should have been said *janiyyatan*, but some of the speech was put in the masculine and some in the feminine." This is open to examination. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that the palm tree had only the trunk, and it had no head. When she shook it, the palm fronds had come out, then she looked at the spathe emerging from between the fronds, then it turned green and became *balah* (unripe dates), then it reddened and became *zahw* (ripening dates), then *rutab* (fresh dates), all in the twinkling of an eye, and the fresh dates began to fall before her. They were *barni* (a kind of dates). It was said *'ajwah* (a kind of dates), and this is what is related from Abu 'Abd Allah, may God be pleased with him.

Apparently she did not carry anything but fresh dates. It was said that there was also a banana with it, and this is related from Abu Rawq. The reason it was limited to dates is its extreme benefit for women after childbirth. From al-Baqir, may God be pleased with him: "A woman after childbirth has never sought healing with the like of fresh dates, for God fed them to Maryam in her childbirth."

They also said: "Nothing is better for a woman after childbirth than fresh dates, nor for a patient than honey." It was said: "When a woman's delivery is difficult, nothing is better for her than fresh dates." It is mentioned that eating dates for women after childbirth is a custom from that time, and likewise *tahnik* (rubbing the newborn's palate with dates). In her being commanded to shake there is an indication that seeking sustenance in general is required, and this does not contradict trust in God (*tawakkul*). How beautiful is what has been said:

*Have you not seen that God revealed to Maryam: "Shake towards you the trunk, so that fresh dates will keep falling"?*

*If He had willed, He could have bent the trunk without a shake towards her, but everything has its cause.*

[Page 86]

﴿So eat﴾ from that fresh date, ﴿and drink﴾ from that stream. It is also said: from the juice of the fresh dates, which was extremely tender, so the argument from the mention of drinking does not conclusively establish that al-sariyy means a stream (jadwal). How subtle is what the noble verse guides to: bringing the water first, then the food second, then eating third, and drinking fourth. Concern for water is greater than concern for food, especially for one who wants to eat something that requires water, such as sweet and hot things. Custom dictates that eating comes after drinking, and for this reason eating was given precedence
[Page 87]
over drinking wherever it occurs. It is also said that water was given precedence because it is the origin of benefit, and its benefit is general, for cleaning and the like, and it was flowing, and it is more evident in removing sorrow. Drinking was delayed due to custom. It is also said that eating was given precedence so that it would be adjacent to what resembles it, namely the fresh dates. The command, it is said, may admit of obligation or recommendation, and that depends on her circumstances. It is also said it is for permissibility. ﴿So be cool of eye﴾, that is, be content and at ease, and cast off from yourself whatever has grieved you. It was also read with a kasra on the qaf (qurri), and this is the dialect of Najd, who pronounce the 'ayn of the past tense with a fatha and the 'ayn of the present tense with a kasra, while others use a kasra for both. This is derived from qarr, meaning tranquility, for when the eye sees what gladdens the soul, it becomes calm and stops looking at other things. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿their eyes rolling﴾ from fear, or it means coolness, for the tear of joy is cool and the tear of sorrow is hot. This is supported by the saying: "the coolness of the eye and its heat" for what is loved and what is hated. Her consolation, peace be upon her, through what the verse contained of causing water to flow and bringing forth fresh dates, is because these are two matters that break the customary order. It is as if it were said: do not grieve, for God, exalted is He, is capable, and He will clear your name of what passes through the hearts of those bound by ordinary customs, by guiding them to understand the reality of your affair through what He has shown them of elemental simples and plant compounds that break the natural customs of creation. He follows the consolation with the command to eat and drink, because the grieving person may not be free for such things, and He reinforced this with the final command. As for one who interprets al-sariyy as one of elevated rank and high status, he makes the consolation through the bringing forth of fresh dates as you have heard, and through al-sariyy in that the elevation of rank is something that is followed by clearing one's name. It is as if it were said: do not grieve, for God, glorified is He, has shown you what clears your name, in word and in state.

This may be supported in general by what is reported from Ibn Zayd, who said: 'Isa, peace be upon him, said to her: "Do not grieve." She said: "How could I not grieve, when you are with me and I have no husband and am not a slave-woman? What excuse will I have before the people? Would that I had died before this!" He, peace be upon him, said to her: "I will suffice you in speech." ﴿If you see any human being﴾, that is, any human being, whoever he may be. Abu 'Amr read, as transmitted from him by Ibn al-Rumi, ( taraʾinna ) with the replacement of the yā' by a hamza. Ibn Khalawayh claimed that this is a grammatical error according to most grammarians. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is from the dialect of those who say labba'tu bil-hajj and halla'tu al-sawiq, due to the affinity between the hamza and the letters of softness in substitution. Talha, Abu Ja'far and Shayba read ( tarīn ) with a sukun on the yā' and a fatha on the nūn, lightened. Ibn Jinni said: it is anomalous, and the analogy would have been to delete the nūn for the jussive, as in the saying of al-Afwah al-Awdi:

"Do you not see my head, which the misery of a time of reversal and despair has disfigured?"

(Then say) to him, if he questions you: ﴿I have vowed a fast to the Most Merciful﴾. Zayd ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, read ( ṣiyāman ), and the meaning is one, that is, silence, as in the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), and Anas ibn Malik also read with it. So the meaning of fasting here is abstention, and its application to what has been mentioned is by consideration that it is one of its instances, like the application of "human" to Zayd, and this is literal usage. It is also said that its application to it is figurative, and the indicator is the following consequence, which is clear according to this. Some said: what is meant is fasting from the known nullifiers and from speech, and they did not speak during their fasting, and it was an act of devotion in their religion, so its vow is valid. The Prophet ﷺ forbade it, so it is abrogated (mansukh) in his law, as al-Jassas mentioned in the book Ahkam al-Qur'an.

It is reported from Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, that he entered upon a woman who had vowed not to speak, and he said: "Islam has demolished this, so speak."
