In Ibn Hajar's commentary on al-Bukhari, from Ibn Qudama, it is stated that it is not part of the law of Islam, and the apparent sense of the reports is its prohibition. If one vows it, he is not obligated to fulfill it, and there is no disagreement about this between the Shafi'is and the Hanafis, because of the restriction it contains, and it is not in our law, even though it was an act of devotion in the law of those before us. The hesitation of al-Qaffal regarding its permissibility or impermissibility arises from a lack of knowledge. And in some reports there is what indicates, by its apparent meaning, that the vow of silence was specific to Maryam, peace be upon her. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Haritha ibn Mudarrib, who said: I was with Ibn Mas'ud when two men came. One of them greeted and the other did not greet. Then they sat down. The people said: "What is wrong with your companion that he did not greet?" He said: "He has vowed a fast, that he will not speak to any human today." Ibn Mas'ud said to him: "Evil is what you have said. That was only the woman's words, she said that so it would be an excuse for her if she were asked, for they used to deny that a child could be born without a husband except through fornication. So speak, and enjoin the good and forbid the evil, for that is better for you." The apparent meaning, on the last interpretation of the fast, is that it is based on the silence in it, a consequence of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So I will not speak today to any human﴾, that is, after I have informed you of my vow. So she would have vowed not to speak to a human without this announcement, and so it would not invalidate it, because it is not something vowed. It may be that this is an explanation of the vow by mentioning its formula. A group said: she was commanded to inform them of her vow by sign. It is said: this is the more apparent. Al-Farra' said: the Arabs call everything that reaches a person speech by whatever means it reaches, as long as it is not emphasized with the verbal noun (maṣdar); if it is emphasized, it is only literal speech. It is understood from His saying, exalted is He, ("human") rather than ("anyone") that what is meant is: "So I will not speak today to any human," and that she would speak only to the angel and converse with her Lord. She was commanded, peace be upon her, to do this, as many have said, because of her aversion to disputing with the foolish, and to rely on the speech of 'Isa, peace be upon him, for it is a decisive text in cutting off criticism.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 27]

﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him.﴾ That is, she came to them with her child, carrying him. The particle *bi* (ب) here expresses accompaniment (*lil-musahabah*), but if it were taken to express transitivity (*lil-ta'diyah*), the meaning would also be correct. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*), either referring to the pronoun of Maryam or to the pronoun of her child. This coming, according to what Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn 'Asakir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, took place after forty days, when she had become clean from her postnatal bleeding (*nifas*). It was said that she longed for her homeland and knew that she would be relieved of her affair, so she came with him. When she entered upon them, they wept. It was also said that they intended to stone her until 'Isa, peace be upon him, spoke.

It is reported in a narration from al-Habr that when she withdrew from her family behind the mountain, they lost track of her from her sanctuary (*mihrab*). They asked Yusuf about her, and he said: "I have no knowledge of her, but the key to the door of her sanctuary is with Zakariyya." So they sought Zakariyya and opened the door, but did not find her, and they accused him. They seized him and rebuked him. Then a man said: "I saw her in such-and-such a place." So they went out in search of her and heard the sound of a magpie (*'aqa'aq*) at the top of the trunk of the palm tree beneath which she was. They went to her, and when she saw them approaching her, she lifted the child towards them, until she met them with him. Then what happened, happened.

The apparent meaning of the verse and the reports is that she came to them with him without any request from them. It was said, however, that they sent to her: "Come to us with your child." Satan had informed them of her delivery, so she came to them with him. When they saw the two of them, ﴿they said, "O Maryam, you have certainly come with a thing"﴾ [*faʻalti*, "you have done"] ﴿"monstrous."﴾ Qatadah said: great. It was also said: strange. Its root is from *fara al-jild*, meaning he cut the hide, either for the purpose of reform or of corruption. It was also said that it derives from *afra-hu* with the same sense. The first view was preferred, because the pattern *fa'il* is formed by analogy only from the triliteral root. The failure to distinguish between it and the derived form in meaning is the view adopted by the author of al-Qamus.

In al-Sihah, from al-Kisa'i, it is said that *al-fary* is cutting in the manner of reform, and *al-ifra'* is in the manner of corruption. Al-Raghib says the same. It was also said that *al-ifra'* is general. Whichever is the case, *al-fary* has been used metaphorically for what has been mentioned in its interpretation. In al-Bahr it is said that it is used for a great matter, whether evil or good, whether in speech or in action. From this is the description of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have not seen a genius (*'abqari*) who performs his *fariyy* (feat)," and in the proverb: "He came performing the *fary*."

The word (*shay'an*) is in the accusative as the object. It was also said that it is in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*), meaning: "You have certainly come with a strange coming." It was expressed as "a thing" in order to emphasize the sense of strangeness.

[Page 88]

Abu Haywah, as transmitted by Ibn 'Atiyyah, read *fariyyan* (فَرْيًا) with a sukun on the *ra'*. As transmitted by Ibn Khalawayh, he read *far'an* (فَرْأً) with a hamzah.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 28:

﴿O sister of Harun﴾ This is a resumption (istinaf) to renew the reproach and emphasize the rebuke. By "Harun" is not meant the brother of Musa son of Imran, peace be upon them both, because of what Ahmad, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Tabarani, Ibn Hibban and others narrated from al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent me to the people of Najran, and they said: "Do you not see what you recite, ﴿O sister of Harun﴾, while Musa was so-and-so many years before Isa?" He said: So I returned and mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: "Did you not tell them that they used to name the prophets and the righteous before them?"

Rather, it is, as narrated from al-Kalbi, a brother of hers from her father. Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah, who said: He was a righteous man among the Children of Israel. It is also narrated from him that he said: It was mentioned to us that forty thousand of the Children of Israel followed his funeral procession on the day he died, all of them named Harun. According to this, "sister" (ukht) is used in the sense of resemblance, and they likened her to him either mockingly or because of the righteousness they had seen in her before. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he was a wicked man, and they likened her to him as an insult to her. It was also said: The intended Harun is the brother of Musa, peace be upon them both. Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated this from al-Suddi and Ali ibn Abi Talhah: she was among the descendants of those who were in the generation of brotherhood, so he described her with brotherhood because she was described by the character of her origin. It is also permissible that Harun is applied generally to his progeny, like Hashim and Tamim, and the intended meaning of "sister" is that she is one of them, as one says "brother of the Arabs," and this is what is narrated from al-Suddi.

﴿Your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother a woman of unchastity﴾ This is an affirmation that what she brought is a monstrous thing (fariyy), or an alert that committing immoralities by the offspring of the righteous is more heinous. In it is evidence that the branches are generally pure when the roots are pure, and they are rebuked when they come with the opposite of that. Umar ibn Baja al-Taymi, the poet who used to satirize Jarir, read: "ma kana abaki imru'u su'in" (ما كان أباكِ امْرُؤُ سَوْءٍ), making the predicate definite and the subject indefinite. This was slightly improved by the existence of a justification for the beginning with an indefinite noun in it, which is the annexation (idafah).

**﴿So she pointed to him﴾**, that is, to Jesus, peace be upon him, [signaling] that they should speak to him. Shaykh al-Islam said: The apparent meaning is that she then made clear her vow, and that she was far removed from conversing with people, as she had been commanded. This indicates that what she was commanded to do was to make her vow clear by gesture, not by speech, and combining the two is something unknown. **(They said)** in denial of her response. In some reports, when she pointed to him that they should speak to him, they said: "Her mockery of us is worse than her fornication," and God forbid that she should be so. Then they said: **﴿How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?﴾** Qatadah said: the cradle is her mother's lap. ʿIkrimah said: it is the cradle (al-marbāh), that is, the rocking one. It was also said: it is his bed. And it was said: it is the place on which he rests. The verse has been found problematic, since everyone whom people speak to was in the cradle as a child before the time of speaking to him, so he would not be a subject for wonder and denial.

Al-Zamakhshari answered this in two ways. The first: the event is tied to a past time that is vague, suitable for both its near and distant past, and here it refers specifically to the near past. What indicates this is that the speech is framed for wonder, so the meaning is: how can we speak to one who was, just yesterday and recently, from this time, in the cradle? Their purpose in this is the continuation of the child's state, that he has not yet left the cradle. Had it been said, "one who is in the cradle," that intensity would not be there, since the preceding [context] serves as evidence for it. And "man" here is a relative pronoun intended to refer to Jesus, peace be upon him. The second: "was" (*kāna*) is a narration of a past state, and "man" is descriptive, so the meaning is: how can we speak to those described as being in the cradle, that is, we have not spoken to them until now, so that we should speak to this one? Shifting from the past to the present conveys depiction and continuity. This, as in *al-Kashshaf*, is a good and fitting explanation.

Page 89
Abu ʿUbayda said: *kāna* is an extra particle used merely for emphasis, without indicating time, and **"a child" (ṣabiyyan)** is an emphatic circumstantial accusative, its governing element being the stability (*al-istiqrar*). So Ibn al-Anbari's claim that *kāna* here governs the predicate, while the extra particle does not govern it, is nothing. The meaning is: how can we speak to one who is now in the cradle, in the state of being a child? According to the view of one who said that the extra *kāna* does not indicate an event but indicates a past time restricted to what it is added to, such as al-Sirafi, the problem is not resolved by saying it is extra.

Al-Zajjaj said: The better view is that *man* is a conditional particle, neither relative nor descriptive, meaning: whoever was in the cradle, how can we speak to him? This is like saying, "How can I admonish one who does not act on my admonition?" The past form has the sense of the future in conditional constructions, so there is no problem in this. Yet its weakness is not hidden.

(قالَ) — "He said." This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) answering a question arising from the context of the noble arrangement, as if it were said: "What happened after that?" So it was said: Jesus, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Indeed, I am the servant of Allah﴾. It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, was nursing, and when he heard what they said, he stopped nursing, turned his face toward them, leaned on his left side, pointed with his index finger, and said what he said. It is also said that Zakariyya, peace be upon him, came to him seeking to make him speak, and he said this, mentioning his servitude to Allah, the Exalted, first, because acknowledging that is, as it is said, the first of the stations of the wayfarers (al-salikin). In it is a refutation of those who claim his lordship (rububiyyah). And in all that he said there is an indication of the innocence of his mother, because it points to his being chosen (al-istifa'), and Allah, glorified is He, is too exalted to choose a child born of fornication, and this is among the matters taken for granted among them. In it is also a glorification of his mother, peace be upon them both, beyond what an explicit statement would convey. It is also said that because He, the Exalted, does not single out with a child described by what has been mentioned except one who is free of blame and chosen.

It is disputed whether, after he spoke what was mentioned, he continued to speak as men customarily do, or whether he did not speak until he reached an age at which children speak. The counting of him, peace be upon him, among those who spoke in the cradle and then did not speak until the time of customary speech, is evidence for the second view.

﴿He has given me the Book﴾ — the apparent meaning is that it is the Gospel (al-Injil). It is also said that it is the Torah (al-Tawrah). It is also said that it is both together.

﴿And has made me a prophet﴾. ﴿And has made me blessed (mubarakan)﴾ wherever I am. Mujahid said: "beneficial (naffa'an)," and from his benefit was the healing of the blind-born and the leper. Sufyan said: "a teacher of good, commanding the right and forbidding the wrong." And from al-Dahhak: "one who fulfills needs." The first is better because of its generality. The expression of the three verbs in the past tense is either in consideration of what is in the decree that is binding, or by treating what is certain to occur as though it had already occurred.

It is also said that Allah, exalted is He, perfected him in intellect and made him a prophet while still a child. This is narrated from al-Hasan.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Anas that Jesus, peace be upon him, studied the Gospel and mastered it while in his mother's womb, and this is what is meant by his saying ﴿He has given me the Book﴾.

﴿Wherever I am﴾ — i.e., wherever I may be. In al-Bahr it is stated that this is a conditional (shart), and its response (jaza') is omitted, its estimate being "He made me blessed," and it was omitted because of what precedes it as an indication. It is not permissible for it to be an object (ma'mul) of the earlier "ja'alani," because "ayna" is only used as an interrogative or a conditional, and the first is not permissible here, so the second is determined. The conditional noun does not govern a verb preceding it; rather, it is an object of the verb that follows it.

﴿And He has enjoined upon me prayer and zakat﴾ — i.e., He commanded me with them as an emphatic command. The apparent meaning is that by them is meant what has been legislated concerning the body and property in a specific manner.

It is also said that by zakat is meant the zakat al-fitr. It is also said that by prayer is meant supplication, and by zakat the purification of the soul from vices. This is required in the case of zakat according to what is related from Ibn 'Ata' Allah, though it is open to objection, since there is no zakat for the prophets, peace be upon them, because Allah, the Exalted, has exempted them from worldly things, so what is in their hands belongs to Allah, the Exalted, and for this reason they are not inherited from; or because zakat is purification and their earnings are pure. It is also said that it is not required, because that would be a command to him to impose zakat on his community, which is contrary to the apparent meaning. And if zakat is taken in its apparent sense, then the apparent meaning is that the intended sense is "He enjoined me" to pay the zakat on wealth if I possess it. There is no objection to his words, glorified is He, ﴿as long as I am alive﴾ including the period of his, peace be upon him, being in heaven, and it would be necessary to say that prayer upon him is obligatory there, peace and blessings be upon him. So it is said.

You know that the apparent and immediately understood meaning of the stated period is the period of his, peace and blessings be upon him, being alive in this world, as is customary, and that does not include the period of his, peace be upon him, being in heaven. Ibn 'Atiyyah reported that the people of Medina, Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr recited "dimtu" with a kasra on the dal, and we have not found this attributed to anyone else. Yes, it is said that this is a dialect (lughah).

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on surah 19, verse 32:

﴿And dutiful to my mother﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with "blessed" (*mubarakan*), according to what al-Hufi and Abu al-Baqa' said. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that it involves a distance caused by the intervening separation, and that in general he preferred to supply a verb for the phrase and its complement, meaning: "and He made me dutiful to her." It has been said that this is almost explicit that he (peace be upon him) had no father, and so it is the clearest of the sentences in indicating her innocence (peace be upon her).

It was also recited as *birran* (with a kasra on the *ba'*). The grammatical basis for its accusative case is like what has been mentioned in the widely transmitted (*mutawatir*) recitation. Making his own person (peace be upon him) into "dutifulness" is a figurative usage, as in "they are only turning away and turning back" (*fa-innama hiya iqbal wa-idbar*). It is also permitted that the accusative is governed by a verb in the sense of "he enjoined upon me" (*awsani*), meaning "and he obligated me" or "and he charged me with dutifulness." This is then of the type of "I fed her straw and cool water." Closer to this, according to what is in *al-Kashshaf*, is that it is like "Zayd, I passed by him," in terms of correspondence, even if it is not of the same type.

It is also permitted that it is coordinated with the position (*mahall*) of "with prayer," as has been said regarding the reading of "and your feet" (*wa-arjulakum*) in the accusative. It has been said that *awsa* may take a second object directly, as occurs in al-Bukhari: "We have enjoined upon you one religion." The apparent view is that the verb in such cases is construed with the meaning of a verb that takes its object directly. Al-Zahrawi and Abu al-Baqa' related that it was also recited as *wa-birran* (with a kasra on the *ba'*), and that it is coordinated with "prayer" and "almsgiving" by unanimous agreement. The indefiniteness is for magnification.

﴿And He has not made me arrogant and wretched﴾, meaning: He, glory be to Him, did not decree this for me in His eternal knowledge. The Prophet (peace be upon him) used to say: "Ask me, for I am gentle-hearted and humble in my own self."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 33:**

﴿And peace is upon me the day I was born, and the day I die, and the day I am raised alive.﴾ The discussion of the reason these occasions are singled out for mention has already been given, so it is not repeated here. The more apparent, indeed the correct, view is that the definite article is for the category (lil-jins), and it was used as an allusion (ta'rid) cursing those who accused Maryam and her enemies among the Jews, peace be upon her. For when one says "the category of peace is for a particular person," he has alluded that its opposite is upon you. A parallel to this is His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And peace is upon those who follow the guidance﴾, meaning that punishment is upon those who deny and turn away. Since the context is one of contention and obstinacy, it indicates this kind of allusion. The claim that the article is for definite reference ('ahd) is contrary to the apparent meaning, and indeed incorrect. This is not because the referent known is the peace of Yahya, peace be upon him, and its very self cannot be a peace for Isa, peace be upon him, since it could be of the type of ﴿This is what we were provided with before﴾. Rather, it is because this statement is separated from that one both in existence and in sequence, so it would be a known referent that has not preceded either verbally or in meaning. Moreover, the context requires the allusion, and that would be lost under that interpretation, since the contrast arises only from the exclusivity of all peace to him, peace be upon him. This is what is found in al-Kashshaf. Restricting the definite reference to his own peace, based on its being mentioned in the narrative, is not sound, and its condition is not hidden.

The peace of Yahya, peace be upon him, was said to be more excellent than this peace (of Isa) because it is from the speech of Allah, exalted is He. It was also said that this peace is more excellent because in it Allah, exalted is He, places Himself in that position, while also conveying the exclusivity of all peace to him, peace be upon him. So reflect.

Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, read (yawma waladat) with the feminine ta' and the verb attributed to his mother.

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the one whose noble attributes have been detailed. In it there is an indication of the elevation of his rank, the loftiness of his station, his distinction from others by those praiseworthy virtues, and his being placed in the position of something perceived and witnessed. It is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is His, exalted is He, saying: (Isa). His saying, glorified is He: ﴿son of Maryam﴾ is either an attribute of Isa, or a second predicate, or an appositive (badal), or an explanatory apposition (‘atf bayan), though most scholars hold it to be an attribute. The meaning is that this is Isa, son of Maryam, not what the Christians describe. This is a refutation of them in the most eloquent manner and the most demonstrative method, since he is described by the opposites of what they ascribe to him, such as servanthood to his Creator, glorified is He, which is contrary to his being a god or a son of Allah, mighty and majestic is He. Thus the restriction (hasr) is derived from the implication (fahwa) of the statement. It was also said that it is derived from the definiteness of both terms, based on what al-Kirmani mentioned, that the definiteness of both terms unconditionally conveys restriction. This, however, is contrary to what the rhetoricians (ahl al-ma'ani, the scholars of the science of meanings) mention, namely that this applies only to a predicate defined by the article or by its being a construct with what it belongs to, as in ﴿Those are the verses of the Book﴾, according to what some commentaries on al-Kashshaf state.

It was also said that its derivation from definiteness, according to what they mention too, is based on the view that "Isa" is interpreted as the defined-by-the-article, i.e., the one named Isa. This is, as you see, not sound. So hold to the first view.

﴿The word of truth﴾ is accusative by way of praise. The meant "truth" is Allah, exalted is He, and "word" is His word, exalted is He. It was applied to him, peace be upon him, in the sense that he was created by the word "Be" without a father. It was also said that it is accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from Isa, and that the meaning of "truth" and "word" is what you have heard.

It was also said that it is accusative as an absolute object (masdar), meaning "I say the word of truth." It was also said that it is a masdar emphasizing the content of the sentence, accusative by a necessarily omitted verb "uhiqqu." Shaykh al-Islam said that it is a masdar emphasizing "qala" (he said), namely "Indeed I am the servant of Allah," etc.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 34:

His saying, glorified is He, ﴿That is Jesus, son of Mary﴾, is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) confirming the content of what precedes it, and there is a remoteness (bu'd) in it. The ﴿truth (al-Ḥaqq)﴾ in all three readings is in the sense of truthfulness (al-ṣidq). The idafa (genitive construction) is, according to a group, explanatory (bayaniyya), and according to Abu Hayyan it is the idafa of a qualified noun to its qualifier (min idafat al-mawsuf ila al-sifa).

Al-Jumhur read ﴿qawlu﴾ with a nominative ending, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: he is the word of truth about which there is no doubt. The implied pronoun refers either to the preceding discourse or to the completion of the story. It has also been said: it is an attribute of Jesus, or a substitute (badal), or a predicate following a predicate for ﴿dhalika﴾; or the predicate is ﴿dhalika﴾ and Jesus is a substitute or an appositive (ʿatf bayan).

What is meant in all of this is the Word of Allah, exalted is He. Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿qala al-haqqa﴾, and ﴿qala Allahu﴾ with the verb ﴿qala﴾ in the nominative in both places.

From al-Hasan (it is read) ﴿qulu al-haqq﴾ with a damma on the qaf and the lam. The words al-qawl, al-qal and al-qul have one meaning, like al-rahb, al-rahab and al-ruhb.

Abu Hayyan stated explicitly that they are verbal nouns (masadir). From Ibn al-Sikkit: al-qal, and likewise al-qil, is a noun (ism), not a verbal noun (masdar). Talha and al-A'mash, in one narration, read ﴿qalu al-haqqa﴾ with a damma on the lam of ﴿qala﴾ as a past-tense verb, and the ﴿al-haqq﴾ in the nominative as the subject (fa'il). On this reading ﴿dhalika Isa ibn Maryam﴾ is the object of the saying: Allah, exalted is He, said that this one described with what was mentioned is Jesus, son of Mary, ﴿about which they dispute﴾, meaning they doubt or contend concerning him. The Jews say: he is a sorcerer, far be it from him; and the Christians say: he is the son of Allah. Glory be to Allah above what they say.

The relative clause (al-mawsul) is an attribute of the saying or of the truth, or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: he is the one who, etc. This varies according to the difference in exegesis and recitation.

ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, al-Sulami, Dawud ibn Abi Hind, Nafi' in one narration, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿kadhalika (tamtarun)﴾ with the second-person ta' (taksh) of address.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 35:

﴿It is not befitting for Allah to take a son; glory be to Him!﴾ That is: it is not correct nor proper for Him, may His majesty be exalted, to adopt such a thing. This is a refutation of the Christians and a declaration of His transcendence, exalted and majestic, above what they have fabricated against Him, blessed and exalted is He. And His saying, may His majesty and loftiness be exalted, ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ is a rebuke to them by making clear that His way, exalted is His way, when He decrees any matter among matters is that it comes into existence in the briefest time. So how can it be imagined that one whose way is this should have a son, which is a sign of need and deficiency? Ibn 'Amir recited ﴿فَيَكُونَ﴾ (fa-yakuna) in the accusative, as an answer (to the imperative, in the grammatical sense of jawab).

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And indeed Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him﴾ is a coordination (ʿaṭf) upon what al-Wahidi said concerning His saying ﴿Indeed, I am the servant of Allah﴾. So it is part of the speech of Jesus (peace be upon him), affirming the meaning of servanthood (ʿubūdiyyah), and the two verses are parenthetical (muʿtariḍatān). This is supported by what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both. Ubayy read it without the waw.

The apparent meaning, on this view, is that with an implied "say" (taqdīr al-qawl), it is an address to the master of those addressed, ﷺ, meaning: "Say, O Muhammad: Indeed Allah..." etc. The two Ḥaramayn (the readers of Makkah and Madinah) and Abu ʿAmr read it as wa-anna, with the waw and a fatḥah on the hamzah. Al-Zamakhshari explained it by deleting the preposition and linking it to uʿbudūhu, meaning: "And because He, exalted is He, is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him." It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the mosques are for Allah, so do not invoke anyone along with Allah﴾. This is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh.

Al-Farra' permitted that inna and what follows it be in the sense of a verbal noun (taʾwīl maṣdar), coordinated upon "the zakah," meaning: "And He enjoined on me the prayer and the zakah, and [enjoined on me] that Allah is my Lord and your Lord," etc. Al-Kisa'i permitted that this be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "And the matter is that Allah is my Lord and your Lord."

Abu ʿUbayda related from Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ that it is a coordination upon "amran" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When He decrees a matter﴾, meaning: "When He decrees a matter, and He decrees that Allah is my Lord and your Lord." This is a confusion in i'rab (grammatical analysis), so it is likely not authentically from Abu ʿAmr, for he holds a high station in the science of grammar. It was also said that it is a coordination upon "the Book." Most of these opinions, as you see, are weak.

In the codex of Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him, it is also read as wa-bi-anna with the waw and the preposition bāʾ. Some explained it as a coordination upon "the prayer" or "the zakah," and some explained it as connected to ʿbudūhu, meaning: "Because of that, so worship Him." The address is either to the contemporaries of Jesus (peace be upon him) or to the contemporaries of our Prophet ﷺ. ﴿This﴾, meaning what has been mentioned of monotheism, ﴿is a straight path﴾, whose follower does not go astray,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 37:

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So the factions differed among themselves﴾, uses the particle fa for the sequencing of what follows upon what precedes, as an admonition to their evil conduct in making that which should necessitate agreement (ittifaq) the source of disagreement (ikhtilaf). For what is related of the statements of ʿIsa, peace be upon him, although they are definitive texts that he is the servant of Allah, exalted is He, and His messenger, the Jews and the Christians differed about them through deficiency (tafrit) and excess (ifrat). So the factions (al-ahzab) are the Jews and the Christians, and this is what is narrated from al-Kalbi. The meaning of ﴿from among themselves﴾ is that the disagreement did not come from outside them; rather they were the ones who disagreed. And "bayn" (between) is a noun-like adverb of place, used as a noun by the entry of min upon it.

It is reported in al-Bahr that min is said to be extra (ziyadah). He also related the view that al-bayn here means distance (bu'd), i.e., they differed concerning it because of their distance from the truth, so that min would be causal (sababiyyah). Its remoteness is not hidden. It has also been said: the factions are the sects of the Christians, for they differed after his lifting up, peace be upon him, concerning him. Nestorius said: he is the son of Allah, exalted is He far above that; He caused him to appear and then lifted him up. Jacob said: he is Allah, exalted is He; He descended and then ascended. Melchior said: he is the servant of Allah and His prophet. And in al-Milal wa al-Nihal it is stated that the Melkites said: the Word, meaning the hypostasis of knowledge (uqnum al-ilm), was united with the Messiah, peace be upon him, and clothed itself with his humanity (nasut).

They also said: the Messiah, peace be upon him, is a universal humanity, not a particular one, and it is eternal, and Mary bore an eternal, everlasting God. The killing and crucifixion befell both the humanity and the divinity together. We have discussed the matter of the Christians sufficiently, so let it be remembered. It has also been said that the intended meaning of them is the Muslims, the Jews and the Christians.

It is related from al-Hasan that they are those who formed factions against the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, when the story of ʿIsa, peace be upon him, was recounted to them, and they differed concerning him among the people. It has been said: they are all disbelievers in general, which includes the Jews, the Christians, the polytheists who were in the time of our Prophet ﷺ, and others. Al-Imam favoured this, saying that there is no specifier for it. He favoured the view that they are the People of the Book, saying that mentioning the disagreement immediately after the story of ʿIsa, peace be upon him, requires this. The saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿So woe to those who disbelieved﴾ supports this. Thus the intended meaning of them is the disputing factions, and He expressed them by this description to announce that they all disbelieved and to indicate the reason for the ruling. When it is said that the Muslims or the Melkites are included, and it is said that they said that he, peace be upon him, is the servant of Allah and His prophet, among the factions, then the intended meaning of "those who disbelieved" is some of the factions, i.e., woe to those among them who disbelieved ﴿from the witnessing of a tremendous day﴾, i.e., from the witnessed event of a tremendous day of terror, reckoning and recompense, which is the Day of Resurrection; or from the time of its witnessing; or from the place of witnessing therein; or from the testimony of that day against them, which is that the angels and the prophets, peace be upon them, and their tongues and all their limbs will testify against them with disbelief and wickedness; or from the time of the testimony; or from its place.

It has been said: it is what they testified to concerning ʿIsa, peace be upon him, and his mother, and its greatness is due to the greatness of what is in it, as in the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿Great is the word that comes out of their mouths﴾. It has also been said it is the day of the killing of the believers when the factions differed, and as you see, it is far-fetched. The truth is that the intended meaning of that day is the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 38:

﴿How keen their hearing and how keen their sight!﴾ This is an expression of wonder at the sharpness of their hearing and their sight on that Day. Its meaning is that their hearing and their sight, ﴿on the Day they come to Us﴾ for reckoning and recompense, that is, the Day of Resurrection, are worthy of being marvelled at, after they were deaf and blind in the world.

This is reported from al-Hasan and Qatadah. ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: it is a warning and a threat, meaning: they will soon hear what will tear their hearts apart, and see what will blacken their faces. And from Abu al-ʿAliyah it is reported that it is a real command to the Messenger (ﷺ) to make them hear and see the promises of that Day and what will befall them therein. The prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa al-majrur) in the first two views is in the nominative position according to the well-known opinion, and in the last view it is in the accusative position, since (asmiʿ) is a real imperative whose subject is an implied pronoun obligatorily. It is also said that in the sense of wonder it is likewise, and the agent is the pronoun of the verbal noun. ﴿But the wrongdoers today﴾, that is, in the world, are ﴿in manifest error﴾, whose extent cannot be grasped, since they utterly neglected hearing and looking. The placing of "the wrongdoers" in the position of the pronoun is to indicate that they are wrongdoers to themselves in this matter.

The istidrak (qualification) upon what was reported from Abu al-ʿAliyah relates to the words of the Exalted ﴿So woe to those who disbelieved﴾,

(And warn them) — that is, the wrongdoers, according to the apparent meaning. Abu Hayyan said: the pronoun refers to all people, meaning, warn them of ﴿the Day of Regret﴾, the Day when the wrongdoers will regret what they neglected concerning God, exalted is He. It was also said: it refers to all people, and the regret of the good-doers is over how little good they did. ﴿When the matter is decided﴾, meaning, when the reckoning has been completed, the people of Paradise have gone to Paradise, the people of the Fire have gone to the Fire, death has been slaughtered, and each of the two groups has been called to eternal abiding.

It is related from al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj that the reference is limited to the slaughtering of death. This is based on what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: (Death will be brought in the form of a white-speckled ram. A caller will call out, "O people of Paradise!" and they will stretch their necks and look. He will say, "Do you recognize this?" They will say, "Yes, this is death," and all of them have seen it. Then a caller will call out, "O people of the Fire!" and they will stretch their necks and look. He will say, "Do you recognize this?" They will say, "Yes, this is death," and all of them have seen it. It will then be slaughtered between Paradise and the Fire, and he will say, "O people of Paradise, eternity without death! O people of the Fire, eternity without death!") Then he recited: ﴿And warn them﴾, the verse.

It is related from Ibn Mas'ud in one narration that the Day of Regret is when the disbelievers see their seats in Paradise, had they been believers. It was also said: it is when they are told while in the Fire, ﴿Be silent therein, and do not speak to Me﴾. It was also said: it is when it is said, ﴿Separate yourselves today, O guilty ones﴾.

Al-Dahhak said: that is when Hell is brought forth and hurls out sparks. It was also said: the intended meaning is the Day of Resurrection in general, and this is related from Ibn Zayd, and in it there are regrets in many stations. From this it was said: the intended meaning of "regret" is its genus, which includes their regret in what has been mentioned, their regret when the books are taken in the left hand, and other things. The intended meaning of "the decision of the matter" is the complete cessation of the affairs of this world, and the time of that is considered to be extended. It was also said: the intended meaning of "the Day of Regret" is the Day of Resurrection, as related from Ibn Zayd, except that the intended meaning of "the decision of the matter" is the cessation of what causes regret. Ibn Atiyya permitted that the Day of Regret be understood as encompassing the Day of Death.

You know that the apparent meaning of the preceding hadith, and similarly other reports, as is not hidden from one who examines them, indicates that the Day of Regret is the Day when death is slaughtered and eternity is proclaimed. Perhaps the specification is because regret on that day is the greatest of regrets, for there hopes are cut off and the door of escape from the terrors is closed. Among the strange things said is that the intended meaning of "the decision of the matter" is the closing of the door of repentance when the sun rises from the west, but this is nothing (of substance).

(And when) according to all the other opinions is a substitute (badal, apposition) for (the Day), or is connected to (the regret). The definite verbal noun (al-masdar al-mu'arraf) governs an explicit object according to some scholars, so how much more so a temporal adverbial (zarf). God's words ﴿while they are heedless and they do not believe﴾: al-Zamakhshari said: it is connected to God's words, exalted is His majesty, ﴿in manifest error﴾, according to al-Hasan. The justification for this is that the two clauses are in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the concealed pronoun in the prepositional phrase, meaning, they are settled in that while they are in those two states. In al-Kashf, the coordination (ataf) with God's words ﴿The wrongdoers today are in manifest error﴾ is preferred, meaning, they are in error and they are in heedlessness. On both views, the clause ﴿warn them﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradiyyah), and the conjunction (waw) is a parenthetical waw. The reason for the parenthesis is that the warning emphasizes what they are in of heedlessness and error. It is also permitted that this phrase be connected to ﴿warn them﴾, as a circumstantial phrase from the object, meaning, warn them while they are heedless and do not believe for the outcome. But this does not fit God's words ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾. In al-Kashf he said: this is not a valid objection, because that is in relation to benefit, while this is in relation to alerting the heedless to show that benefit is in the Hereafter, and this is the duty of the prophets, peace be upon them all. Moreover, even if it were sound, there is no contradiction, as in God's words ﴿And remind, for the reminder benefits the believers﴾. How could there be, when this meaning is repeated in the Qur'an, up to God's words ﴿so that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned, so they are heedless﴾? As for God's words, glorified is He, ﴿and they do not believe﴾, it is an emphatic negation encompassing the past and the future, so it is not sound if made a circumstantial phrase; and even if it were sound, its answer has already been known from what preceded, and upon the Messenger is only the conveying.

Yes, we do not deny that the first view is more preponderant and more fitting to the context. The essential meaning on the last view is: warn them, because they are in a state in which they need warning.

[Page 95]

﴿Indeed, it is We who inherit the earth and whoever is upon it.﴾ No dominion or sovereign remains for anyone besides Him, the Exalted. So all of that belongs to Him, the Exalted, absolutely, outwardly and inwardly, with none other beside Him. He, glory be to Him, takes possession of it in the manner of an inheritance passing from the one who bequeaths it to the heir. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿To whom belongs the dominion today? To God, the One, the Subduer.﴾ Or ﴿We cause the earth and whoever is upon it to die﴾ by annihilation and destruction. The heir dies, having inherited and taken possession of it. ﴿And to Us they will be returned.﴾ That is, they will come back to the recompense, not to anyone other than Us, whether independently or in partnership.

Al-A'raj read ﴿turja'un﴾ with the upper dot (taʾ), i.e., tur'ja'ūn. Al-Sulami, Ibn Abi Ishaq and ʿIsa read it with the lower dot (yāʾ), in the active voice. Al-Dani reported from them that they read it with the upper taʾ. And God the Exalted knows best.

* * *

(From the allusive indications (ishara) in the verses) ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, ʿAyn, Sad.﴾ According to the sound view, this and similar letters are among the secrets of God the Exalted. It has been said, regarding the reason the surah opens with them, that the Kaf is an allusion to the Sufficient (al-Kafi), which the state of Zakariyya's weakness, old age and inability required; the Ha is an allusion to the Guide (al-Hadi), which His care for him and His showing him what he sought required; the Ya is an allusion to the Protector (al-Wali), which the state of his fear of his relatives required; the ʿAyn is an allusion to the All-Knowing (al-ʿAlim), which His manifesting (the answer) despite the absence of means required; and the Sad is an allusion to the Truthful (al-Sadiq), which the promise required. The allusion in the two stories, in general, is that God, His majesty be exalted, grants both upon request and without request.

Some of the people of ta'wil (esoteric interpretation) applied what these letters contain to what is within the souls (anfus), but they overstrained and forced their meanings.

As for the vow of fasting, the intended meaning being silence, it is an allusion to abandoning the defence of the self. It is as if it were said to her, peace be upon her: "Be silent and do not defend yourself, for in your speech and your defence of yourself there is hardship for you, while in your silence there is a display of the power We have over you." So she remained silent. When God, glory be to Him, knew the truthfulness of her severing herself to Him, He made ʿIsa, peace be upon him, speak to clear her.

It is mentioned that he, peace be upon him, folded every beautiful attribute within the folds of his saying ﴿Indeed, I am the servant of God﴾ (19:30). This is because they said that no one claims to be "servant of God" unless he manifests all the divine attributes indicated by the sublime Name. On this basis, His saying ﴿He has given me the Book﴾ etc. is placed as an explanation of this claim.

They mentioned that "servant" (ʿabd) when attributed to His pronoun (ʿabduhu) is a more eloquent praise than what has been mentioned, and that the possessor of that station is our Prophet (ﷺ). It seems their meaning is that "servant" is attributed to His pronoun, glory be to Him, in this way when it is not joined with a proper name, as in "His servant Zakariyya." Otherwise, the claim of exclusivity is not complete. So let it be pondered.

Ibn ʿAta mentioned, regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and has not made me a tyrant, a wretch﴾ (19:32), that the tyrant (jabbar) is one who cannot be advised, and the wretch (shaqi) is one who cannot be admonished. We seek refuge in God, glory be to Him, from His making us like that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 41:

(And mention) is coordinated with (warn them) according to Abu al-Su'ud. It has also been said that it is coordinated with the preceding "udhkur" (mention), and this is probably the more apparent reading. ﴿In the Book﴾, i.e., this surah, or in the Qur'an. (Ibrahim), i.e., recite to the people his story, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And recite to them the news of Abraham﴾. Otherwise, the one who mentions that in the Book is God Most High, as in al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's tafsir). In this there is the point that he, upon him be blessings and peace, is the one who speaks on behalf of God Most High, conveys His commands and prohibitions, and is the greatest of His manifestations and loci of disclosure (majali), so it is as if he is the one who mentions in the Book what his Lord, majestic and exalted, has mentioned. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that it includes the misguiding of those who attribute divinity to inanimate matter, just as what precedes it includes an allusion to the misguiding of those who attribute it to a living being. The two groups, although they share in the error, the second group is more astray.

It may be said, on the first view regarding the coordination, that the meaning is: warn them of that, and mention to them the story of Abraham, peace be upon him, for they claim descent from him, ﷺ, so perhaps by hearing his story they will desist from the vile things they are engaged in. ﴿Indeed, he was a truthful one﴾, i.e., one who constantly adhered to truthfulness and never lied at all, (a prophet) whom God Most High made a prophet. This is a second predicate, and "kana" governs it as a qualifier and specifier of the first, i.e., he combined both attributes.

Perhaps this order serves to emphasize the avoidance of the supposition that truthfulness is restricted to prophethood, for every prophet is truthful. It has also been said: the siddiq is one who confirms by his speech and belief and realizes his truthfulness by his deeds. In al-Kashshaf: "siddiq" is of the intensive forms (ab'iyat al-mubalagha), and what is meant is the extreme of his truthfulness and the abundance of what he confirmed of God Most High's unseen matters, His signs, His books and His messengers, and the preponderance and predominance lay in this confirmation of the books and messengers, i.e., he was confirming all the prophets and their books, and he was a prophet in himself, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, he brought the truth and confirmed the messengers﴾. Or he was eloquent in truthfulness, because the foundation of the prophetic affair is truthfulness, and one who confirms God Most High's signs and miracles is worthy of being so. End of quotation.

In this there is an indication that the intensive form may be taken in terms of quantity and may be taken in terms of quality, and you may intend both, since the context is one of praise and emphasis, and al-Raghib touched upon this. As for the intensification being in terms of the object, as in "qatta'tu al-hibal" (I cut the ropes), al-Kashf counted it among the errors, so reflect. It has been inferred that it derives from truthfulness (sidq), not from confirmation (tasdiq), and this is supported by the reading ﴿innahu kana sadiqan﴾ and by the fact that the form fa'il from af'ala is rarely found, while most are from fa'ala. Some have explained the word "nabi" here as one of high rank with God Most High and among people.

The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to give the reason for the requirement of the command, for describing him, peace be upon him, with this is one of the motives for mentioning him. It is, as has been said, a parenthetical insertion between the substituted term, which is Abraham, and the substitute, which is "idh" in His saying, exalted is He,

﴿When he said﴾. Ṣāḥib al-Farā'id (the author of al-Farā'id) criticized this, arguing that placing an interjection between the substitute (*badal*) and the word it replaces (*mubdal minhu*) without a conjunction *wāw* is far from natural and is clearly objectionable. In al-Bahr, it is said that making *idh* a substitute for *Ibrāhīm* requires that *idh* be declinable (*mutasarrif*), whereas the more correct view is that it is not declinable. There is room for discussion on this. It has also been said that *idh* is an adverbial complement (*ẓarf*) of *kāna* (was), which is built on the view that the incomplete *kāna* and its sisters govern adverbial complements. This is a disputed question. It has also been said that *idh* is an adverbial complement of *nabiyyan* (a prophet), meaning "informing at the time of his saying (*li-abīhi*, to his father)." This is objected to on the grounds that it implies that the informing (*istinbā'*) took place at that time. It has also been said that *idh* is an adverbial complement of *ṣiddīqan* (truthful). In al-Bahr, it is stated that this is not permissible, because the *ṣiddīqan* has already been described by the qualifier *al-a'lā*, according to the view of the Kufans. It is objected that *nabiyyan* is a predicate (*khabar*), as we have mentioned, not a qualifier (*na't*). Yes, restricting *al-ṣiddīqiyyah* (truthfulness) to that time is not free from some difficulty.

It has also been said that *idh* is an adverbial complement of *ṣiddīqan nabiyyan* together, and its apparent meaning is that it governs both of them at once. It is objected that two governing words acting upon one governed word is not permissible according to the correct view. The claim that they were treated as a single compound term, like the treatment of *ḥulw ḥāmiḍ* (sweet-sour) as *mazz* (a single term meaning "a flavour mixing sweet and sour"), so that the meaning is "combining the attributes of the truthful ones and the prophets, peace be upon them, when he addressed his father," is by no means free from problems. What the context requires and what good taste confirms is that *idh* is a substitute, namely a substitute of inclusion (*badal ishtimāl*). The linking of remembrance to times, although the intended purpose is to remind of the events that occurred in them, has had its secret explained many times, so reflect on this.

"O father" (yā abatī), meaning "O my father." The tā' (ta) here is a substitute (ʿiwaḍ) for the ya' of possession, which is why the two are not combined except in rare cases, as in the saying: "yā abatī arraqanī al-qudhdhān" (O my father, the gnats have kept me awake). Combining them in "yā abatā" is said by some to be a combination of two substitutes, which is permissible, like the combining by the one wearing a splint (ṣāḥib al-jabīra) of wiping (al-masḥ) and tayammum, which are two substitutes for ghusl (ritual washing). It is also said that what is combined in it is a single substitute, and it is said that the alif is for lengthening the vowel (al-ishbāʿ). You know the state of the grammatical reasons (al-ʿilal al-naḥwiyya).

Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Aʿraj and Abū Jaʿfar read "yā abatі" with a fatha on the tā', and Hārūn claimed that this is a grammatical error (laḥn), but the truth is contrary to that. In the codex of ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd) it is "wa-abatı" with a waw in place of the ya'. Addressing someone with it outside of lamentation (nudba) is rare. He (peace be upon him) addressed his father with this to appeal to his compassion (istiʿṭāfan lahu).

Abū Nuʿaym and al-Daylamī reported from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The right of the parent over his child is that he should not name him except by what Ibrahim (peace be upon him) named his father: 'yā abatī', and that he should not call him by his name." This is apparent in indicating that he was truly his father. A group of scholars held that he was his paternal uncle, and the application of "father" to him is metaphorical.

﴿Why do you worship that which does not hear﴾ your praise of it when you worship it and your supplication to it, ﴿and does not see﴾ your humility and submission before it, or: does not hear or see anything of what is heard or seen, so that what was mentioned enters into this primarily. "Mā" is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), and they permitted that it be an indefinite qualified noun (nakira mawṣūfa). ﴿And cannot avail you﴾, meaning, is not able to avail you ﴿anything﴾
Page 97
of things, or some kind of availing; it is then in the accusative as an object or as a verbal noun (maṣdar).

He (peace be upon him) followed in his call the finest method and argued against him with the most wondrous argument, with good manners and character, having no method of the kind that would cause him to ride the back of obstinacy and stubbornness, nor to fall utterly away from the path of right guidance, in that he was asked for the reason for his worship, though it is something that the intellect of every sane person, learned or ignorant, finds ridiculous and refuses to incline toward, let alone to worship it, which is the furthest extreme of veneration, while such worship is only due to one who has complete self-sufficiency and comprehensive bounty: the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life, the Giver of death, the Rewarder, the Punisher. He also drew attention to the fact that the sane person must do everything that is done for a sound motive and a sound purpose. And the thing, even if it were living, discerning, hearing, seeing, capable of benefit and harm, would, if it were possible, be rejected by the person of sound intellect from worshipping it, even if he were the most noble of creatures, since he sees his like in need and subjection to the overpowering, necessary Power. So what is your opinion of a made, lifeless stone that has no trace or sign of the attributes of living things?

Then he called him to follow him, so that he might guide him to the clear truth, since he (his father) had not been favored with divine knowledge, nor was he independent in sound reflection; he began his call with the appeal mentioned earlier, saying: ﴿O father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge what has not come to you﴾. He did not call his father utterly ignorant, though he was so in the extreme, nor did he describe himself as having surpassing knowledge, though he did; rather he presented himself in the guise of one who is a gentle servant to him, who would know better the states of the path they both were on, and so he won him over gently, saying: ﴿So follow me; I will guide you to a straight path﴾, meaning a right path leading to the most excellent aims, removing one from error which leads to the pits of destruction and perils. His saying "there has come to me" (jāʾanī) clearly indicates that this discourse took place after he had been made a prophet (peace be upon him). As for what came to him, it is said to be knowledge of what is necessary for God Most High, what is impossible regarding Him, and what is permissible, in the most complete and perfect form. It is said: knowledge of the affairs of the Hereafter, its reward and its punishment. It is said: knowledge encompassing all of that. Then he dissuaded him from what he was upon by portraying it in a form that every sane person would find repugnant, by explaining that it, despite being utterly devoid of benefit, draws a great harm, for in reality it is worship of Satan, since he is the one who commands it. So he said:

O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, your worship of idols is worship of him, since it is he who adorns them for you and incites you to them.

And His saying, ﴿Indeed Satan has been disobedient to the Most Merciful﴾, is a justification for the prohibition's binding force and a confirmation of it, by making clear that he is rebellious against the one whom His mercy has encompassed and whose blessing has overspread you. There is no doubt that whoever obeys a disobedient one is himself disobedient, and whoever is disobedient deserves to have blessings taken back from him and to be punished. To point to this meaning, "the Most Merciful" was used. In it there is also an indication of the utmost heinousness of his disobedience. As for restricting mention to his disobedience among all his other offences, this is either because it is the root (milak) of them, or because it is the consequence of his enmity toward Adam, peace be upon him; so reminding him of it serves as a call to his father to beware of allying with him and obeying him. And the use of the explicit noun in place of a pronoun is for the sake of greater emphasis.

And His saying: ﴿O my father, I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you﴾ is a warning against the evil outcome of what he is engaged in, namely worshipping idols. As al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, fear (khawf) is the expectation of something disliked, based on a presumed or known sign, so it is not definitively certain that what is feared will occur. From this it has been said that his choice of this expression contains courtesy (mujamalah). Al-Farra' and al-Tabari took it to mean knowledge, but that is not the case. The indefiniteness of ﴿punishment﴾ (ʿadhab), according to what al-Sa'd (al-Sa'd al-Taftazani) chose in al-Mutawwal, admits of either magnification or minimization, i.e., a terrible punishment or the least thing of it. He said: The word "touch" (mass) and the attribution of the punishment to the Most Merciful do not indicate a preference for the second meaning, as some have claimed, because of the Almighty's saying: ﴿Surely a great punishment would have touched you for what you plunged into﴾, and because punishment from the Generous and Forbearing is more severe. (End of quotation.)

Page 98

Abu al-Su'ud chose that it is for magnification. He said: The word "min" (from) is connected to an implied element that occurs as a qualifier of "punishment," confirming what the indefiniteness conveys of inherent grandeur with relational grandeur. The explicit mention of "the Most Merciful" serves to indicate that the attribute of mercy does not prevent the arrival of punishment, as in the Mighty and Majestic's saying: ﴿What has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ (End.) In al-Kashf it is said that taking "ʿadhab" as magnification, as the author of al-Miftah (al-Sakkaki) permitted, is something the context rejects, because the context is one of displaying utmost compassion, observing good manners, and good treatment. He said "from the Most Merciful" because of his earlier saying ﴿he was disobedient to the Most Merciful﴾, and to indicate that it is not by way of retribution; rather, this too is a mercy from God Most High toward His servants, and an alert that mercy precedes wrath, and that the attribute of "Rahmaniyyah" (being the Most Merciful) does not contradict punishment; rather, it is "Rahimiyyah" (being the Merciful) according to what the Sufis hold. For al-Muhaqqiq al-Qunawi said in his commentary on al-Fatihah: "al-Rahim, as we have explained, is for the people of the right and beauty, while al-Rahman combines gentleness and subjugation for the people of the other case and majesty," and so on to the end of what he said. He supported taking it as magnification by His saying: ﴿so you would become a companion to Satan﴾, i.e., a partner whom he follows and who follows you in punishment, for the guardianship (wilayah) of Satan in this sense results only from touching a great punishment.

It may be answered regarding the claim that the context is one of displaying utmost compassion, which seems to contradict it, that harshness is sometimes also a form of compassion, as it has been said:

"So he was harsh that they might be restrained, and whoever is wise, let him at times be harsh toward one he loves."

This has already been mentioned, along with other verses to this effect. In observing good manners and courtesy, it suffices that he did not assert with certainty that the punishment would overtake him. Although "mass" indicates little for the great, they said that abundance and greatness are considered with respect to what it entails and follows, not by looking at it in itself, for it is not intended in itself; rather, it is like a foretaste preceding the intended goal, so it may be described by either of the two aspects according to different considerations. It seems to me that you would choose magnification, because it is more suitable to intimidation, and you would claim that here it is from the source of compassion. So reflect.

It has also been permitted that "so you would become" and what follows is consequent upon touching the lesser punishment, and "walī" (guardian/companion) derives from "muwalah," which is following and befriending. The intent is that the persistence (in that state) is a consequence of the ruling of that companionship and the continuation of its effects, namely God's displeasure and wrath. There is no obstacle to a great outcome following from a small matter. Then, the apparent meaning is that "punishment" refers to the punishment of the Hereafter. Some have interpreted it as the punishment of this world, meaning abandonment (khidhlan) or something else of the afflictions that befell the disbelievers in this world, but that is not the case. Some have claimed that the sentence has an inversion, and the original would be: "Indeed I fear that you would become a companion of Satan," i.e., a follower of him in this world, "so a punishment from the Most Merciful would touch you," i.e., in the afterlife. It seems that the matter of the consequence was difficult for him, so he was compelled to this. God Most High has already sufficed you from that with what we have mentioned.

(قالَ) "He said." This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), answering a question that arises from the preceding discourse, as if it were said: "So what did his father say when he heard from him, peace be upon him, these advice that must be accepted?" It is said: he said, insisting on his obstinacy, countering gentleness and kindness with harshness and coarseness: ﴿Do you turn away from my gods, O Ibrahim?﴾ Al-Zamakhshari (al-Zamakhshari) chose that (راغِبٌ, raghib) is a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and (أنتَ, anta) is the subject (mubtada'), and in this there is a directing of the denial to the very act of desiring, together with a kind of amazement. Abu al-Baqa' (Abu al-Baqa'), Ibn Malik (Ibn Malik) and others went to the view that (أنتَ, anta) is the agent (fa'il) of the adjectival form (sifah), because the interrogative particle precedes it, and it dispenses with the predicate; this is so that there would not be a separation (fasl) between (أراغِبٌ, ara-ghibun) and its complement, which is ﴿from my gods﴾, by something foreign, namely the subject. And it is answered that (عَنْ, 'an) is connected to a deleted element after (أنتَ) that is indicated by (أراغِبٌ).

The author of al-Kashf (sahib al-Kashf) said: the subject is not foreign in every respect, especially since the separated element is an adverbial phrase (zarf), and the fronted element is in the intention of being delayed; and the eloquent speaker turns the attention to the meaning after what he commits has a permissible aspect in Arabic, even if it is weaker. Perhaps adopting this style is close to preferring istihsan (juristic preference) because of the strength of its effect over qiyas (analogy). And there is no doubt that the increase in denial arises only from the fronting of the predicate, as if it were said: "Do you desire to turn away from them, while no one seeking them desires them?" alerting him to the error in his aversion. And if it were said: "Do you desire?" it would not be of this category at all. End of quotation.

Abu Hayyan (Abu Hayyan) preferred the parsing of Abu al-Baqa' and those with him, because there is no necessity of separation in it, and because the speech remains free of departure from the original arrangement in fronting and delaying. Al-Badr al-Damamini (al-Badr al-Damamini) hesitated regarding the permissibility of the delayed element being an inceptive subject (ibtida'iyyah) in a construction like this, even if it is free of separation or another objection, as in "Is the sun rising?" (أطالعٌ الشمسُ), and that is like "Is standing Zayd?" (أقائمٌ زيدٌ), because of the risk of confusing the subject with the agent, as in "Zayd struck" (ضرب زيدٌ), where it is not permissible for Zayd to be an inceptive subject. Al-Shumunni (al-Shumunni) answered that Zayd in the first case allows two possibilities, each of which is contrary to the original, and that is an ambiguity that causes no confusion, unlike the second case. So reflect.

﴿If you do not desist, I will surely stone you﴾: a threat and a warning regarding what he was upon of admonition and reminder; meaning: "By God, if you do not desist from what you are upon of forbidding their worship and calling to what you called me to, I will surely stone you with stones," according to what is narrated from al-Hasan (al-Hasan). It was also said: "with the tongue," and the intended meaning is "I will surely revile you." This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (Ibn 'Abbas), al-Suddi (al-Suddi), al-Dahhak (al-Dahhak) and Ibn Jurayj (Ibn Jurayj). Some scholars supposed that the object of the prohibition is the desire to turn away from the gods, meaning: "If you do not desist from turning away from my gods, I will surely stone you," but that is not correct. (واهجرني, wahjurni) is a conjunction upon a deleted element indicated by the threat, meaning: "So beware of me and leave me," and to this al-Zamakhshari went.

Perhaps the reason for this, and for not considering it a conjunction with what was mentioned, is that it is not valid, or it is not good, to have a disagreement between the two conjoined elements, one being declarative and the other imperative; and the answer to an oath that is not a request for something cannot be an imperative; and the fa' in (فاحذرني, fa-hdharni) is not a conjunctive particle, lest the threat be returned. Some people conjoined it to the preceding sentence, based on Sibawayh's (Sibawayh) permission of conjunction despite a difference between declarative and imperative; and the estimate is more fitting to the soul. (مَلِيًّا, maliyyan) means a long time, according to al-Hasan, Mujahid and a group; al-Suddi said: "forever," and this seems to be the intended meaning. Its root, according to what has been said, is from "imla'," i.e., "imdad" (extension); likewise "mala'ah," with the mim vowelled in three ways, has the same meaning, and from this comes "al-malawan," the night and the day. It is in the accusative as an adverb of time, as in the saying of Muhalhil:

So the deaf mountains were split at his death, and the veiled women wept for him at length (maliyyan).

Ibn al-Anbari (Ibn al-Anbari) narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he explained it as "long" (tawilan) without mentioning the qualified noun. It was said that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "a long abandonment." In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas, the meaning is "safe and sound," and the intended sense is "able to abandon, capable of it." In that case it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of (اهجرني), meaning: "Abandon me for a long time, by forsaking and departing from me, before I inflict upon you blows so that you cannot move." It seems that on this basis it derives from "tamalla bi-kadha," meaning he enjoyed it for a long time.

(قالَ) is a resumptive clause (istinaf), as before. ﴿Peace be upon you.﴾ is a farewell and a disengagement, in accordance with the principle of repaying evil with good, since leaving off harm to one who harms you is itself a kindness. The meaning is: I will not afflict you with anything disagreeable hereafter, nor will I speak to you in a way that hurts you. This is similar to His saying, ﴿To us are our deeds, and to you your deeds. Peace be upon you. We do not seek the ignorant.﴾ [28:55]. It was also said that it is the greeting of one who parts ways. The one who advanced this view permitted greeting a disbeliever, and that one may begin with the prescribed greeting of peace. This is the view of Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, who relied on His saying, ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you...﴾ [60:8] and His saying, ﴿There has certainly been for you an excellent example in Ibrahim...﴾ [60:4]. What he relied upon is an interpretation that is refuted by what is established in Sahih Muslim: "Do not begin the Jews and the Christians with the greeting of peace." It is also read as "salaman" in the accusative, as a verbal noun (masdariyyah), and in the nominative, as a subject (ibtida').

﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you.﴾ That is, I will petition Him, glorified is He, to forgive you by granting you the tawbah (repentance) and guiding you to faith. This is indicated by the reason given for his saying, "And forgive my father," in His saying, ﴿Indeed, he was among the astray.﴾ So it is said. Thus his seeking forgiveness is in effect equivalent to saying: "My Lord, guide him to faith and bring him out of error."

Seeking forgiveness in this sense for a disbeliever, before it becomes clear that he will die in disbelief, is undoubtedly permissible, just as there is no doubt that it is impermissible once that has become clear, because it involves seeking the impossible. What Allah, exalted is He, has informed us will not occur is impossible to occur. For this reason, when it became clear to him, peace be upon him, through revelation, according to one of the two opinions mentioned in Surat al-Tawbah, that his father would not be forgiven if he died in that state, the promise and its fulfillment took place before the clarification. Therefore they were not commanded to follow him in seeking forgiveness.

The Allamah al-Tibi said: Allah, exalted is He, made clear to the believers that those people are the enemies of Allah, exalted is He, by His saying, ﴿Do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies, showing them affection...﴾ [60:1], and that there is no room for showing affection in any way. Then He, glorified is His majesty, went to great lengths in detailing their enmity by His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿If they overcome you, they will be enemies to you and will extend against you their hands and tongues with evil, and they wish that you would disbelieve﴾ [60:2]. Then Allah, exalted is He, urged them to sever ties of kinship by His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Your relatives and your children will not benefit you on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [60:3]. Then He, mighty and majestic is He, consoled them by urging them to follow Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and his people in severing ties, by His saying, blessed and exalted is He, ﴿There has certainly been for you an excellent example in Ibrahim and those with him, when they said to their people, "Indeed, we are free of you and of what you worship other than Allah. We have disbelieved in you...﴾ [60:4], up to His saying, exalted is His glory, ﴿except for the saying of Ibrahim to his father, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you"﴾ [60:4]. So He excepted from what was mentioned that which the context does not permit, just as the context permits the rest. This is because of the decisive text, meaning: for you there is an example in following Ibrahim, peace be upon him, together with these disbelievers in severing ties and abandoning them, and nothing else. So do not show them courtesy or display toward them compassion and mercy, as Ibrahim, peace be upon him, displayed toward his father in his saying, "I will ask forgiveness for you," because it had not then become clear to him that he would not believe, as the disbelief and enmity of these people has become clear to you. End of quotation.

It was objected that what has been mentioned clearly indicates that the forgiveness-seeking that the believers performed for their close relatives was forbidden because it took place after the clarification. It was like Ibrahim's seeking forgiveness, in the sense of asking for the granting of repentance and guidance to faith. What most scholars have relied upon is that His saying, ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to seek forgiveness for the polytheists...﴾ [9:113], was revealed concerning his (ﷺ) seeking forgiveness for his uncle Abu Talib after his death. That forgiveness-seeking cannot in any way mean seeking guidance at all. How can guidance be conceived after death? Moreover, even if it were supposed that his (ﷺ) seeking forgiveness for him took place before death, it still cannot be conceived in this sense, because the verse implies that it occurred after it became clear that he was among the companions of the Blazing Fire. And if it is interpreted as the inevitability of death upon disbelief, then it would be a supplication for guidance to faith together with knowledge of the inevitability of death upon disbelief and its impossibility, if these are known to us from what has passed. Then this is the most evident thing to him (ﷺ) and to those who draw from his niche of light, peace be upon him. This objection is strong on its face. Accordingly, Ibrahim's seeking forgiveness for his father in that sense must have occurred during the father's lifetime, because it cannot be conceived after death, and this is clear.

Al-Zamakhshari, in answering the question of how it was permissible for him, peace be upon him, to seek forgiveness for a disbeliever and to promise him that, said: They intended it as conditional upon repentance from disbelief. They said: He sought forgiveness for him only by his saying, "And forgive my father," because he had promised him that he would believe. They cited His saying, ﴿And the request of forgiveness by Ibrahim for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him﴾ [9:114]. Then he said: One may say that what prevented seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever is only the revealed text, whereas the judgment of reason does not reject it. So it is permissible that the promise to seek forgiveness and its fulfillment took place before the revealed text came. What confirms its soundness is that He excepted Ibrahim's saying, peace be upon him, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you," in the verse, "There has certainly been for you an excellent example in Ibrahim..." and so on, from that in which the example is required. Had it been conditional upon faith and repentance, the exception would not have been valid. As for the promise being from his father, it contradicts the apparent meaning, which is supported by the reading of al-Hasan and others, "wa'adaha abahu," with the letter ba' (waw ba'), meaning "He promised it to his father." Said the author of al-Kashf:

The Imam objected to the hadith of the exception, saying that the verse indicates a prohibition from following him, not that it was a sin. So it may be among his particular privileges, like many permissible things specific to the Prophet (ﷺ). This is not valid, because al-Zamakhshari did not hold that what Ibrahim, peace be upon him, committed was reprehensible. Rather, it is reprehensible for us, due to the revealed text.

The author of al-Taqrib objected that negating the necessary implication is not accepted, since the exception from what following is required only indicates that it is not obligatory, not that it is impermissible. So it should have been: "except for that in which following is permitted," instead of "except for that in which following is required," and the verse contains no indication of obligation. The answer: making it reprehensible and excepted indicates that it is reprehensible, not merely that the exception is from what following is required. The reprehensibility arises because it was excepted from the good example, so if one were to follow him in it, it would be a bad example. As for the indication of obligation, it is clear from His saying, exalted is He, later, ﴿There has certainly been for you in them an excellent example for whoever hopes in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [60:6], as is established in the principles of jurisprudence.

The conclusion is that the action of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, indicates that it is not in itself reprehensible. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to seek forgiveness...﴾ and so on, indicates that it is now reprehensible by revelation, and that it was also reprehensible in the time of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, after having been permissible. Therefore he disassociated himself from it. This is clear. However, al-Zamakhshari made the basis of permissibility before the prohibition to be reason, and this is a disputed question. Many have said it is revelation, since it falls under filial piety and compassion toward the community of the call. Indeed, it was said that the first view is the position of the Mu'tazilah, and this is the position of the People of the Sunnah. End of quotation, with slight alteration.

It was objected to the view that it became reprehensible in the time of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, after having been permissible: if this were so, our Prophet (ﷺ) would not have done it, yet it has come down that he, peace be upon him, did it for his uncle Abu Talib. It is answered that it is possible that the ruling had not reached him at the time he did it, peace be upon him. The truth on this question is that seeking forgiveness for a living disbeliever whose end is unknown, in the sense of seeking his guidance to faith, involves nothing prohibited, rationally or textually. But seeking that for a disbeliever known to have had a seal set upon his heart, whom Allah, exalted is He, has informed will not believe, and it is known that there is no conditionality in his matter at all, has no legitimate basis, rationally or textually.
