Similar to this is seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever while he remains in disbelief, as some verifiers have mentioned. It was said that this is because it nullifies the matter of disbelief, which is the gravest of sins, and turns the obligation of faith, which is the greatest of acts of obedience, into something futile, along with what is unbecoming to the majesty of Allah, mighty and majestic is He. Close to this, in what has been mentioned, is seeking forgiveness for the rest of the sinners while they remain in sin, except that one distinguishes between disbelief and other sins. As for seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever after his death in disbelief, the judgment of reason does not reject it; only the revealed text prevents it. He distinguished between this and seeking it for a disbeliever who remains in disbelief, by the absence of the earlier reasoning applying to it. This requires reflection.

It has been argued that this is permissible rationally by his (ﷺ) saying to his uncle: "I will not cease to seek forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden." Then the verse was revealed, ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to seek forgiveness for the polytheists...﴾ [9:113]. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire﴾ [9:113] is understood to mean: after it had become clear to them that they died as disbelievers. It was held necessary to say that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [4:48], was revealed afterward. Otherwise, his (ﷺ) seeking forgiveness for his uncle after knowledge of his death as a disbeliever would not be conceivable, and it had already been heard that Allah, exalted is He, does not forgive disbelief. It was also said that there is no need to hold that, because it is possible that he, peace be upon him, out of his great compassion and intense mercy, understood the verse to mean that Allah, exalted is He, does not forgive polytheism when it is not interceded for, or the abandonment in which the heart and all the limbs agree, and he knew of his uncle that his polytheism was not of that kind, so he sought forgiveness until he was forbidden, (ﷺ). Other views were also mentioned, so reflect. The matter still requires further discussion, and Allah, exalted is He, is the Granter of success.

﴿Indeed, He has ever been kind to me.﴾ That is, abundantly generous in goodness and honor. One says "hafiyy bihi" when one takes care to honor him. The clause is a reason for what precedes it. The fronting of the adverbial phrase (bi) is for the sake of the rhyme (fawasil), together with emphasis.

(And I will withdraw from you) The apparent meaning is that it is conjoined (ʿatf) to "I will ask forgiveness for you," and what is meant is: I will distance myself from you and from your people ﴿and from what you call upon besides Allah﴾ by emigrating with my religion, since my counsel has not had any effect upon you.

It is related that he, peace be upon him, emigrated to al-Sham (Greater Syria). It is also said that he emigrated to Harran, which is close to that, and they were in the land of Kuthā. During this emigration he married Sarah, and he met the tyrant who gave Hagar to Sarah as a servant. It is also permissible to take the withdrawal (iʿtizal) as withdrawal in the heart and in belief, though this is contrary to the apparent, transmitted meaning. ﴿And I will call upon my Lord﴾, that is, I will worship Him, glorified be He, alone, as is understood from avoiding other objects of worship besides Him, the Exalted. And because of the difference between the two acts of worship, a variation has been made between the two expressions. Some have mentioned that he expressed it as "worship" first because that is more suitable to the words of his father ﴿Do you turn away from my gods?﴾ together with his statement earlier ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which does not hear...﴾ etc. And he expressed it a second time as "calling upon" because it is more evident in the sense of turning toward, which is the opposite of withdrawal.

It is also permissible that by this is meant supplication in general, or what He, glorified be He, related in Surat al-Shuʿara, which is his saying ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous﴾. It has also been said: it is not far-fetched that the request for offspring is also meant by his saying ﴿My Lord, grant me a righteous [son]﴾, as the context and the sequence support. ﴿It may be that I will not be, in calling upon my Lord, unfortunate﴾, that is, disappointed and with my effort lost. In this there is an implicit reference to their wretchedness in worshipping their gods. In beginning the statement with "it may be" (ʿasā) there is a display of humility, observance of good manners, and an alert to the truth of the matter: that reward and answer come by way of His grace, mighty and majestic, not by way of obligation, and that what matters is the final outcome, and that is among the unseen matters specific to the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, which is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 49:

﴿So when he withdrew from them and from what they worshipped besides Allah﴾ by the emigration (hijrah) to the place mentioned earlier, ﴿We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾. The phrase is a substitute (badal) for "he withdrew from them": from his father and his disbelieving people, but not immediately after the emigration. It is well known that the first child granted to him, peace be upon him, was Isma'il, peace be upon him, based on Allah's words ﴿So We gave him good news of a forbearing boy﴾, following his supplication, "﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] among the righteous﴾." He had emigrated, and Sarah became jealous, so he married Hajar, and then she conceived Isaac, peace be upon him. When he grew old, Jacob, peace be upon him, was born to him.

Perhaps the ordering of their granting here, after his withdrawal, is to show the full magnitude of the blessings Allah Most High gave him in exchange for those among his family and relatives whom he left. For they are the two trees of the prophets, and they had descendants and grandchildren of great importance and great numbers. Moreover, Glorified is He, wished to remind Isma'il, peace be upon him, of his favour upon him individually.

It is also reported that when he, peace be upon him, headed for al-Sham (the Levant), he first came to Harran, married Sarah, she bore him Isaac, and Isaac had Jacob. The first view is the closest and most apparent.

﴿(And each of them)﴾, i.e., each one of Isaac and Jacob, or both of them together with Abraham, peace be upon him. It is the first object (maf'ul awwal) of Allah's words ﴿We made [him] a prophet﴾. It is placed before the verb for emphasis (takhsis), but not in relation to those other than them; rather, in relation to some of them, meaning that each one of them, ﴿We made [him] a prophet﴾, not some of them to the exclusion of others. In this arrangement, according to the second view regarding "(each)", the fact that Abraham, peace be upon him, was a prophet before the withdrawal does not become apparent.

﴿And We bestowed upon them of Our mercy﴾. Al-Hasan said: "It is prophethood."

Page 103

It may be that mentioning this after the mention of their being made prophets is to indicate that prophethood is among the mercy which He bestows specially on whom He wills. Al-Kalbi said: "It is wealth and children." It was also said: "It is the Book." The most apparent view is that it is general to every good, religious and worldly, that they were given, of what none among the worlds had been given. ﴿And We made for them a tongue of truth, exalted﴾, by which people take pride in them and praise them, in response to his supplication, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿And make for me a tongue of truth among the later generations﴾, and in addition to that. By "tongue" is meant the speech by which it is produced, so it is a metaphor (majaz, a figurative usage) through the relation of causation (ʿalaqah al-sababiyyah), like the hand in the sense of a gift, and the "tongue of the Arabs" is their language. It is also applied to a fine message, as in the verse of A'sha Bahila:

"There came to me a tongue that does not gladden me by it"

And from it is the saying of another:

"I regretted a tongue that was from me"

Its being attributed to truth and its description as exalted serve to indicate that they deserve what is said in praise of them, and that their virtues are not hidden, as if they were a fire upon a mountain, despite the long distance of the eras, the change of dynasties, and the variation of religions and sects. Some scholars restricted "the tongue of truth" to what is recited in the tashahhud: "As You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim," but generality is preferable.

﴿And mention in the Book Moses﴾. It is said that his mention was placed before that of Isma'il, peace be upon them both, so that it would not be separated from the mention of Ya'qub, peace be upon him. It is also said: this was done to hasten the attraction of the People of the Book, after what precedes it, which attracts the Arabs.

﴿Indeed, he was sincere﴾: a monotheist who made his worship sincere, free from shirk (associating partners with God) and riya' (showing off), or who submitted his face entirely to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and turned away from anything other than Him.

The Kufans, Abu Razin, Yahya and Qatadah read *mukhlasan* (مُخْلَصًا) with a fatha on the lam, meaning that Allah made him sincere (chosen). ﴿And he was a messenger﴾: sent by Allah, Exalted, to creation to convey whatever rulings He willed. ﴿A prophet (nabiyyan)﴾: of high rank above many of the messengers, peace be upon them, or above all the people to whom he was sent. Thus *nabi* (prophet) is derived from *nubuwwah* in the sense of elevation. It is also permissible that it derives from *naba'* (news), its original form being *nabi'*, meaning one who gives news from Allah, Exalted, of monotheism and the sacred laws. The first meaning is preferred because it is more eloquent. It is said that for this reason he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace (ﷺ), said: "I am not the *nabi'* of Allah (with a hamza), but the *nabi* of Allah," addressing someone who pronounced it with a hamza and intended to belittle him.

According to what al-Jawhari mentioned, the speaker meant that he, peace be upon him, had been expelled by his people from a *naba'* (a place of news/notoriety), and he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace (ﷺ), answered him with what removes that possibility. The reason for mentioning *nabi* after *rasul* is clear according to the first view. According to the second view, the reason is conformity with reality, on the basis that the meaning is that Allah sent him to creation and he informed them of Him, glorified be He.

Some scholars chose that both words are meant in their linguistic senses, and that the mention of *nabi* after *rasul* is because not every messenger is a *nabi*, since one may be sent with a gift, a written message, or the like.

﴿And We called him from the right side of the mountain﴾. The Tur is a mountain between Egypt and Madyan. Al-Aymanu (the right) is an attribute of janib (side), in accordance with His saying, Exalted is He, in another verse, ﴿the right side of the mountain﴾, with janib in the accusative. That is, We called him from its right-hand direction, which is opposite the left. What is meant is the right of Musa, peace be upon him, that is, the direction adjacent to his right side, since the mountain itself has no right or left. It is also permissible for al-Aymanu to derive from al-Yumn, which means blessing, and then it is likewise an attribute of janib, meaning from its blessed and auspicious side.

It has been permitted that it be an attribute of al-Tur, but the first is preferable. What is meant by His calling him from that place is the manifestation of His speech, Exalted is He, from that direction. Apparently, peace be upon him, he heard only the spoken word. Some have said that what he heard was without letters or sound, and that peace be upon him heard it with all his limbs from all directions. By this one is certain that the one calling was Allah, Exalted is He. From here it has been said that what is meant is: We called him while he was approaching from the side of the blessed Tur, which is a mount beyond the mount of the intellect. Yet the reports contain what calls against this view.

﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾. This is an drawing near of honour, similar to the state of him, peace be upon him, being like one whom a king has brought near for private conversation, chosen for companionship, and with whom intermediaries have been removed between them. Najiyyan is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of mufa'il, like jalis in the sense of mujalis (companion) and nadim in the sense of munadim (boon-companion). Al-munajah is private speech with someone. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from one of the two pronouns of Musa, peace be upon him, in nadaynahu and qarrabnahu. That is, We called him or brought him near while he was conversing in private. Many have said: "elevated", as it is derived from al-najw, which means elevation.

(It has been reported by Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that Jibril, peace be upon him, lifted him up until he heard the scratching of the pen while the Torah was being written for him, that is, a second writing. Otherwise, in the sound hadith concerning the dispute between Adam and Musa, peace be upon them both, it is stated that it was written forty years before the creation of Adam, peace be upon him. The report that he, peace be upon him, was raised to the heavens until he heard the scratching of the pen was transmitted by more than one narrator, and al-Hakim authenticated it from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. On this basis, the Mi'raj is not absolutely exclusive to our Prophet (ﷺ); rather, the most complete Mi'raj belongs to him.) It has also been said that the meaning of najiyyan is naji (one who is saved) through his truthfulness. This was reported from Qatadah, but its remoteness is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 53:

﴿And We bestowed upon him, out of Our mercy﴾ i.e., out of Our mercy toward him, (his brother) i.e., the support of his brother and his assistance, in response to his supplication when he said: ﴿And appoint for me a minister from my family, ﴿Aaron, my brother﴾﴾ — not himself, peace be upon him, because he was older than Moses, peace be upon him, in age, so his existence preceded Moses's existence. And (bestowed) is the object of "We bestowed," and His, the Exalted's, saying "Aaron" is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to it, and His, glorified is He, saying "a prophet" is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) from it. It is also permissible for "min" (out of) to be partitive (li-l-tab'īḍ). It has been said that in that case "(his brother)" is a partial substitution (badal baʿḍ min kull) or a total substitution (badal kull min kull) or an inclusive substitution (badal ishtimāl) from "min." It has been objected that if it is a noun meaning "some of," then this is contrary to what is apparent, and if it is a particle, then substituting a noun for a particle is something not found in their speech. It has also been said: the estimated meaning is "We bestowed upon him something of Our mercy," so "his brother" is a substitution (badal) from the implied "something" (shay'an), and you know that the apparent reading is that it is an object.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 54:

﴿And mention in the Book Isma'il.﴾ The apparent meaning is that he was the son of Ibrahim, peace be upon them both, as the majority of scholars held, and this is the truth. Mentioning him separately from his father and his brother, peace be upon them, serves to show the complete care given to his matter by presenting him on his own. It has been said that he was Isma'il son of Hizqil, whom Allah sent to his people. They flayed the skin of his head, so Allah gave him the choice of whatever punishment he wished to inflict on them. He asked Him to pardon them, and he was content with the reward of the Glorified and entrusted their affair to the Mighty and Majestic, to pardon or punish. The Imamiyyah (the Twelver Shi'is) narrated this from Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, but it is most likely that this is not authentically attributed to him. ﴿Indeed he was true to his promise.﴾ This is a reason for the command, and his being described with this attribute, peace be upon him, is because of the complete fame he had for it.

It has come in some reports that he promised a man that he would wait for him at a place, then he was absent from him for a year. When he came, he said to him: "Have you not moved from your place?" He said: "No, by Allah, I would not break my appointment." It has been said that he was absent for twelve days, and from Muqatil that it was three days, and from Sahl ibn Sa'd that it was one day and one night. The first is the best known. The Imamiyyah also narrated it from Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him. If he was the one who was sacrificed, then it is enough as proof of his truthfulness that he promised his father patience in the face of the slaughter, when he said: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast,﴾ and he fulfilled it.

Some of the intelligent scholars, may their lives be long, said: It is not far-fetched that this is an allusion to this promise, and truthfulness in it is among the greatest that can be imagined.

﴿And he was a messenger and a prophet.﴾ The discussion regarding this is like the discussion regarding the previous verse, except that they said here: this indicates that a messenger (rasul) need not necessarily be a bringer of an independent law (shari'ah), for the sons of Ibrahim, peace be upon them, followed his law, though the opposite is well known. Some even stipulated that he must also be a bearer of a scripture (kitab), but the truth is that this is not necessary. It has also been said that what is meant by being a bringer of a law is that he has a law in relation to the people to whom he was sent, and Isma'il, peace be upon him, was like this, for he was sent to Jurhum with the law of his father, and Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was not sent to them. The problems in this are not hidden.

Page 105

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 55:

﴿And he used to enjoin on his family the prayer and the zakat﴾, giving priority to what is most important, which is that a man, after perfecting himself, should begin with perfecting those who are closest to him. God Most High said: ﴿And warn your nearest kinsfolk﴾, ﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family﴾, ﴿Save yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾; or with the intention of perfecting all of them by perfecting them, because they are a model to be emulated (qudwah).

Al-Hasan said: what is meant by "his family" is his community (ummah), since the Prophet stands in the position of a father to his community. This is supported by the reading in the codex of Abdullah (Mushaf 'Abd Allah): "and he used to enjoin his people". As for the meaning of "the prayer and the zakat", it has been said that their meaning is the well-known one. It has also been said that what is meant by zakat is charity in general. It is related that he, peace be upon him, used to enjoin his family to pray at night and to give charity by day. It has also been said that what is meant by them is the purification and cleansing of the soul. ﴿And he was pleasing to his Lord﴾ because of the uprightness of his words and deeds. It is a passive participle (ism maf'ul), and its original form is marḍuwwun, which was made weak (i'lal) by converting its waw into a ya', since it is a final letter after a sakin waw. So the waw and the ya' came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the waw was changed into a ya', the ya' was assimilated into the ya', and the damma was changed into a kasra.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read (marḍiyyan) without i'lal. It is reported from the Arabs that they said: arḍun musniyatun and musniwatun, meaning land that is irrigated by the sawani (water-wheels).

And mention in the Book Idris (﴿واذْكُرْ في الكِتابِ إدْرِيسَ﴾). He was a prophet before Noah, and between them, according to what is in al-Mustadrak (al-Mustadrak 'ala al-Sahihayn) from Ibn 'Abbas, there were a thousand years. He is Ukhnukh (Enoch), son of Yard, son of Mahla'il, son of Anush, son of Qinan, son of Shith (Seth), son of Adam, peace be upon him. From Wahb ibn Munabbih, he was the grandfather of Noah, peace be upon him. The well-known view, however, is that he was the grandfather of Noah's father, for he was the son of Lamak, son of Mutawshalakh, son of Ukhnukh. He was the first to study the stars and calculation, and God made this one of his miracles, according to what is in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit). He was also the first to write with the pen, the first to sew garments, and the first to wear stitched clothing; he was a tailor. Before him, people used to wear hides. He was the first messenger after Adam, and God sent down to him thirty scrolls (suhuf). He was also the first to make scales, measures, and weapons, and he fought the descendants of Qabil (Cain). From Ibn Mas'ud, he was Ilyas (Elijah), who was sent to his people to say: "There is no god but God," and they may do whatever they wish. They refused and were destroyed. The reliable view, however, is the first, although Ibn Abi Hatim narrated the saying that he was Ilyas, with a sound chain (isnad hasan), from Ibn Mas'ud. This name is Syriac according to most scholars, and it is not derived from al-dars (study), because derivation (al-ishtiqaq) from a non-Arabic word is something no one has said. That it is Arabic and derived from that root is refuted by its being diptote (mana' al-sarf, the grammatical state of not taking tanwin and certain endings). Yes, it is not far-fetched that its meaning in that language was close to that, so he was called by it because of his great study (of scripture). ﴿إنَّهُ كانَ صِدِّيقًا نَبِيًّا﴾ ("Indeed he was a man of truth and a prophet"). As previously mentioned, this is so.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 57:

﴿And We raised him to a lofty station﴾. This is the nobility of prophethood and nearness to God, Exalted is He, as is narrated from al-Hasan. Al-Jubba'i (a Mu'tazili theologian) and Abu Muslim (al-Isfahani, a Qur'anic exegete) also held this view. From Anas, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Ka'b (al-Ahbar) and Mujahid it is said: the fourth heaven. From Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak: the sixth heaven. In another narration from al-Hasan: Paradise, for nothing is higher than Paradise.

It is also narrated from al-Nabigha al-Ja'di that when he recited to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) the poem whose last line is:

*We have reached the heavens with our glory and our eminence, and indeed we hope for a manifestation beyond that.*

[p. 106]

The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "To where is the manifestation, O Abu Layla?" He said: "To Paradise, O Messenger of God." He said: "Indeed, if God, Exalted is He, wills."

It is also narrated from Qatadah that he (peace be upon him) worships God, Exalted is He, along with the angels, peace be upon them, in the seventh heaven, and sometimes roams in Paradise wherever he wishes. Most of those who hold that his raising was physical (hissan) say that he is alive where he was raised. From Muqatil it is narrated that he is dead in the heaven, but this is an anomalous (shadhdh) view.

The cause of his raising, as narrated from Ka'b and others, is that he once passed by on some errand and was struck by the heat of the sun. He said: "O Lord, I walked one day in the sun and was affected by what affected me. How then will it be for one who carries it (the sun) a distance of five hundred years in a single day? O God, lighten its weight and heat from him." When the angel awoke, he found from the lightness and heat of the sun what he did not know, and he said: "O Lord, You created me to carry the sun, so what is the matter You have decreed concerning it?" He said: "Indeed, My servant Idris asked Me to lighten its load and heat from you, and I granted him that." He said: "O Lord, bring me together with him, and make between me and him a friendship." So He gave him permission, until he came to Idris. Then he asked him to raise him to the heaven, and God, Exalted is He, permitted him to do so, and he raised him.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Umar, client of Affrah, who traced the report to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said:

("He said: 'Rather, I am with you, and I take the soul of whoever I am commanded to take the soul of, in the east and west of the earth. The entire world is to me only like a table before a man, from which he takes whatever he wishes.' Then he (Idris) said to him: 'O Angel of Death, I ask you by the One in whom you loved me and for whose sake you loved me, that you grant me a need I ask of you.' He said: 'Ask me, O Prophet of God.' He said: 'I wish that you make me taste death, then return my soul to me.' He said: 'I cannot, except that I seek permission.' So he sought permission from his Lord, Exalted is He, and He permitted him. So he took his soul, then God, Exalted is He, returned it to him. The Angel of Death said to him: 'O Prophet of God, how did you find death?' He said: 'Greater than what I used to be told and to hear.' Then he asked him to show him the Fire, so he went to one of the gates of Hell and called out to some of its guardians. When they knew that he was the Angel of Death, their muscles trembled, and they said: 'Have you been commanded concerning us with a command?' He said: 'If I had been commanded concerning you with a command, I would not have debated with you. But the Prophet of God Idris asked me that you show him a glimpse of the Fire.' So they opened for him a hole the size of a needle's eye, and the heat of it struck him until he fainted. The Angel of Death said: 'Close it!' So they closed it. The Angel of Death began to wipe the face of Idris and say: 'O Prophet of God, Exalted is He, I did not wish that this should be your share from my companionship.' When he recovered, he asked him: 'How did you see it?' He said: 'Greater than what I used to be told and to hear. Indeed Idris was a pious, purified prophet, and he divided his time into two halves: three days he taught people good, and four days he traveled in the earth and worshipped God, Exalted is He, with diligence. From his deed alone there would ascend to heaven good equal to what ascends from all the deeds of the children of Adam.' And the Angel of Death loved him for the sake of God, Exalted is He, so he came to him when he went out for travel and said to him: 'O Prophet of God, I want you to permit me to accompany you.' Idris said to him, not knowing who he was: 'Indeed you will not be able to bear my company.' He said: 'Yes, I hope that God, Exalted is He, will strengthen me for that.' So he went out with him that day, until at the end of the day they passed by a shepherd of goats. The Angel of Death said: 'O Prophet of God, we do not know where we will be at evening. If we took a young goat from these goats and broke our fast on it...' He said to him: 'Do not return to the like of this. Do you invite me to take what is not ours? Where we will be at evening, God, Exalted is He, will bring us sustenance.' When evening came, God, Exalted is He, brought him the provision that used to come to him. He said to the Angel of Death: 'Go forward and eat.' He said: 'No, by the One who honored you with prophethood, I do not desire it.' So he ate alone, and they both stood for prayer. Idris became weary and drowsy, but the angel did not become weary nor drowsy. He was amazed at him, and his worship seemed small in his eyes compared with what he saw. Then they both rose in the morning and traveled. When the end of the day came, they passed by a vineyard, and he said to him the same as he had said at first. When they reached evening, God, Exalted is He, brought him the provision, and he invited him to eat, but he did not eat, and they stood for prayer. The matter between them was as it had been at first. Then Idris said to him: 'No, by the One in whose hand is my soul, you are not from the children of Adam.' He said: 'Yes, I am not one of them.' And he mentioned to him that he was the Angel of Death. He said: 'Have you been commanded concerning me with a command?' He said: 'If I had been commanded concerning you with a command, I would not have debated with you. But I love you for the sake of God, Exalted is He, and I accompanied you for His sake.' He said to him: 'While you have been with me this period, you have not taken the soul of anyone from creation.'")

[p. 107]

(He said:) "Rather, I am with you..." (the same report continues) ... When they opened for him, he was struck by its coolness, its fragrance and its scent, which captivated his heart. He said: "O Angel of Death, I wish to enter Paradise and eat one morsel of its fruits and drink one sip of its water, for perhaps that would be more intense for my desire and longing." He entered and ate and drank. The Angel of Death said to him: "Come out, O Prophet of God, Exalted is He, you have attained your need, so that God, Mighty and Majestic, may return you with the prophets, peace be upon them, on the Day of Resurrection." He embraced the trunk of one of its trees and said: "I will not come out. If you wish to dispute with me, I will dispute with you." God, Exalted is He, revealed to the Angel of Death: "Judge the dispute between them." He said to him: "With what do you dispute with me, O Prophet of God, Exalted is He?" Idris said: God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾ and I have tasted it. He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿There is none of you but will pass through it﴾ and I have passed through it. He, Majestic and Exalted, said concerning the people of Paradise: ﴿And they will not be removed from it﴾. So I will not come out from something that God, Mighty and Majestic, has brought to me." God, Exalted is He, revealed to the Angel of Death: "My servant Idris has defeated you. By My might and My majesty, it is in My pre-eternal knowledge that it should be so. So leave him, for he has argued against you with a strong proof."

(The report ends.) God, Exalted is He, knows best its soundness, and likewise the soundness of what precedes it from the report of Ka'b. This raising, because it implies the exaltedness of rank and loftiness of station, contained in it that which is praise. Otherwise, mere raising to a high place physically is nothing:

*So the fire is overtopped by smoke, and often the dust is overtopped by the turbans of horsemen.*

Some have claimed that the closer view is that the elevation is physical, because an elevation linked with a place cannot be figurative. It has been objected that this is open to question, since the like of it occurs, and even something more evident than it, such as his saying:

*And be in a place where, if you fall, you will stand up with your leg in safety.*

So reflect.

(أُولَئِكَ) is a demonstrative referring to those mentioned in the noble surah, and the distance implied in it indicates the elevated status of these people and the exalted rank they hold in virtue. It is the subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and His saying, ﴿those upon whom Allah bestowed favor﴾, that is, with the various kinds of religious and worldly blessings, as has been hinted at in summary form, is its predicate (*khabar*, the grammatical predicate), according to what al-Andalusi (Abu Hayyan) in *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*, "The Surging Sea") considered most likely. The restriction (*hasr*, exclusivity) according to the one who holds this view is relative, with respect to non-prophets, because those who remain are known for being those upon whom favor was bestowed, so the bestowing of favor on others is treated as if it did not exist. It has also been said that a noun is to be understood before it, meaning: some of those upon whom Allah bestowed favor. His saying, ﴿of the prophets﴾, is an explanation of the relative clause (*bayan*, an explicative specification of the relative pronoun). It has also been said that *min* is partitive (*tab'idiyyah*, indicating a part of a whole), based on the view that what is meant is those mentioned, upon whom Allah the Exalted bestowed the known blessings mentioned here. In that case the subject and predicate are restricted to those you have heard about, and they are some of the prophets. The generality of the concept meant by the predicate, considered in itself and as it exists in the mind, does not preclude that a particular matter in external reality is intended by it, as is not hidden. It was preferred to take the definite article in the predicate as generic (*jins*, referring to the whole category) for emphasis, as in His saying, ﴿That is the Book﴾, and the objection is removed by what we have mentioned. As for *min* in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿of the offspring of Adam﴾, it has been said that it is explicative, and the prepositional phrase is a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for the earlier prepositional phrase, and the prepositional phrase is a substitute for the prepositional phrase with the preposition repeated. This is a partial substitution (*badal ba'd min kull*) based on the view that what is meant by its offspring are the prophets, and this does not include Adam, peace be upon him. Its remoteness is not hidden. It has also been said that it is partitive, because the one upon whom favor was bestowed is more specific than the offspring in one respect, since the offspring include, according to the apparent and immediate meaning of the word, those other than the one upon whom favor was bestowed, and it does not conflict with this that it is more general than them in one respect, since it includes Adam and the angel, and the believers among the jinn, but not the offspring. ﴿And of those whom We carried with Noah﴾, meaning: and of the offspring of those whom We carried with him, peace be upon him, specifically, and they are all except Idris, peace be upon him, because of what you have heard, that he was before Noah and Abraham, peace be upon them both, and by consensus he was of the offspring of Sam son of Noah, peace be upon them both. ﴿And of the offspring of Abraham﴾, and they are the rest.

(Israel) is coordinated (*'atf*, conjunction-linked) with (Abraham), meaning: and of the offspring of Israel, that is Jacob, peace be upon him. Among them were Moses, Aaron, Zechariah, John, and Jesus, peace be upon them all. The verse contains evidence that the children of daughters are included in the offspring, since Jesus, peace be upon him, is included though he had no father. Taking the term "offspring" for him by way of predominance (*taghlib*, applying a term to a case by extension because of a dominant element) is contrary to the apparent meaning. ﴿And of those whom We guided and chose﴾ is coordinated with His saying, ﴿of the offspring of Adam﴾, and *min* is partitive, meaning: and of the totality of those whom We guided to the truth and chose for prophethood and honor.

It has been permitted that it be coordinated with His saying, glorified is He, ﴿of the prophets﴾, with *min* explicative. It was objected to this that the apparent sense of coordination is difference, so it is necessary to say that what is meant is: those for whom We combined prophethood, guidance, and being chosen for honor, and this is contrary to the apparent meaning. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿When the verses of the Most Merciful are recited to them, they fell down in prostration and weeping﴾, is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence beginning independently), brought to explain their fear of Allah the Exalted and their humility before Him, glorified is He, together with their high rank, lofty station, nobility of lineage, perfection of soul, and nearness to Allah, mighty is His authority.

It has been said that it is a predicate after a predicate for the demonstrative. It has also been said that the speech ended at His saying, the Exalted, (and Israel), and His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and of those whom We guided﴾, is the predicate of an omitted subject, and this clause is a qualifier (*sifah*, adjective) of that omitted subject, meaning: and of those whom We guided and chose are a people who, when the verses are recited to them, etc. This was reported from Abu Muslim. Some of the Imamiyya narrated from Ali ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: "It is we who are meant by these people." It is not hidden that this is extremely contrary to the apparent meaning, and the state of the narrations of the Imamiyya is not hidden from those who understand distinction. The apparent practice of some of the verifiers is to choose that the relative clause be a qualifier of the demonstrative, as is common after a demonstrative, and this clause is the predicate, because that is more praiseworthy for them. The reason for this is clear to one who knows the rules of qualifiers and predicates.

*Sujjadan* is the plural of *sajid* (one prostrating), and likewise (*bukiyyan*) is the plural of *baki* (one weeping), like *shahid* and *shuhud*. Its original form was *bukuwwa*; the *waw* and *ya'* came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the *waw* was changed into *ya'*, the *ya'* was assimilated into the *ya'*, and the *kaf* was vocalized with a kasra to harmonize with the *ya'*. Its regular plural is *bukat*, like *kirām* and *rumāt*, except that it is not attested, according to what is in *al-Bahr*, and this contradicts what is in *al-Qamus* and elsewhere. Some have permitted that it be a verbal noun (*masdar*) of *baka* (to weep), like *julusan*, the verbal noun of *jalasa* (to sit). This is contrary to the apparent meaning. Yes, perhaps what Ibn Abi al-Dunya recorded in *al-Buka'* and Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, suggests it: that he recited Surah Maryam, prostrated, and then said, "This is the prostration; so where is the weeping?" Ibn Atiyya claimed that this is definite in the reading of Abdullah, Yahya, al-A'mash, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i, (*bikiyyan*) with a kasra on its first letter. This is not as he claimed, because that is assimilation (*ittiba'*, a vowel harmonizing with a following vowel), and it is apparent that it does not specify the verbal noun.

The accusative of the two nouns is the circumstantial state (*hal*) from the subject of (they fell), meaning: prostrating and weeping. The first is a provisional circumstance (*hal muqaddarah*), as al-Zajjaj said. The apparent meaning is that by prostration is meant its legal sense, and by the verses is meant what the heavenly books contain, whether it includes mention of prostration or not, and whether it includes mention of the punishment sent down on the disbelievers or not. From here the verse has been used as evidence for the recommendation of prostration and weeping when reciting the Qur'an.

Ibn Majah, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, and al-Bazzar recorded in their *Musnads*, from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Recite the Qur'an and weep; and if you do not weep, then feign weeping." It has also been said that by prostration is meant the prostration of recitation, according to what we have been commanded to do upon hearing some Qur'anic verses. Then by the verses of the Most Merciful are meant specific verses containing mention of prostration. It has also been said that by it is meant prayer, and this is an extremely weak view. It has also been said that by it is meant humility and submission, and by the verses is meant what contains the punishment sent down on the disbelievers, and this is close to the previous view. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti transmitted from al-Razi that he used the verse as evidence for the obligation of the prostration of recitation, and this, as al-Kiya said, is remote. They have mentioned that the one prostrating should supplicate in his prostration with what fits the content of the verse. So here he says: "O Allah,

[p. 109]

make me among Your servants who have been favored, the guided, who prostrate to You and weep when Your verses are recited." In the verse of the Night Journey he says: "O Allah, make me among those who weep toward You and are humbled before You." In the verse of the Prostration (Surah al-Sajdah) he says: "O Allah, make me among those who prostrate to Your face, glorifying You with Your praise and Your mercy, and I seek refuge in You from being among those who are arrogant toward Your command."

Abdullah, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Shibl ibn Abbad, Abu Haywa, Abdullah ibn Ahmad al-Ijli, from Hamza, Qutayba in one transmission, Warsh in the transmission of al-Nahhas, and Ibn Dhakwan in the transmission of al-Taghlibi read (*yutla*) with the underlined *ya'* (third person masculine), because the feminine is not real (*ghayr haqiqi*, a grammatical feminine not referring to a biologically female entity), and because there is an intervening element (the pronoun *alayhim*).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 59:

﴿Then there succeeded them an evil successor﴾, meaning that after them came an evil offspring. The well-known usage is that *khalf* with a sukun on the lam (*khalf*) has this sense, while *khalf* with a fatha on the lam (*khalaf*) is its opposite. Abu Hatim said: "*khalf* with a sukun means offspring, and the singular and plural are the same in it, while with a fatha it means a replacement, whether a son or other than a son." Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "*khalf*, whether vocalised or with a sukun, means a bad generation, but for a good one only the vocalised form is used." Ibn Jarir said: "Most of what is used in praise has a fatha on the lam, and in blame it has a sukun, though it may be reversed." The use of the fatha form in blame is shown in the verse of Labid:

*They have gone, those among whom one lived in their shelter,*
*and I remain in a khalf like the hide of a mangy camel.*

﴿They neglected the prayer﴾. Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud), al-Hasan, Abu Razin al-Uqayli, al-Dahhak and Ibn Miqsam read *al-salawat* (the prayers) in the plural, which is clear. The singular is perhaps used because the category is the same. As for what is meant by neglecting it, it is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i, al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymirah, Mujahid, Ibrahim, and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that it means delaying it past its time. This was also related by the Imamiyyah (the Twelver Shi'i school) from Abu Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him). Al-Zajjaj chose that neglecting it means failing to meet its conditions, including its time and other requirements. It was also said that it means performing it not in congregation. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that neglecting it means abandoning it. It was also said that it means not believing it to be obligatory. According to this view, the verse concerns the disbelievers, and regarding the preceding verses there is no certainty. It was inferred that it applies to Muslim people, on the basis that disbelievers are not obligated to the subsidiary rulings (*furu'*), unless it is said that what is meant is that it is their habit, so reflect on this. As for the preceding verses, they concern Muslim people with no disagreement.

It is well known from Ibn Abbas and Muqatil that the verse concerns the Jews, and from al-Suddi that it concerns them and the Christians. Its applying to disbelievers in general was preferred, for reasons that will come shortly, God willing, and Hasan based on this the placement of the narration of the words of Jibril (peace be upon him) that follows. That it concerns Muslim people of this community is reported from Mujahid, Qatadah, Ata and others, who said: "They will come when the righteous have passed away, rushing into fornication, mounting one another in the alleys like cattle, not ashamed before people and not fearing Allah the Exalted."

﴿And followed their desires﴾, that is, they plunged into various kinds of sins. In *al-Bahr* (the tafsir of Abu Hayyan), *al-shahawat* (the desires) is general to every appetite that distracts from the prayer and from the remembrance of Allah the Exalted. Some counted among these the marriage to a half-sister from the father's side. This is on the view that the verse covers the Jews, because it is said that this is part of their religion, but this is not correct. What is established from them is that they permit marriage to a brother's daughter, a sister's daughter, and the like.

It is reported from Ali (may Allah ennoble his face): "Whoever builds the lofty, rides the showy, and wears the famous..."

﴿So they will meet error﴾. Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and others transmitted from the hadith of Abu Umamah, traced to the Prophet, that: "It is a river at the bottom of Hell in which flows the pus of the people of the Fire. In it, if a rock the weight of ten 'ushrawat were hurled from the brink of Hell, it would not reach its bottom in seventy autumns. Then it ends in *ghayy* and *athama*." From this is known the secret of the expression "they will meet", with *sawfa* (will).

Page 110

A group transmitted through several chains from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "*al-Ghayy* is a river or a valley in Hell, of pus, deep in its bottom and foul in taste, into which those who follow their desires are cast." Al-Kirmani mentioned that it is wells in Hell into which pus and matter flow.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah that *al-ghayy* is evil. From this is the saying of Muraqqish al-Asghar:

*Whoever meets good, people praise his affair,*
*and whoever goes astray will not lack one who blames him for the error.*

It is also reported from Ibn Zayd that it is misguidance, which is the well-known meaning. On this basis it was said that what is meant is the reward of error. This was reported from al-Dahhak and chosen by al-Zajjaj. It was also said that what is meant is error away from the path of Paradise. It was recited, as al-Akhfash transmitted, as *yulaqqawna* (with a damma on the ya, a fatha on the lam, and a shadda on the qaf).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 60:

﴿Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds﴾ is an exception that is disjunctive (munqati') according to al-Zajjaj (munqati' (disjunctive exception), i.e., the exception is not of the same kind as what precedes it). Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: its apparent meaning is that it is connected (muttasil) (muttasil (connected exception), i.e., of the same kind as what precedes it). This is supported by the mention of faith, and by the fact that the verse concerns disbelievers or is general to them and to others, since one who believes is not described as such unless he was previously a disbeliever, except figuratively for the sake of emphasis. Taking faith to mean perfect faith is contrary to the apparent meaning. Likewise is the view that the intended meaning is "except one who combines repentance and faith." It has also been said that by faith is meant prayer (salah), as in the words of God Most High: ﴿And God would not let your faith go to waste﴾ and the mention of it is in contrast to neglecting prayer, while the mention of righteous deeds is in contrast to following desires. ﴿Those﴾ who are described with repentance, faith and righteous deeds ﴿will enter Paradise﴾ by the necessary force of the binding promise. And there is no hidden grace in omitting any delay while mentioning "those."

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr and Ya'qub read ﴿yudkhalun﴾ (they will be made to enter) in the passive voice from adkhala (to cause to enter). Ibn Ghazwan, on the authority of Talhah, read ﴿sayadkhulun﴾ (they will enter) with the future particle sin, in the active voice. ﴿And they will not be wronged in the least﴾ means they will not be deprived of any of the reward of their deeds, or they will not be diminished in any way at all. In this there is a warning that their former act does not harm them and does not diminish their rewards. The Mu'tazilah used this verse as evidence that deeds are a condition for entering Paradise. It is answered that the intended meaning is ﴿they will enter Paradise﴾ without delay, as indicated by the contrast, and this is by treating the time preceding entry, during which they are preserved from what befalls others, as if it were non-existence; so deeds are a condition for this entry, not for entry absolutely. Also, it is possible that it is a condition for entering the Garden of Eden specifically, not for entry into Paradise in general. It has been said that it is a condition for not losing anything of the reward of deeds, and this, as you see, is weak. Others have said other things. Some objected to the conditional view, saying that it would follow that one who repents and believes but is unable to perform righteous deeds would not enter Paradise. It is answered that this is among the rare cases, and rulings are attached to what is general and usual, so reflect.

﴿Jannāti ʿadnin﴾ (Gardens of Eden) is a substitute (badal) for ﴿al-Jannah﴾ (the Garden), a substitute of part (badal al-baʿḍ, partial substitution), because the Garden includes them, the inclusion of the whole over the part (ishtimāl). This is based on what has been said: that ﴿Jannāti ʿadnin﴾ is a proper name (ʿalam) for one of the eight Gardens, like the proper nouns Banāt Awbar (the name of a tribe or a place).

It has also been said that the proper name is Jannat ʿAdnin, but the second element was placed, after the first was omitted, in the position of the whole, as in Shahru Ramaḍān and Ramaḍān. The original form was therefore Jannāti Jannati ʿAdnin. What makes this substitution acceptable is that the definiteness of the construct (manqūl iḍāfī) is considered in its second element, as though it had been transferred alone, as established in its place in the detailed grammar books.

In al-Kashshāf (of al-Zamakhsharī): when naming with a construct phrase (muḍāf wa muḍāf ilayhi), they treat the second term (muḍāf ilayhi) in such constructions as having an implied proper-name status, because the usual practice in their speech in this matter is the annexation to proper names and kunyas (patronymics). When they annex to other than these, they treat it in the manner of those, such as Abū Turāb. Do you not see that they do not permit the insertion of the definite article (al-) in Ibn Dāyah and Abū Turāb, but they require it in such examples as Imru' al-Qays and Mā' al-Samā', all of this in view of the fact that it does not change from its state, like a proper name, to the end of what is in it?

This also indicates that it is not declined (mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf) in Banāt Awbar, Abī Qatarah, Ibn Dāyah and so on. So ﴿Jannāti ʿadnin﴾ is definite according to both views: according to the first, by virtue of its being a proper name; according to the second, by virtue of the aforementioned annexation. Even though ʿadn was not originally a proper name nor definite, but is rather the verbal noun (maṣdar) of ʿadana bil-makān, yaʿdinu and yaʿdunu, meaning "he dwelt in the place."

Considering that ʿadn before the compounding was a proper name for one of the Gardens requires that the annexation in "Jannat ʿAdn" be an annexation of the more general absolutely to the more specific, based on the view that what is understood from "al-Jannah" is the known place, not trees and the like. Such annexation is not absolutely good: some of it is good, like "shajar al-arāk" (the tree of the miswak) and "Madīnat Baghdād," and some of it is ugly, like "insān Zayd." There is no difference between these except taste, which is not precisely defined.

It is also permitted that ʿadn be a proper name for ʿadn in the sense of dwelling, like siḥr being a proper name for magic, and ams for yesterday. The definiteness of ﴿Jannāt﴾ is also evident on this view. They only said this to validate the substitution, because if the definiteness were not considered, it would require substituting an indefinite noun for a definite noun, and according to the view of the one who said it, this is not permitted except when the indefinite noun is qualified. The qualifying relation is supported by the verse ﴿allatī waʿada al-Raḥmānu ʿibādahu﴾ (which the Most Merciful promised to His servants).

Abū Ḥayyān permitted considering ﴿Jannāti ʿadnin﴾ as indefinite, in the sense of gardens of dwelling and settlement, and said: the claim that ʿadn is a proper name for the meaning of "ʿadn" needs a revelation (tawqīf) and transmission from the Arabs, together with what is in that which suggests the requirement of indeclinability (binā'). Likewise the claim of personal proper-name status in it. The impermissibility of substituting an indefinite noun for a definite one except when qualified is something the Baghdadis said, and they are refuted by transmitted usage. The view of the Basrans is that substitution is permitted even if the indefinite noun is not qualified. Abū ʿAlī said: that is permitted when substituting an indefinite noun gives a benefit not derived from the noun being substituted, and the substitution is not thereby fixed, since the accusative is permitted by way of praise (naṣb ʿalā al-madḥ). Likewise, the relative clause is not fixed as a qualifier, since substitution is permitted. End of quotation, with slight addition.

The substitution of the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) has been criticised on the grounds that it has the status of a derived noun (mushtaqq), and they have stated explicitly that substituting a derived noun is weak. Perhaps Abū Ḥayyān does not accept this. Then he permitted ﴿Jannāti ʿadnin﴾ to be a substitute of the whole (badal kull). Likewise he permitted it to be an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān). The clause ﴿lā yuẓlamūna﴾ (they will not be wronged) is in the two cases of substitution. The conjunction is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

Al-Ḥasan, Abū Ḥaywah, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, al-Aʿmash and Aḥmad ibn Mūsā, from Abū ʿAmr, read ﴿Jannātu ʿadnin﴾ with the nominative (rafʿ). Abū Ḥayyān explained it as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "those are gardens"; others explained it as a subject whose predicate is the relative clause. Al-Ḥasan ibn Ḥayy and ʿAlī ibn Ṣāliḥ read ﴿Jannata ʿadnin﴾ with the accusative and in the singular. It was also transmitted from al-Aʿmash, and it is so in the codex (muṣḥaf) of ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd).

Al-Yamānī, al-Ḥasan in one transmission, and Isḥāq al-Azraq from Ḥamzah read ﴿Jannatu ʿadnin﴾ with the nominative and in the singular, and the returning pronoun to the relative pronoun is omitted, i.e., "which the Most Merciful promised it." The mention of the title "the Most Merciful" is to signal that His promise of it and its fulfilment come from the completeness of the vastness of His mercy, glory be to Him and exalted. The preposition bi- in His saying, mighty and majestic, ﴿bil-ghayb﴾ (in the unseen), indicates accompaniment (mulābasah), and it is connected to a hidden element that is a circumstantial clause from the returning pronoun, or from ﴿ʿibādahu﴾ (His servants). That is: He promised it to them accompanied by, or they being accompanied by, the unseen, i.e., it being absent from them and not present, or they being absent from it and not seeing it. Or the preposition indicates causation (sababiyyah), and it is connected to "waʿada" (promised), i.e., He promised it to them because of their believing in the unseen and faith in it. It has also been said that it is the complement of ﴿ʿibādahu﴾, in the sense of those who worship Him, glory be to Him, in secret, i.e., privately; and that, as you see, is weak.

﴿Innahu﴾ (indeed He, i.e., the Most Merciful) — it is permitted that the pronoun be for the matter of the situation (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), ﴿kāna waʿduhu﴾ (His promise was), i.e., His promised thing, glory be to Him, which is the Gardens, as narrated from Ibn Jurayj; or His promised thing being whatever it was, so that what was mentioned enters into it at the first level, as has been said. It is also permitted to keep "waʿd" (promise) as a verbal noun and apply it to what was mentioned, for emphasis.

The expression with kāna (was) is to indicate the certainty of its occurrence, i.e., that was ﴿maʾtiyyan﴾ (coming), i.e., it comes to him of a promise made to him without doubt. It has been said that ﴿maʾtiyyan﴾ is a passive participle in the sense of an active participle, i.e., coming. It has been said that it is a passive form from atā ilayhi iḥsānan, i.e., he did to him what is counted as kindness and goodness, and the promise is in its literal sense.

The meaning of its being passive is that it is executed (munjazan), because the verb of promising, after its issuance and existence, is only its execution (tanjīz), i.e., that His promise to His servants was executed.

﴿They hear therein no idle talk﴾: vain speech with no benefit in it. Rather, it is like *al-lighaa'* (the chirping), which is the sound of sparrows and similar birds.

The statement is a metaphor (*kinaayah*) for the fact that idle talk does not come from its people. It also alerts the reader that idle talk is something one should avoid in this world as far as possible. Mujahid explained *al-laghw* as speech that includes abuse, meaning that they do not revile one another. However, the general meaning is preferable.

﴿except "Peace"﴾ is a disjunctive exception (*istithnaa' munqati'*, an exception not of the same kind as what precedes it). "Peace" (*salaaman*) may be taken in its well-known sense, meaning: but they hear the angels greeting them with peace, or some of them greeting others with peace. Or it may mean speech free from defect and imperfection, meaning: but they hear speech free from defect and imperfection. It has also been permitted that the exception be a connected one (*muttasil*), and this is an emphasis of praise through something resembling blame, as in the verse of the poet:

*"There is no fault in them, except that their swords are notched from the clashing of battalions."*

This construction conveys the negation of hearing idle talk by the strongest demonstrative method. On this reading the connection is hypothetical: the meaning is, "Were it not for that, it would not have fallen into its place of beauty and emphasis." It has also been said that the exception is connected, with "peace" meaning the supplication for safety from afflictions. Since the people of Paradise have no need of that, because there is no affliction in it, the greeting would be idle in outward appearance, though not in reality, when considered in terms of its purpose, which is honouring and displaying mutual affection. For this reason it is fitting for the people of Paradise.

﴿And for them is their provision therein, morning and evening﴾: this is in the manner of those who live in luxury in this world. Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Yahya ibn Kathir, who said: "The Arabs in his time had only one meal. Whoever obtained two meals was called 'So-and-so the Pampered.' So Allah the Exalted sent this down, encouraging His servants toward what is with Him."

Something similar is reported from al-Hasan. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the continuity and abundance of their provision, since there is no morning or evening in Paradise. However, some reports state that the people of Paradise know the measure of night by the lowering of veils and the closing of doors, and know the measure of day by the raising of veils and the opening of doors.

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi reported in *Nawadir al-Usul* through the chain of Aban, from al-Hasan and Abu Qilabah, who both said: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is there night in Paradise?' He said: 'What has moved you to this?' He said: 'I heard Allah the Exalted mention in the Book: ﴿And for them is their provision therein, morning and evening﴾, and I said: night is part of the morning and the evening.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'There is no night there; rather, there is light and radiance. Morning comes after evening and evening after morning. The gifts of Allah the Exalted come to them at the times of the prayers they used to perform in the world, and the angels greet them with peace.'"

[Page 113]

﴿That is the Garden which We shall bequeath from among Our servants, those who were God-fearing.﴾ It is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*, a sentence newly begun, not grammatically dependent on what precedes it), brought in to magnify the status of the Garden and to specify its people. The demonstrative *tilka* is the subject (*mubtada'*), and *al-jannah* (the Garden) is its predicate (*khabar*). The relative clause is a qualifier of it, and the sentence following the relative pronoun is its complement (*silah*). The returning pronoun is omitted, meaning "We shall bequeath it."

In accordance with this, al-A'mash, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Qatada, Ruways, Humayd, Ibn Abi Abla, Abu Haywa, and Mahbub (from Abu 'Amr) read *nuwarrithu* (نُوَرِّثُ) with a fatha on the *waw* and a shaddah on the *ra'*. The intended meaning is that We preserve it for the one who was God-fearing, from the fruit of his piety, and We grant him enjoyment of it, just as the heir is left the property of the one who bequeathed it and is allowed to enjoy it. Thus *al-iritha* (inheritance) is used metaphorically for preservation. The choice of this word over other expressions that convey the same idea, such as sale or gift, is because it is the most complete form of ownership, in that it is not followed by cancellation, reclaiming, or annulment.

It has also been said: the God-fearing inherit from the Garden the dwellings that were meant for the people of the Fire had they believed.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Shawdhab, who said: "There is no one except that he has in the Garden a dwelling and spouses. When the Day of Resurrection comes, God, exalted is He, bequeaths to the believer so-and-so many dwellings from the dwellings of the disbelievers." This is the meaning of His words, exalted is He: ﴿That is the Garden which We shall bequeath﴾, to the end of the verse. It is not hidden that this, if a report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is authentically transmitted concerning it, then it is to be accepted wholeheartedly. Otherwise, it has been said against it that it is weak, because it indicates that only part of the Garden is inherited, whereas the sublime wording indicates that all of it is so. Also, inheritance points to a prior ownership, which is not supposed here, and there is no need for such supposition here. However, it has been objected that it suffices for inheritance that the thing inherited existed, but on the condition of piety, according to what some have held regarding His words, exalted is He: ﴿Gardens of Eden, which the Most Merciful promised to His servants﴾, where he said: the intended meaning of "servants" includes the God-fearing believer and others, and the promise to the non-God-fearing believer is conditioned on faith and piety. Yes, the majority have chosen that the intended meaning of "servants" there is the God-fearing, and the intended meaning of them here is the more general. The intended meaning of "those who were God-fearing" is those who believed and did righteous deeds, as has been said. The verse contains no indication that anyone else is absolutely excluded from entering the Garden.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from Dawud ibn Abi Hind that it refers to the one who professes God's oneness (*muwahhid*). So reflect upon this, and do not be heedless.

[p. 114]

﴿And We do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ is a quotation of the words of Jibril, may the blessings and peace of Allah the Exalted be upon him. It is narrated that he withheld himself from the Prophet (ﷺ) for days, when he was asked about the story of the People of the Cave, Dhul-Qarnayn and the Spirit, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) did not know how to answer. He grieved and it weighed heavily upon him. The polytheists said: "His Lord has forsaken him and abandoned him." When (Jibril) descended, the Prophet (peace be upon him) said to him: "O Jibril, you withheld yourself from me until my thoughts became bad and I longed for you." He said: "I was more eager (to come), but I am a servant who is commanded. When I am sent, I descend, and when I am held back, I withhold." Then Allah the Exalted sent down this verse and the surah of al-Duha. So said more than one scholar. Thus it is a connection of one narrative to another, according to what al-Khafaji said.

In al-Kashshaf, the reason this verse is placed in this position is that when Allah the Exalted had finished the accounts of the prophets, peace be upon them, as a consolation to him (ﷺ), and as a warning concerning what the successors (al-khuluf) introduced after them, and He had excepted the righteous successors and mentioned the reward of both groups, He followed it with the narration of Jibril's descent and what the polytheists had accused him of, namely that his Lord, glory be to Him, had bid him farewell. This was an increase in consolation, and an indication that the matter is not as these successors claimed. It also incorporated its relevance to the discourse on piety, by indicating that they (the angels) are commanded in movement and rest, submissive and entrusted, as a kindness to him and to his community (ﷺ). For this reason, He stated after it: ﴿So worship Him and be steadfast in His worship﴾. And in it is the meaning that you should not care about the words of those who oppose you until you meet your Lord in happiness. He connected to it the saying of the disbelievers, to clarify the difference between the two sayings, and between the state of the infallible angel and the state of the ignorant, wrongdoing human. Thus it is a digression resembling an interjection, well placed. End of quotation.

This does not contradict what was mentioned about the occasion of revelation, which Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and a group reported regarding its cause from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Jibril (peace be upon him): 'What prevents you from visiting us more often than you visit us?' Then ﴿And We do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ was revealed." This is possible because the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) may have said that in the course of his earlier conversation as well, and each narration mentioned only one part of what occurred in the conversation. It has also been said that the descent may have been repeated. Yes, what was mentioned in the explanation (of the connection) is appropriate only according to some of the previous narrations concerning the meaning of "the successors who neglected the prayer and followed their desires."

Some have said: the implied meaning is this: Jibril said, "And we do not descend," etc. Through this the goodness of the connection becomes apparent, and its aspect. This was refuted by saying that it has no real benefit. Al-Naqqash related from a people that the verse is connected to the earlier words of Jibril (peace be upon him): ﴿I am only a messenger of your Lord, to grant you a pure boy﴾. This view is far below the level of acceptance.

Al-Tanazzul means descending gradually, because it is the reflexive form (mutawi') of nazala. One says nazzaltuhu, so tanazzala. It may also be used in the general sense of descending, just as nazala is used in the sense of anzala (to cause to descend). On this basis is the verse of the poet:

"You are not of mankind, but of an angel who has descended from the air of the sky, pouring down (rain)."

Since there is no effect of gradualness in the poet's intention. The meaning is: "We do not descend at one time after another except by the command of Allah, according to what His wisdom requires, glory be to Him." Al-A'raj recited (وما يَتَنَزَّلُ) with the ya' (third person), and the pronoun refers to the revelation, by the context of the situation and the occasion of revelation, and the speech is for Jibril (peace be upon him). It has also been said that the pronoun refers to him (Jibril, peace be upon him) and the speech is for Him, Mighty and Majestic. He, glory be to Him, informed that Jibril does not descend except by His command, saying: ﴿To Him belongs what is before us﴾, meaning what is in front of us of future time, ﴿and what is behind us﴾, meaning past time, ﴿and what is between that﴾, meaning the present time mentioned. So we do not descend in one time rather than another except by His command and will, Mighty and Majestic.

Ibn Jurayj said: what is before us is what passed of time before creation; what is behind us is what comes after their death until the continuation of the Hereafter; and what is between them is the duration of life. Abu al-'Aliyah said: what is before us is the whole of this world up to the first blast; what is behind it is the Hereafter from the time of resurrection; and what is between them is what is between the two blasts, which is forty years. In the book al-Tahrir wal-Tahbir: what is before us is the Hereafter, and what is behind us is this world. Al-'Awfi related this from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Muqatil and Sufyan also said this. Al-Akhfash said: what is before us is what was before creation; what is behind us is what is after annihilation; and what is between is what is between this world and the Hereafter. So the possibilities according to these sayings are the various ranges of time.

The author of al-Fanniyan said: what is before us is the sky, what is behind us is the earth, and what is between is what is between the earth and the sky. It was said: what is before us is the earth, and what is behind us is the sky. It was also said: what is before us is the place to which they move, what is behind us is the place from which they move, and what is between is the place where they currently are. So the possibilities are various places. Some chose to interpret these terms as encompassing both time and place, and the intended meaning is that He, Exalted, is the owner of all of that, so we do not move from one place to another, nor descend at one time rather than another, except by His permission, Mighty and Majestic.

Al-Baghawi said: the intended meaning is that to Him belongs knowledge of what is before us, etc., that is, we do not advance to what is not in accordance with His wisdom, glory and exalted be He.

Some chose the generalization, that is, to Him, glory be to Him, belongs all of that by ownership and knowledge. ﴿And your Lord is never forgetful﴾, that is, He does not abandon His prophets, peace be upon them. And the Prophet (ﷺ) is included in this inclusion in the first place: that is, the non-descent was only due to the absence of a command for it, and it was not due to Allah the Exalted abandoning you or bidding you farewell, as the disbelievers claimed. Rather, it was for a far-reaching wisdom. It has also been said: forgetfulness is to be taken in its literal sense, meaning that He, glory be to Him, because of the all-encompassing extent of His knowledge and His dominion, is not subject to heedlessness or forgetfulness such that He would neglect you or the revelation to you. Rather, the delay in revelation was for a wisdom known to Him, exalted be His majesty. The first meaning was preferred, because this meaning is not permissible for Him, glory be to Him, so there is no need to negate it from Him, Mighty and Majestic, together with the fact that the first meaning is the more suitable to the occasion of revelation.

The second was preferred on the ground that it is more suitable to the intensive form (of the word), for it is, with regard to abundance, connected to the one who supposes that it applies to Him, and it is more complete on the second view, together with what this entails of keeping the word in its literal meaning. Many times the Qur'an negates what is not permissible for Him, glory be to Him, and exalted be He. But there is room for examination in this. Yes, there is no doubt that the second meaning is the more evident, and the matter of its suitability to the occasion of revelation is easy. In the repetition of the name of the Lord, which indicates the communication of perfection that befits Him, attached to the pronoun referring to him (peace be upon him), there is an honour to him (ﷺ) and an indication of the cause of the ruling, which is not hidden.

Abu Muslim and Ibn Bahr said: the beginning of the verse up to ﴿and what is between that﴾ is the speech of the righteous when they enter Paradise. The "descent" in it is from descending in a place. The meaning is: "We do not settle in Paradise and take it as dwellings except by the command of your Lord, Exalted, and His kindness. He, glory be to Him, is the owner of all matters, the past, the awaited, and the present. So what we have found, and what we are finding, is of His kindness and bounty." His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿And your Lord was never forgetful﴾ is an affirmation from Him, Exalted, of their saying, that is: "He, glory be to Him, did not abandon the reward of the worlds, nor was He forgetful of their deeds and the reward for them, as He promised, Majestic and Exalted." In this, the interpretation of "descent" as mentioned is against the apparent meaning. Also, its implication would be "by the command of our Lord," because the address to the Prophet (ﷺ), as in the first view, is not apparent, unless Allah the Exalted related it according to its meaning, since their Lord and his Lord is one. Had it been related according to their wording, it would have said "our Lord." It was related in this manner only to make it a preparation for what follows. That this is an address by a group of the righteous to one of them is far-fetched, and likewise ﴿And your Lord was never forgetful﴾, since it did not say "their Lord." Also, this does not agree with the occasion of revelation in any way. It seems that the one who chose it did so in order to make the speech fit with what precedes it and to show its connection to it. It has been confirmed that I am free from resorting to it for this purpose.

[p. 116 of the original edition is marked here.]

And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾, is an explanation of the impossibility of forgetfulness on His part, for how could heedlessness or forgetfulness, or the abandonment and neglect of one whom He has chosen and selected to convey His message, approach the precincts of His greatness and majesty, when He in whose hand is the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them...? The word "Lord" (rabb) is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: He is the Lord of the heavens, etc. Or it is a substitute (badal) for "your Lord" in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And your Lord was never forgetful﴾. The "fa" (fa') in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿So worship Him and be steadfast in His worship﴾ is for the sequencing (tartib) of what follows, namely the requirements of the two commands, upon what precedes it, namely His being the Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them. It has been said that it is based on His not abandoning you, peace be upon him, or not forgetting the deeds of those who act. The meaning is: when you have come to know Him, Exalted is He, through what has been mentioned of His perfect lordship, then worship Him, etc., for the obligation to know Him, glorified is He, in this way, in order to worship Him, is beyond doubt. Or: when you know that He, Mighty and Majestic, does not forget you, or does not forget the deeds of those who act, then devote yourself to His worship and be steadfast in its hardships, and do not grieve over the delay of revelation and the words of the disbelievers, for He, glorified is He, watches over you, looks after you, and is gentle with you in this world and the Hereafter.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "Lord of the heavens" be the subject (mubtada') with "so worship Him" as its predicate, the "fa" being superfluous (za'ida) according to the opinion of al-Akhfash. This, as you see, is not [a sound view].

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And your Lord was never forgetful﴾, be part of the speech of the righteous (al-muttaqun), on the assumption that "Lord" is the predicate of an omitted subject. He did not permit this on the assumption of substitution (badal), because then the sequencing of His saying, glorified is He, "so worship Him", etc., upon it would not be apparent, since it is, without doubt, speech of God, Exalted is He, to His Prophet, peace be upon him, in this world. Making it the response (jawab) of an omitted conditional clause (shart), on the assumption: "And when you knew the states and speech of the people of Paradise, then devote yourself to action", does not suit, as stated in al-Kashf, the eloquence (fasahah) of the Revelation, because it turns away from the apparent cause to the hidden one. The verb "istibar" (be steadfast) is construed with the preposition "lam" (li-), although the familiar construction is with "ʿala" (upon), as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and be steadfast upon them﴾, because it implies the sense of firmness in worship in the face of the hardships and difficulties that confront it, like your saying to one who is facing an opponent in combat: "Stand firm against your opponent," i.e., hold your ground against him in the onslaughts that come upon you. In this there is an allusion to the striving (mujahadah) that one endures, and that the upright is one who stands firm for that and does not waver, with a hint of the sense of "we have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad."

﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾ That is, any equal (mithl), as came in a narration of a group from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and Qatada. Its root meaning is a partner in the name, and its application to that is because sharing in a name requires likeness. Ibn Attiyya said: "The samiyy (namesake) in this sense means the one who is equal to and resembles." Some have kept it to its original meaning and inclined to say that what is intended here is a partner in a specific name by which He has referred to Himself, namely "Lord of the heavens and the earth." It has been said: what is meant is a partner in the glorious name (al-ism al-jalil, i.e., Allah), for the polytheists, despite their extreme obstinacy, never named an idol with the name of Majesty (al-Jalalah) at all. It has been said: what is meant is a partner in what is specific to Him, Exalted is He, such as the Glorious Name and al-Rahman, and this was also transmitted from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. It has been said: it is a partner in the name "Ilah" (God), and what is meant by naming (tasmiyah) is naming upon the truth; as for naming upon falsehood, it is as if there were no naming at all. Al-Tastari transmitted from Ibn Abbas that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked him about this, and he said: "The samiyy is the son." He recited to him the verse of the poet:
