"As for the samiyy, you have from him many [sons/offspring]; and wealth is wealth that goes and comes."

This was also narrated from al-Dahhak. Whichever of these is the case, the intent of denying knowledge and negating it is the denial and negation of the thing known in the most eloquent and emphatic manner. The sentence confirms the obligation of worshipping Him, Mighty and Majestic, even though the consideration differs according to the differing opinions, so reflect.

The two brothers (al-Akhawan, i.e., Hamzah and al-Kisa'i), Hisham, Ali ibn Nasr and Harun, both transmitted from Abu Amr, al-Hasan, al-A'mash, Isa and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿hal ta'lamu﴾ with the lam assimilated into the ta' (هَتَعْلَمُ). According to what Abu Ubaydah said, this is a dialectal form (lughah) like the clear pronunciation (al-izhar). They cited for this the verse of Muzahim al-Uqayli:

"So leave this aside, but you will afflict (hut'in) the lovesick one, over the light of a lightning flash at the end of the night, standing (nasib)."

﴿Those who disbelieve say, "When I have died, shall I really be brought forth alive?"﴾ Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij that it was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il. It is also narrated from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, that it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. It has been said that it was about Abu Jahl. And it is narrated from al-Kalbi that it concerned Ubayy ibn Khalaf, who took a decayed bone, crumbled it with his hand, and scattered it in the wind, saying: "So-and-so claims that we will be resurrected after we die and become like this. This is something that will never happen."

The alif-lam in (al-insan, "the human being") is, as has been said, the alif-lam of prior reference (al-'ahd), and what is intended is one of these individuals. It has also been said that what is intended by "al-insan" is a specific group, namely the disbelievers who deny the resurrection.

Others have said: it is permissible that the alif-lam be the alif-lam of genus (al-jins), and that there is a figurative usage in the sense of the part (majaz fi al-taraf), whereby the genus of human beings is mentioned and some of its members are intended, just as the whole is sometimes mentioned for some of its parts. Or there may be a figurative usage in the attribution (majaz fi al-isnad), whereby what proceeded from some is attributed to all, as one says, "The Banu so-and-so killed a slain man," while the killer was only one of them. From this is his saying:

*"The sword of the Banu 'Abs, when they struck,*
*was blunted in my hand, from the head of Khalid."*

This was objected to: for such an attribution to be valid, the approval of the rest must actually be present, or their support for it, so that it is regarded as if it proceeded from them. And there is no doubt that the rest of humankind, the believers, did not approve of this statement. One of those who stipulate this for validity answered that denial is inherent in the natures of all before any consideration of the evidence, so approval is present by reference to natural disposition and innate constitution.

Al-Khafaji said: The correct view is that such a condition is not required for its validity; it is only required for its eloquence, when a rhetorical purpose demands it, so that the act is regarded as if it proceeded from all. Approval may be the case, or joint support, or the withholding of aid and assistance; this is why the Law prescribed the qasama (the oath of fifty men in cases of unknown killing) and the diyya (blood money). It may also be other than these. The rhetorical purpose here seems to be that, since a statement was openly made among them that should not be said, and whoever says such a thing should not be left without being prevented or killed, this was treated as if it were approval, to urge them to reject it, whether by word or deed. End of quotation.

It has been said: perhaps the truth is that the attribution to all here is to indicate the scarcity of those who believe in the resurrection in the manner that the Truthful One (the Prophet ﷺ) reported. ﴿But most people will not believe, even if you should strive eagerly﴾ (12:103). Consider this carefully.

He expressed it with the present tense (yaqulu, "says"), either to bring to mind the past scene because of its strangeness, or to convey continuous renewal, for this statement will keep being renewed until the Trumpet is blown.

The hamza is for denial (al-istinkar). Idha is an adverbial of time (zarf) dependent on a verb omitted, indicated by (ukhraju, "shall I be brought forth"). They did not permit its dependence on the verb that is stated, because what follows the lam (of emphasis) does not govern what precedes it. Ibn 'Atiyya also counted the interposition of sawfa as an obstacle to governance, and he was answered with the line:

*"When she saw him secure, her grief eased,*
*and she said: 'Our father is like this; he will do so.'"*

and other examples that have been heard. It is reported from al-Radi that he took idha here to be a conditional particle, and took its governing element to be the apodosis (jaza'), saying that the conditional particle indicates the necessity of the apodosis for the protasis. To achieve this purpose, the apodosis governs idha, even though it comes after a particle whose following element does not govern what precedes it, like the fa in (fa-sabbih, "so glorify") and inna in your saying: "If you come to me, then I honor you" (idha ji'tani fa-inni mukrim), and the lam of initiation in His saying, exalted is He: (a-idha ma mittu la-sawfa ukhraju hayya, "When I have died, shall I really be brought forth alive?"). But the preferred view of most scholars is that idha here is a temporal adverb, and what al-Radi mentioned is not agreed upon; its verification is in the books of Arabic grammar. In the sentence there is an omitted conjoined element, indicated by the presence of a context: i.e., "when I have died and become dust, shall I really be brought forth," and so on.

The lam here is merely for emphasis (li-mujarrad al-tawkid), and for this reason it was permissible for it to be combined with the particle of future time (sawfa). This is on the view that when it enters the present tense it makes it specific to the present; but on the view that it does not make it specific, there is no need to claim that it is stripped for emphasis. However, the first view is the well-known one. What is in (idha ma) is also for emphasis.

What is meant by "bringing forth" (ikhraj) is bringing out of the earth, or out of the state of annihilation. On the first interpretation it is literal, and on the second it is figurative, meaning transition from one state to another. The placing of the adverbial of time before the hamza of denial, rather than the bringing forth, is because that bringing forth is not denied absolutely; what is denied is its occurrence at the time when both matters are combined. Therefore the adverbial was put first, because it is the locus of the denial, while the original position of what is denied is to come immediately after the hamza. It is also permissible that what is intended is the denial of that very time, i.e., the denial of the coming of a time in which there is life after death, meaning that this time will not exist. This is more eloquent than denying life after death, because it indicates denial through a demonstrative argument. Some did not posit an omitted conjoined element and took the time of death to be extended until the first departure of the soul, as is the obvious meaning. It has been said: there is no need for all of that, because if they deny it at the moment of death, it is known that they deny it when they have become crumbled bones, by a fortiori reasoning. In any case, there is no difficulty in the verse.

Ibn Dhakwan, along with a group, read, with a variant from him, (idha, "when") without the hamza of interrogation, and it is implied with him by the meaning. It has been said that nothing is implied, and that what is intended is a statement in the manner of mockery and derision toward the one who says this. Talha ibn Musarrif read (sa-ukhraju, "I will be brought forth") with the sin of future and without lam, and on this reading idha is connected to the verb mentioned according to the correct view. In another transmission from him, it is (la-sa-ukhraju, "I will surely be brought forth") with both sin and lam. Al-Hasan and Abu Haywa read (ukhruju, "bring forth") in the active voice. (Awa-la yadhkuru al-insan, "Does not man remember?") is from remembrance, which is meant as reflection and recognition, placed in the position of the pronoun for added emphasis and to indicate that humanity itself is a motive for reflection upon what has happened to him of the matters of his creation, which prevent him from the statement mentioned. This is the secret of attributing it to the genus or to the individual under that title, according to what has been said. The hamza is for rebuking denial (al-istinkar al-tawbikhi), and according to one of the two well-known views regarding such a construction, it enters upon an omitted element to which what follows is conjoined. The estimate here is: "Does he say that?" (a-yaqulu dhalika).

[p. 117]
[p. 118]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 67:

﴿Does not man remember that We created him before, while he was nothing?﴾ That is: before the state he is in now, which is the state of his existence. It is said: that is, before his resurrection (ba'th). ﴿While he was nothing﴾ That is, and the case is that he did not exist at that time. So since We created him when he was in that state, which is wholly incompatible with creation, and it being even more remote from occurring, then how much more so will We resurrect him by restoring what had ceased to be in him, since he had previously been characterized by existence at some time, according to what some of the people of the Sunnah have chosen; or by gathering the scattered materials and bringing into being the like of what accidents were in them, according to what another of them has also chosen, which is more fitting and more evident. So what is wrong with him that he does not remember it, and so falls into what he falls into of denial? It is also said: the conjunction is upon the earlier mentioned "says" (yaqulu).

The interrogative hamza is for denying the combining, since it enters upon the waw which indicates it. This does not disturb its being placed first, because it is in relation to the whole sentence. So it is as if it were said: Is it combined between the aforementioned saying and not remembering? Its summary: Does he say that and not remember that We created him, etc.?

Many of the Seven Readers recited (yadhdhakaru) with a fatha on the dhal and the kaf and with shadda on both, and its origin is yatadhakkaru; the ta was assimilated into the dhal. Ubayy also recited thus.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 19, verse 68:**

﴿So by your Lord﴾: His swearing by His own Name, may His names be exalted, with the pronoun referring to him (ﷺ), is to confirm the matter by indicating its cause and to magnify his station (ﷺ) and elevate his rank, may peace and blessings be upon him. ﴿We will surely gather them﴾, meaning: We will surely assemble those who made the statements mentioned earlier, driving them to the place of gathering (al-mahshar) after We have brought them forth alive. In swearing to this, and not to the resurrection itself, there is an affirmation of it in the most eloquent and emphatic form, as if it were a clear matter needing no explicit statement, once its possibility has been shown by the conclusive proof mentioned earlier. What needs explanation is only what follows it of terrors. That the pronoun refers to the disbelievers who made the statements is the most apparent reading in view of the context, and Ibn 'Atiyyah and a group of scholars adopted it. This does not exclude that the intended reference is to one individual of mankind, as is not hidden.

Abu Hayyan preferred that it refers to all people, believers and disbelievers alike. ﴿And the devils﴾ is either conjoined (ma'tuf) to the pronoun in the accusative, or is a direct object with ma'a (maf'ul ma'ah, the object of accompaniment). It has been narrated that the disbelievers will be gathered together with their companions among the devils who used to lead them astray, each one with his devil, in chains. The reasoning for this, on the assumption that the pronoun refers to mankind, is that when they are gathered, and the disbelievers are among them bound to the devils, they have been gathered together with them, in the manner of what is said about attributing a statement to a whole category. It was also said: every one of mankind, believer and disbeliever, will be gathered with his companion from among the devils, and the disbeliever is not singled out for this. This may be supported by what is in the two Sahihs from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, in a raised (marfu') narration: "There is none of you but that a companion of his from among the jinn is assigned to him." They said: "And you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "And me, but Allah has helped me against him, so he has submitted, and he does not command me except to good."

﴿Then We will surely bring them forth around Hell on their knees﴾: kneeling (jathiyan), meaning sitting back on their knees. Its original form is juthuww with two waws. Because the coming together of the two was burdensome after two dammas, the tha' was given a kasra for lightness, so the first waw became a ya' because it was sukun and preceded by a kasra. Thus a waw and a ya' came together, and one of them was preceded by sukun, so the waw was changed into a ya', and the ya' was assimilated into the ya', and the jim was given a kasra to match what follows it.

Most of the Seven Readers recited it with a damma, and it is the plural of jathin in both readings. Al-Raghib allowed that it could be a verbal noun (masdar), like the saying about bakā, which has passed. Perhaps bringing the disbelievers in this state is a humiliation for them, or because of their inability to stand due to the severity that has overcome them.

[Page 119]

Some have said: the reckoning takes place around Hell, so they kneel in order to dispute with one another, and then some of them disown others. Al-Suddi said: they kneel because of the narrowness of the place for them. The state (hal) is thus described as something determined (muqaddarah) on both opinions, in contrast to what was mentioned earlier. It was also said that it is determined on this view as well, because the intended meaning is kneeling around Hell. Whoever makes the pronoun refer to the disbelievers and others says: the fortunate and the wretched will be brought around Hell, so that the fortunate may see what Allah, exalted is He, has saved them from, and so they may increase in gladness and joy, and so the wretched may receive what they stored up for their return, and may increase in rage at the fortunate turning away from them to the abode of reward, and at their gloating over them. All of them will kneel, then because of the terror that overwhelms them at the sight of it, or because of the narrowness of the place, or because that belongs to the consequences of standing for the reckoning and mutual speech before arriving at reward and punishment. It was also said: they kneel on their knees to show humility in that great station. The general kneeling of all the people of the place of standing is indicated by the apparent sense of the words of the Exalted: ﴿And you will see every nation kneeling﴾. However, there will soon come, if Allah the Exalted wills, what is apparent in the non-kneeling of all of them from the reports. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

The state (hal) has been said to be determined, and it has been said to be not determined, except that what belongs to some is attributed to all. To make it determined with respect to the fortunate and not determined with respect to the wretched is not valid. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he explained (jithiyyan) as "in groups," taking it to be the plural of jathwah, which is a heap of earth and stones. That is, "We will surely bring them forth in groups."

Then We will surely drag out from every group (*shi'ah*), i.e., every company that rallied together and cooperated in falsehood, or that followed and adhered to falsehood, according to what the context requires if the verse concerns disbelievers; or every company that followed a religion in general, according to what the context requires if the verse concerns believers and others. ﴿Which of them is most insolent toward the Most Merciful?﴾ i.e., most rebellious against obedience and most disobedient. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it means audacity, and from Mujahid that it means disbelief. It was also said that it means slander, in the dialect of the Banu Tamim. The majority follow the first explanation. On all the other explanations, *'itiyy* is a verbal noun (*masdar*), and in it are the two readings mentioned earlier concerning *jithiyyan* (جِثِيًّا).

Some scholars claimed that in both readings it is the plural of *jathin* (جاثٍ), but this is contrary to the apparent meaning here. *Naz'* means extraction, as in God's words ﴿and he drew out his hand﴾. The intended meaning is the continuation of this action, i.e., We will continually extract and separate out from every company of disbelief the most rebellious among them, and then the next most rebellious, until they are surrounded. When they have all been gathered, We will cast them into the Fire in order, beginning with the first of them for punishment, then the next, and so on, and the first of them ...

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 70:**

[p. 120]

God Most High says: ﴿Then We will surely know best those most deserving of burning therein.﴾ The intended meaning of "those most deserving" is those who are drawn out in order, and it may also refer to those people as a whole. It is as if it were said: "Then We know best the burning of these people, and they are the most deserving of the Fire among all the astray, and their ranks are lowest and their punishment is most severe." So in the speech there is the placing of an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun. Some scholars explained *naz'* (drawing out) as *ramy* (shooting), from "I drew the arrow from the bow," meaning I shot it. So the meaning is: "We will surely shoot into the Fire the most rebellious from every group of those groups, then We know best their burning." Interpreting the verse as "beginning with the most severe, then the most severe" is related from Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him.

It is also permitted that by "those most severe in rebelliousness" are meant the leaders of the sects and their imams, because their sin is multiplied by being astray and leading others astray. God Most High says: ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of God, We will increase them in punishment upon punishment for what they used to corrupt﴾ [16:88], and ﴿They will surely carry their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [29:13].

Ibn Abi Hatim related this from Qatadah, and it does not necessarily require universality and comprehensiveness. An objection to the view of generality is that God's words ﴿They will surely carry their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ imply that all share in rebelliousness, indeed in its extreme degree, and this does not suit the believers. It is answered that this is ascribing to the whole what belongs to some of them, and preference over a group does not require that every single individual share in it. When you say, "He is the bravest of the Arabs," it does not necessarily mean that bravery exists in every one of them. On this view, the verse contains an allusion to forgiving many, since the punishment is specifically assigned to the most disobedient. (*Ayyuhum*) is the object of (*lananzi'anna*, "We will surely draw out"), and it is a relative pronoun meaning "who," built on *dammah*, and its place is in the accusative. (*Ashaddu*) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "he is most severe," and the sentence is a relative clause, with the returning pronoun being the subject. And ﴿against the Most Merciful﴾ is connected to (*ashaddu*). (*'Itiyyan*) is a specifier (*tamyiz*) transferred from the subject. Whoever claims it is a plural makes it a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). It is permitted that the prepositional phrase be explanatory, so it is connected to an omitted verb, as in *saqyan laka* ("watering for you"). It may also be connected to (*'itiyyan*). As for if it is a descriptive, then it is by agreement. As for if it is a verbal noun, then according to those who permit the fronting of the complement of a verbal noun, especially if it is an adverb of place or time. The same discussion applies to (*biha*) in His words ﴿they are most deserving of it, burning﴾, for he permitted that the preposition be explanatory, or connected to (*awla*, "most deserving"), or connected to (*saliyyan*, "burning"). It has been read with *dammah* and with *kasrah*. Both the verbal noun and the descriptive status are permitted. On the descriptive status it is a circumstantial accusative, and on the verbal noun status it is a specifier, in the same manner as what was said about (*'itiyyan*), except that it is permitted that it be a specifier of the relation between (*awla*) and the prepositional object. This was already indicated in what has passed.

*Al-Saliyy* comes from *saliya al-nar* (like *radiya*), meaning he suffered its heat by it. Al-Raghib said: it is said *salia bil-nar* and *bi-kadha*, meaning he was afflicted with it. It is related from al-Kalbi that he explained *al-saliyy* as entering, and from Ibn Jurayj that he explained it as abiding. Neither of the two meanings is literal, as is not hidden. Then, what has been mentioned about the indeclinability of *ayy* here is the view of Sibawayh. Its proper status would be to be indeclinable in every position, like the rest of the relative pronouns, because it resembles a particle in needing what follows it as its relative clause. But since it necessarily takes an annexed genitive, either verbally or in implication, and annexation is one of the distinctive features of nouns, after that resemblance it returned to the original status of nouns, which is inflection. Also, when it is annexed to an indefinite noun it has the meaning of "every," and when it is annexed to a definite noun it has the meaning of "some," so it is treated in inflection according to what its meaning is. Here, according to him, it returned to what is the proper status of relative pronouns, which is indeclinability, because when the first part of its relative clause is omitted, its semantic deficiency increases, namely vagueness and need for a relative clause, through the deficiency of the clause which is like its part. Thus its resemblance to the particle became stronger. Many scholars did not approve of what he held.

Abu 'Amr al-Jurmi said: "I left Basra and from when I parted from al-Khandaq until Mecca I did not hear anyone say: '*La-adribanna ayyuhum qa'im*' (I will surely strike whichever of them is standing)" with *dammah*. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: "I know of no grammarian except that he has judged Sibawayh in error on this issue."

Al-Zajjaj said: "It has not become clear that Sibawayh erred in his book except in two places, and this is one of them, for he says that *ayy* is inflected when it is separated from annexation, so how can he make it indeclinable when it is annexed?" Our teacher 'Ala' al-Din, may God Most High exalt his station in the highest of the high, exerted himself in defending Sibawayh on this point with arguments not worth the trouble of relating, and we have mentioned some of it in our glosses on the commentary of *al-Qatr* by its author.

Yes, what Sibawayh held regarding its being in the object position is supported by the reading of Talhah ibn Musarrif, Mu'adh ibn Muslim al-Harra' the teacher of al-Farra', and Za'idah from al-A'mash: *ayyahum* with *fathah*. But this reading refutes what was transmitted from him about the necessity of indeclinability when it is annexed and its relative clause's first part is omitted. And it is necessary, if one stops on this reading, that one say that both cases are permitted in it at that point.

Al-Khalil said: the object of *lananzi'anna* is an omitted relative pronoun, and *ayy* here is interrogative, a subject, and *ashaddu* is its predicate, and the sentence is reported by a saying which occurred as a relative clause to the omitted relative pronoun, meaning: "We will surely draw out those about whom it is said: 'Which of them is most severe?'" This was objected to on the grounds that there is no sense in making "drawing out" apply to one who asks about him with this question. It is answered that this is a metaphor for the closeness of their conditions and their resemblance in extreme rebelliousness, so that it deserves that one ask about them; or the intended meaning is those who are answered with respect to this question. Its summary is: "We will surely draw out the most severe in rebelliousness." Yet this, along with its strained character, involves omitting the relative pronoun together with part of its relative clause, which is strain upon strain, and such a thing is not to be used as a general rule. Yes, a similar omission, according to what has been said, is the poet's verse:

*Wa-laqad abitu min al-fataa bi-manzilin / fa-abitu la harajun wa-la mahrumu*
(And indeed I spend the night with the girl in a position, so I spend the night neither troubled nor deprived.)

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' went to what al-Khalil said, except that they made the sentence in the position of an accusative governed by *lananzi'anna*, and the meaning is: "We will surely draw out those who fall in the answer to this question." The verb is suspended by the interrogative, and this suspension was permissible in their view because the meaning is "we will surely call out," and they [the two] held that the suspension of calling is permitted even though it is not one of the verbs of the heart. To this view al-Mahdawi also went.

It has been said: since drawing out includes the meaning of separating and distinguishing, and this necessarily involves knowledge, it was treated as the treatment of knowledge, and so suspension of it was permitted. Yunus does not hold that suspension is restricted to one kind of verb; rather all kinds are equal in permissibility of suspension in his view.

It has been said: the interrogative sentence is resumptive (*isti'nafiyyah*), and the verb has as its object "every group" with the addition of *min* in affirmative speech, as al-Akhfash holds, or with the meaning of "We will surely draw out some of every group," making *min* an object by treating it as a noun. Then, if the resumption is explanatory, arising in answer to "Who are those drawn out?", interpretation is needed, as if it were said: "The intended meaning is those who fall in answer to 'Which of them is most severe?' or something like that." If *ayy* is on the assumption of resumption and the verb has as its object what was mentioned, then it is a relative pronoun, and interpretation is not needed. However, in saying resumption there is a deviation from the apparent sense that the speech is one sentence to a departure from the apparent sense that it is two sentences.

Some transmitted from al-Mubarrad that *ayyuhum* is the subject of *shi'ah* (party), because its meaning is "those who support," and the estimate is: "We will surely draw out from every group that supports, which of them is most severe." On this view, *ayy* is in the sense of "who" according to what Abu al-Baqa' said. It was transmitted from al-Radi that it is in the sense of *alladhi* ("who"). In *al-Bahr* it is said: al-Mubarrad said: *ayyuhum* is connected to *shi'ah*, and for this reason it is in the nominative case, and the meaning is that those who support one another, which of them is most severe, as if they hasten to this. It necessarily requires that the object of *lananzi'anna* be an omitted noun. It was also estimated in this view: "from those who support one another, which of them is most severe," meaning "from those who cooperate, then look at which of them is most severe." Al-Nahhas said: "This is a good view," and it ended. This is contrary to what was transmitted first. By my life, what was attributed to al-Mubarrad, both first and last, is more insipid than *yakh* (an expression of disgust).

It has been said: the sentence is interrogative and occurred as a descriptive of *shi'ah*, with the meaning: "We will surely draw out from every group, about whom it is said: 'Which of them is most severe?'" That is, from every group whose conditions are close to one another. *Min* is extra, and *naz'* means shooting. Abu Bakr ibn Shuqayr reported that some Kufans say: in *ayyihim* there is the meaning of a condition. You say: "I struck the people, whichever of them was angry," and the meaning is "if they became angry or did not become angry." Abu Hayyan said: "On this view the estimate here is: 'if their rebelliousness became severe or did not become severe.'" It ended. And this, as you see, is not right. The view that the mind is led to and that the wording supports is what Sibawayh held. The basis of what he held regarding the inflection and indeclinability of *ayy* is, in reality, what is heard, and the explanations of the grammarians, whatever flaws they contain, come only after the usage occurred, and the absence of hearing does not discredit its being heard. So consider this carefully.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 71:**

﴿And there is none of you﴾: this is a shift (iltifat, a change of grammatical address) to address to mankind, whether the intended meaning is generality or specifically the disbelievers, in order to show greater concern for the content of the statement. It has also been said that it is an address to the people, and that it is a new statement from Him, exalted and majestic, after He had completed the purpose of the first, so there is no shift at all. The latter is perhaps the one that comes to mind first. But it has been said that the first view is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and a group: ﴿And there is none of them﴾, meaning, "and there is none of you ﴿except that he will come to it (warid)﴾", meaning, will enter it, as a large number of the earlier exegetes (salaf al-mufassirin) and the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) held. To this also points His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; you will come to it (waridun)﴾. And His saying, concerning Pharaoh: ﴿He will precede his people on the Day of Resurrection and will lead them into the Fire, and wretched is the place to which they are led (al-wird al-mawrud)﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas used what has been mentioned as evidence against Ibn al-Azraq when he denied his interpretation of warid as "entering." This is also applicable on the assumption that the address is general, so the believer too will enter it, but it will not harm him, as has been said. Ahmad, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), and a group have related from Abu Sumayyah, who said: "We disagreed about warid. Some of us said, 'No believer will enter it.' Another said, 'They will all enter it, then Allah, exalted is He, will save those who had taqwa.' So I met Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, and mentioned this to him. He said, and he pointed with his finger to his ears (as a sign of certainty): 'If I have not heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Neither the righteous nor the wicked will remain but that he will enter it. It will be cool and safe for the believer, as it was for Ibrahim, peace be upon him, so much so that the Fire will cry out from their coolness. Then Allah, exalted is He, will save those who had taqwa."'" Al-Imam al-Razi mentioned several benefits of this entry in his tafsir, so let it be consulted.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Anbari and al-Bayhaqi related from al-Hasan: "Warid is passing by it without entering." This was also related from Qatadah, and it means passing over the Sirat (bridge) laid over its back, as a group related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him. The believer passes over it without feeling it, based on what Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim and others related from Khalid ibn Ma'dan, who said:

"When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, they will say: 'Our Lord, did You not promise us that we would come to the Fire?' He will say: 'Yes, but you passed by it while it was extinguished.'"

This does not contradict what al-Tirmidhi, al-Tabarani and others related from Ya'la ibn Umayyah from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "On the Day of Resurrection the Fire will say to the believer: 'Pass over, O believer, for your light has extinguished my flame.'" This is because it is possible that he will not be recalling this saying when asked, or that he did not hear it due to being preoccupied.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Zayd that he said concerning the verse: "The warid of the Muslims is passing over the bridge between its two sides, and the warid of the polytheists is that they enter it." On this view one must resort to a general metaphor (umum al-majaz), according to those who do not consider it permissible to use a single word in two meanings.

From Mujahid: the warid of the believer into the Fire is the touch of fever upon his body in this world, because of what is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ: "Fever is from the heat (fayh) of Hell."

It is not hidden that the evidence for this is weak with respect to the point to be proven.

Some have argued for this from what al-Tabari related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out to visit a man from among his companions who had a fever, and I was with him. Upon him be prayers and peace, he said: 'Allah, exalted is He, says: It is My fire, which I impose upon My believing servant, so that it may be his share of the Fire in the Hereafter.'" In this too there is also obscurity.

The truth is that there is no indication in it that a believer who has a fever in this world does not come to the Fire in the Hereafter. At most, what it indicates is that he will be protected from the pain of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr that warid means presence and nearness, as in His saying: ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan (warada ma'a Madyan)﴾. Some have chosen that what is meant is their presence around it, on their knees, and they have cited for this what you will learn, if Allah wills. There is no contradiction between this verse and His saying: ﴿Those will be kept far away from it (mub'adun)﴾, because what is meant is that they will be kept far from its punishment. It has also been said that what is meant is their being removed from it after having been near it.

﴿(It was) upon your Lord a decree (kana) (hatman)﴾: a binding matter, as related from Ibn 'Abbas. What is meant by "in the status of the obligatory" is in its certainty of occurrence, since nothing is obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, according to Ahl al-Sunnah. ﴿(Maqdiyyan)﴾: a matter decreed, with its occurrence definitively determined.

Al-Khatib related from 'Ikrimah that the meaning of "kana hatman maqdiyyan" is "it was an obligatory oath (qasam)." This was also related from Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Qatadah. It has been said: what is meant by it is the initiation of an oath. It has also been said: It may be said that the phrase "upon your Lord" is intended as an oath, just as you say, "It is incumbent upon Allah, the Exalted, on me to do such-and-such," for it has no meaning except the emphasis of obligation, and an oath is mentioned only in such a context. And "'alayya" (upon me) occurs frequently in their speech for oath, as in the saying of the poet:

"Upon me, whenever I come to visit Layla, a visit to the House of Allah, on two feet, barefoot."

For the form of a vow (nadhr) may be intended as an oath, as they have explicitly stated. It is also permissible that what is meant by this clause is an oath, as in their saying: "I have insisted upon you (azamtu 'alayka) that you do such-and-such." This ends his words. What is meant by the oath is known from what al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and others related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No three of a Muslim's children die and he enters the Fire, except for the dissolving of the oath (tahillat al-qasam)."

Abu 'Ubaydah, Ibn 'Atiyyah, and others following them said: the oath in the predicate is an allusion to the oath in the opening, namely ﴿And there is none of you except that he will come to it﴾. Some have explicitly stated that the waw in it is the waw of oath. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that no grammarian holds that such a waw is an oath-waw, because that would entail deleting the genitive noun while retaining the preposition, which is not permissible except in poetry or rare speech, on the condition that the attribute of the deleted noun stands in its place, as in the saying: "By Allah, my night does not let its companion sleep."

He also said: The grammarians have stated that one cannot dispense with the oath by the answer (jawab) for the meaning's sake, except when the answer has the lam or an (that), and neither of these is in the verse. Ibn Hisham took "tahillat al-qasam" as a metaphor for paucity, which is widespread in that usage, including the saying of Ka'b:

"You strike upon swift (camels), while they are pursuing, dhawabil (lean with exertion), whose touching the ground is a slight dragging."

The meaning is: their touching the ground is a little. This is like a person who swears to do something and then does a little of it, so that he thereby dissolves his oath. Then he said: What some exegetes said, that the oath is in its original sense and refers to His saying, ﴿And there is none of you except that he will come to it﴾, etc., is open to question, because the sentence contains no oath unless it is conjoined with the clauses to which the oath was answered in His saying: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them﴾ to its end. And in this there is a distance (bu'd). This ends his words. Al-Khafaji permitted both the circumstantial (hal) reading and the conjunctive (ʿatf) reading, and said: The objection of distance is not heard, since no intervening separator occurs. And this is as you see. Perhaps the safest course, away from much contention, is to take it as a metaphor for paucity, which is a well-known metaphor in what has been mentioned. This is not disturbed by what Ahmad, al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, al-Tabarani and others related from Mu'adh ibn Anas, from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, that he said: "Whoever stands guard behind the Muslims in the cause of Allah, exalted is He, voluntarily, not being seized by a ruler, will not see the Fire with his eyes except for the dissolving of the oath, for Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And there is none of you except that he will come to it﴾."

For the causal explanation is correct even with paucity intended from that too. It is as if it were said: he will not see the Fire except a little, because Allah, exalted is He, has informed that everyone will come to it, and what He has informed must occur. Were it not so, it would be permissible that he would not see it at all.
