Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 72:

﴿Then We shall deliver those who were mindful of God﴾ by bringing them out of it, according to what the great majority of scholars hold. ﴿And We shall leave the wrongdoers therein, kneeling﴾ on their knees, as related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. In my view, this verse clearly indicates that the meaning of "wurud" (arrival/coming upon) is entering (al-dukhul), which is the common meaning.

Some have said: it is evidence that the meaning of "wurud" is kneeling around it (al-juthuw hawalayha). This is because "nunajjy" (We deliver) and "nadharu" (We leave) constitute a detailed specification of the genus, as if it were said: We deliver these and leave those in the state in which they were brought, kneeling. On this view, it is necessary to assume the implied phrase "around it" (fi hawalayha), and you know that the apparent reading does not include this implied phrase, and kneeling does not necessitate it. The address "those who were mindful" (ittaqaw) and the address "the wrongdoers" (al-zalimin) are varied, to indicate the preponderance of the aspect of mercy, and that monotheism is what delivers and polytheism is what destroys. It is as if it were said: "Then We shall deliver whoever is found to have some measure of God-consciousness, namely abstaining from shirk, and We shall destroy whoever is characterized by wrongdoing, that is, by shirk, and persists in it." The placement of "nadharu" as the counterpart of "nunajjy" also hints at this subtle point. Al-Raghib said: one says "fulan yadharu al-shay'" meaning he casts it away, out of little regard for it; from this comes the term "dharr" for a piece of flesh that is of no account. "Thumma" is used to indicate the difference between the act of the creature, which is their arrival at the Fire, and the act of the Truth, glory be to Him, which is deliverance and destruction, in time and in rank. This was said by the scholar al-Tibi, may God sanctify his resting place.

Page 124

The traditions that have come concerning sinful believers indicate that the aforementioned deliverance is not instantaneous; rather, it occurs gradually, in accordance with the strength or weakness of God-consciousness, until whoever has in his heart the weight of an atom's worth of good emerges from the Fire. This occurs after punishment in proportion to his disobedience. As for what the apparent reports say, such as the earlier report of Jabir: "Indeed the believer is not harmed by the Fire," it is interpreted by taking "the believer" to mean the complete believer, because of the abundance of reports indicating that some believers will be punished.

From this same category is what al-Tirmidhi transmitted from Jabir, may God be pleased with him, who also said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Some people from among the people of monotheism will be punished in the Fire until they become charred cinders; then mercy will overtake them and they will be brought out and cast at the gates of Paradise. The people of Paradise will sprinkle water upon them, and they will sprout as the debris sprouts in the flood-carried sediment."

From here, some scholars prohibited saying in supplication: "O God, forgive all of the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ all their sins," or "O God, do not punish anyone of the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ," and so on. Some have said: on the supposition that the address is specific to the disbelievers, the meaning of deliverance is that those who were mindful are driven to Paradise after having been on the brink of the Fire; "thumma" is used to show the difference between the arrival of the disbelievers in the Fire and the driving of those mentioned to Paradise, and that the former is for humiliation and the latter for honor. You know that those who are taken to Paradise from among those who were mindful, without entering the Fire at all, are none but the elite. The Mu'tazilah restricted "those who were mindful" to those other than the people of major sins, placed them among the wrongdoers, and used this verse as evidence for their eternal abiding in the Fire, since they are wrongdoers.

ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud, and Ubayy, may God be pleased with them, al-Jahdari, Muʿawiyah ibn Qurrah, and Yaʿqub read "thamma" with a fatha on the tha', meaning "there" (hunak). Ibn Abi Layla read "thammata" with a fatha together with the silent ha' (ha' al-sakt), and it is an adverb of place related to what follows it. Yahya, al-Aʿmash, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Muhaysin and Yaʿqub read "nunjī" with a light jim (takhfif al-jim). It has also been read as "yunjī" and "yunajjā," with shaddah and without, in the passive form. A group read "nujjiya" with a single damma-d nun and a shaddah on the jim. ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, read "nunahhī" with an unpointed ha', and this reading, by its apparent sense, supports the interpretation of "wurud" as nearness and presence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 73:

﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾ — to the end of the verse — is a report of what they said upon hearing the verses that recount to them the awfulness of their state and the gravity of their end. That is: when Our verses are recited to the polytheists, among which are the preceding verses, ﴿clear﴾, meaning manifest in their inimitability, by which they were challenged and were unable to oppose them; or clear in their well-arranged words, summarizing the meaning and making the purposes plain, whether they are muhkamat (clear in meaning) or mutashabihat (ambiguous), the clarification by the muhkamat following them, or the clarification of the Messenger (ﷺ) by word or deed. The view, as in al-Kashshaf, is that ﴿clear﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) emphasizing the content of the sentence, even though it did not form it from two nouns, because the meaning requires this.

Abu Haywa, al-A'raj and Ibn Muhaysin read (وإذا يُتْلى) with the yā' (ي), because the subject is feminine in a metaphorical sense and there is a separator.

﴿those who disbelieved said﴾, that is, they said. The relative pronoun was placed in the position of the pronoun to draw attention to the fact that they said what they said while disbelieving in what was recited to them and rejecting it. Or: ﴿those who said﴾ refers to those among them who were persistent in disbelief and insisted on defiance and obstinacy, namely al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and his wicked followers, for the verse was revealed concerning them. The lam in His words, exalted is He, ﴿to those who believed﴾ is the lam of conveyance (li-l-tabligh), as in "I said to him such-and-such" when you address him with it. It has also been said that it is the lam of cause (lam al-ajal), meaning they said it for their sake and concerning them. The first is preferred, because their statement was not only concerning the believers, as indicated by His words ﴿which of the two groups﴾, that is, the believers and the disbelievers, as if they said: which of us (is better) — we or you — in station (maqaman), that is, place and dwelling. Its origin is the place of standing, then it was used for place in general. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-Ju'fi and Abu Hatim, from Abu 'Amr, read (مُقامًا) with a ḍammah on the mīm. Its origin is the place of dwelling, and it also refers to dwelling and place, so the two readings agree.

In al-Bahr it was permitted that both the fatḥa and ḍamma forms could be verbal nouns: the original is the verbal noun of qāma yaqūmu, and the second is the verbal noun of aqāma yuqīmu. I saw in some collections a passage attributed to Abu al-Su'ud, may God have mercy on him, on the difference between maqām with a fatḥa and muqām with a ḍamma, and one of them asked him about it saying:

O unique one of the age, O shaykh of mankind, we seek the difference between maqām and muqām.

It is that the first, with a fatḥa on the mīm, is the place of a thing's standing, more general than whether its standing is by itself or by the establishment of another, and whether that is by way of being fixed in it or without it. The second is the place of another's establishing it, or the place of its own standing in a lasting manner. If the governing verb is triliteral, the required form is the first, and likewise if it is quadriliteral and it is not intended to show that the place is where the standing of the annexed noun occurs through the establishment of another, or its lasting standing. But if that is intended, the required form is the second, as when you say: "The tā' of the oath was placed (uqīmat) in the position (maqām) of the waw, to indicate that it is a substitute for the bā', which is the original of the particles of oath."

The positions of words, all of them, although they are bound to the imposition of the one who imposed them, their original position bound to the original imposition has descended to the status of the place of their own standing, and making their positions bound to later usage take the place of compelled positions for those of free choice. This is when the position is an adverbial noun of place. But if it is a mīmi verbal noun and the governing verb is quadriliteral, its rule is to take a ḍamma on the mīm. End of what is intended from it.

You know that in this context it is not in the accusative as an adverb of place nor as a verbal noun, but in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), transferred from the subject, as it is said: that is, whichever of the two groups its station is better ﴿and better in assembly (nadiyy)﴾, that is, in gathering and congregation. In al-Bahr it is the gathering in which people meet for an incident or consultation. It has been said: the assembly of people of generosity. Likewise the nādī. It is related that they used to comb their hair, anoint it, perfume themselves, and wear the finest garments, then they would say this to the poor believers who could not afford that when the verses were recited to them. Al-Imam said: their purpose in this was to oppose the believers, as if they said: if you were upon the truth and we upon falsehood, your condition in this world would be better and more pleasant than ours, because the Wise does not fittingly place His allies, the sincere ones, in punishment and humiliation, and His enemies who turn away from His service in honor and ease. But the disbelievers were in blessing and ease, and the believers were the opposite, so it is known that the truth is not with the believers. This, though it is clearly a barren syllogism arising from a sickly opinion, God, exalted is He, refuted and nullified it with His words, glorified is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 74:

﴿How many generations We destroyed before them, who were better in furnishings and in appearance.﴾

The gist is that many who were greater in blessing than you in this world, such as ʿAd, Thamud and their likes among the rebellious nations, were destroyed by God Most High. Therefore, if the attainment of worldly blessing indicated that a person is honoured by God Most High, it would be necessary that He not destroy anyone among those who live in luxury in this world. There is in this a threat and warning that is not hidden; it is as if it were said: let these people also look at the like of that. ﴿How many﴾ is informative (khabariyyah), for multiplicity, and is the object of ﴿We destroyed﴾; it was placed first because it has the right of initial position (sadarah). It has also been said that it is interrogative (istifhamiyyah), but the first view is the apparent one. ﴿From a generation﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of its vagueness. The qarn (generation) is the people of every age, and its duration has been disputed; it is from the qarn of an animal (the horn), named so because it precedes. From it is qarn al-shams (the horn of the sun), for the first part that rises from it. The phrase ﴿they were better﴾ is in the place of accusative according to what al-Zamakhshari held, and Abu al-Baqa' followed him, as a description (sifah) of ﴿you﴾; Abu Hayyan rejected this, saying that the scholars have stated explicitly that ﴿kam﴾, whether informative or interrogative, is not described and does not describe; and he made it a description of ﴿qarn﴾. The plural pronoun is used because the generation includes many individuals; had the pronoun been singular, it would also have been correct Arabic. It is not refuted by what al-Khafaji said: "kam min rajulin qama" and "kam min qaryatin halakat," on the basis that the prepositional phrase must be construed as attached to an omitted element that is a description of ﴿you﴾, as some claimed al-Radi indicated, because it is permissible for the prepositional phrase to be the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is explanatory with no place in i'rab; so what he claimed is not accepted by him. ﴿Athath﴾ (furnishings) is a specification (tamyiz), and it is the household goods of the house, including bedding, clothing and other things; its singular is ﴿athathah﴾. It has been said there is no singular for it. It has also been said that athath is what is new of goods, and khurthi is what is old and worn out. al-Hasan ibn ʿAli al-Tusi recited:

"The passing of time from Umm al-Walid over us for an age has made the furnishings of the house into worn-out things."

Al-Ri'y (appearance) is the sight, as Ibn ʿAbbas and others said, and it is a form (fiʿl) in the sense of maf'ul from seeing, like al-tahn (grinding) and al-saqy (watering). al-Zuhri, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Talha in the transmission of al-Hamdani, Ayyub, Ibn Saʿdan and Ibn Dhakwan recited ﴿riyyan﴾ with a shaddah on the yaʾ without hamzah. It is possible that this is from that form, with the hamzah changed to yaʾ and assimilated. It is also possible that it is from al-riyy, the opposite of thirst, and what is meant is freshness and beauty.

Abu Bakr, in the transmission of al-Aʿmash, recited ﴿riy'an﴾ with a sakin yaʾ followed by hamzah, and this is by transposition (qalb), its pattern being fil'an. It was also read ﴿ri'aan﴾ with a yaʾ followed by an alif and then hamzah, related by al-Yazidi. Its meaning, as in al-Durr al-Masun, is that some of them show off to one another.

Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, recited ﴿riyyan﴾ with the hamzah removed and shortened. Some people presumed to say it is a solecism (lahn), but this is not so; it has two valid analyses. One is that the original is ﴿riyyan﴾ with a shaddah on the yaʾ, lightened by deleting one of the two yaʾs, namely the second, because it is the one that produced the heaviness, and because the final position is the place of change; this is like its deletion in "la siyyama". The second is that the original is ﴿ri'an﴾ with a sakin yaʾ followed by hamzah, the vowel of the hamzah was moved onto the yaʾ, and then it was deleted according to the well-known rule.

Ibn ʿAbbas also recited, as did Ibn Jubayr, Yazid al-Barbari and al-Aʿsam al-Makki, ﴿ziyyan﴾ with a zayn and a shaddah on the yaʾ, meaning gathered attractions; it is said: "zawāhu zayyan" (with a fatha), i.e. he gathered it. The meaning may also be furnishings, as al-Mubarrad mentioned in the verse of al-Thaqafi:

"Did the litters distress you on the day they departed, with the fine adornment of furnishings?"

The apparent meaning in the verse is the first meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 75:

﴿Say: Whoever is in error, let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension﴾ and so on. This is a command from Him, exalted is He, to His Messenger ﷺ to answer those who boast of the worldly portions they possess over the believers, by explaining the outcome of the matter of both groups. This may be in a general form encompassing them and others who are immersed in and delighted by fleeting pleasure, with "man" (من) taken in its general sense; or in a specific form pertaining to them, with "man" taken as referring to them, and describing them as firmly established in error in order to censure them and to indicate the cause of the ruling, i.e., whoever is settled in error, overwhelmed by ignorance and heedlessness of the consequences of affairs. ﴿Then let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension﴾, i.e., He, glorified is He, extends for him and gives him respite by lengthening his life, granting wealth, and enabling him to act freely. The imperative here carries the meaning of a report, and it was chosen to indicate that this is something that ought to be done in accordance with the requirement of wisdom, in order to cut off excuses, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did We not give you a life long enough for whoever would remember to remember?﴾ So the resulting meaning is: whoever is in error, there is no excuse for him, since the Most Merciful has given him respite and extended for him an extension. It is also permissible that this is for the purpose of istidraj (gradual enticement), as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾. The resulting meaning: whoever is in error, it is God's custom, exalted is He, to extend for him and lead him gradually so that he may increase in sin. It has also been said: the intended meaning is a supplication for extension, to show that no excuse remains after this clear explanation; thus it follows the style of ﴿Our Lord, that they may lead astray from Your way﴾ if it is taken as supplication. In al-Kashshaf it is said: the first aspect is more suited to this context. The mention of the title "the Most Merciful" is because its rulings are what apply... ﴿until, when they see what they are promised﴾ and so on is a goal (ghayah) for the extension. The plural of the pronoun in the two verbs is in view of the meaning of "man", just as the singular in the first two pronouns is in view of its wording. "Ma" is a relative pronoun and the clause after it is its relative clause, with the returning pronoun omitted, i.e., "that which they are promised". Taking "ma" as a verbal-noun (masdariyyah) is contrary to the apparent sense.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿either the punishment or the Hour﴾ is a substitute for ("ma") and a detailing of what is promised, in the manner of excluding the absence of either. By "the punishment" is meant the worldly punishment, through the victory of the believers and their domination over them. By "the Hour" it has been said: the Day of Resurrection, and this is the apparent meaning.

It has also been said: it includes the time of death and the witnessing of punishment, and whoever dies, his resurrection has come; this is so that the goal is connected to what is goaled, since extension does not connect to the Day of Resurrection. It is answered that the matter of the intervening is easy, because the affairs of this world, by their passing and ending, are not counted as an intervening, as has been said. That is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They were drowned, then they were made to enter fire﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so they will know﴾, which is the answer of the condition; and these two are in reality the goal, if we say that the whole is the speech, or its meaning alone, if we say that the speech is the condition and the conditional clause is a qualifier of it. ("Hatta") according to Ibn Malik is a preposition indicating mere goal, and it is neither a preposition nor a conjunction according to the majority. Likewise it is whenever it enters upon the conditional "idha", and it is in the accusative by the condition or the answer, according to the well-known disagreement; and the clause is a resumed clause with no grammatical place. The intended meaning: until, when they witness what they are promised of punishment, whether worldly or otherworldly, only then will they know, ﴿who is worse in place﴾ of the two groups, by seeing the matter contrary to what they were estimating; so they will know that they are worse in place, not better in station. The use of "place" here rather than "station", which is used there, is an intensification in showing the badness of their condition. ﴿And weaker in host﴾, i.e., in group and helpers, not better in assembly. The point of contrast is that the goodliness of the assembly lies in the gathering of the people's faces and notables, the manifestation of their power, and their being backed.

It has also been said: the intended meaning of "assembly" there is the one who is in it, as one says "the high assembly" for honour, and it does not mean that he has a weak host. Nay: ﴿and they had no group who would help them besides God, nor was he among those who could help himself﴾. This was mentioned only to refute what they claimed, that they had helpers among their associates. The apparent view is that "man" is a relative pronoun in the accusative position as object of "they will know", and it is transitive to one object because "knowing" here means "recognizing". The clause ﴿he is worse﴾ is the relative clause. Abu Hayyan permitted that it be interrogative, with knowing in its proper sense, and the clause in the position of an accusative substituting for the two objects. According to Abu al-Baqa', it is a separator, not a subject.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted, and his practice apparently favours it, that what preceded is a goal for the statement of the disbelievers: ﴿which of the two groups is better in station﴾ and so on.

His saying, exalted is He: "how many We destroyed" and so on, and ﴿Say: whoever is in error﴾ and so on, are two parenthetical clauses for rebuke against them; that is, they do not cease saying this statement and persisting in it, not refraining from it, until they witness the promised thing with their own eyes: either the punishment in this world at the hands of the believers, or the Day of Resurrection, and what they will suffer therein of disgrace and torment. Then they will know that the matter is the reverse of what they had estimated. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr criticised this as being very remote, because of the long separation between the goal and what is goaled, together with the fact that separation by two parenthetical clauses is contrary to the view of Abu Ali, who does not permit it. You also know, after resolving the matter of the speech ending at the time of death and not extending to the Day of Resurrection, that considering the continuation and repetition of the statement does not hold without considering the continuation of the recitation, since the statement falls within the scope of the answer to "idha", and that is, as you see, [problematic].

[Commentary of al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on surah 19, verse 76]

﴿And Allah increases in guidance those who are guided﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new clause not grammatically dependent on what precedes it), brought to explain the state of the guided after the explanation of the state of those astray, as Abu al-Su'ud chose. Al-Zamakhshari chose, and Abu al-Baqa' followed him, that it is a conjunction (ʿatf) with the position (mawdi') of ﴿then let him extend﴾ etc. Abu Hayyan did not permit this, whether ﴿then let him extend﴾ is a supplication or a statement in the form of a command, because it occupies the position of a predicate if man is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), and the position of a response to a condition if man is a conditional (shartiyya). The position of the conjoined element would then be the position of the element conjoined to, and the clause made conjoined would be free of a pronoun linking the predicate to the subject and the response to the condition. It was also said against this: the conjunction is unsuitable in meaning, just as it is unsuitable in grammatical construction (i'rab), since it is not sound to say: "Whoever is in error, Allah increases those who are guided in guidance." This is answered by saying that the meaning is: whoever is in error, his error is increased, and the guidance of his enemies is increased, because that is among the things that enrage him. As for what preceded, that man is a conditional and not a relative pronoun: stipulating a pronoun returning from the response to the conditional noun, other than a adverb of time, is prohibited, and it is not agreed upon among the grammarians, as in al-Durr al-Masun, although it is implied, as you have heard. It should not be hidden that this conjunction is not free from artificiality (takalluf). Al-Baydawi chose that it is a conjunction with the whole of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Whoever is in error, let the Most Merciful extend [his term]﴾ etc., so that the contrast (taqabul) is complete, for he (ﷺ) was commanded to answer them concerning their saying to the believers: "Which of the two groups?" etc. So he should bring mention of the two categories originally. Al-Tibi said: It is as if it were said: "Say: whoever among the two groups is in error, let Allah grant him respite and prolong for him the duration of his life, so that he increases in misguidance, and Allah gathers for him the punishment of both abodes. And whoever among them is in guidance, Allah increases his guidance, so that He, glory be to Him, gathers for him the best of both abodes." This answer is of the wise approach (al-uslub al-hakim, a method of addressing the listener according to what is most fitting), and in it is the meaning of the saying of Hassan:

"Do you satirize him, while you are no match for him? Then may your evil be the ransom for his good,"

in supplication and in avoiding direct confrontation. In al-Kashf it is stated that this is better than what al-Zamakhshari chose.

﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾: the traditional reports concerning its interpretation have already been mentioned. It has been chosen that they are the acts of obedience whose benefits endure and whose returns last, because of its generality. All of them are ﴿better in reward with your Lord﴾ in its familiar meaning. It was said: they return from what the disbelievers have been granted of the blessings that are deficient and perishing, in which they take pride. ﴿And better﴾ than that too ﴿in return (maradd)﴾, that is, in place of return and in outcome, because their outcome is everlasting joy and enduring bliss, while the outcome of that is eternal regret and painful punishment.

In mentioning the title of Lordship together with its addition to his pronoun (ﷺ), there is a gentleness and honour that is not hidden. The repetition of "better" is for greater care in explaining the superiority and for emphasizing it.

In the verse, according to what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, there is a kind of mockery of the disbelievers, in that it refers to naming their recompense "reward." The comparative form (al-mufadala), as he said, is according to the pattern of "summer is hotter than winter," meaning that its heat is more intense than the cold of winter. It is not mockery, because if you said, "Fire is better than the freezing cold," or the reverse, as mockery, the mockery would apply to the comparative and the object of comparison, and that does not work here. The essential point of what he intended is that the reward of these is more eminent than the reward of those, that is, their punishment. As for the statement of the author of al-Taqrib concerning it: that its answer is not known; how not, when mercy has preceded wrath, and in Paradise is of bounty and grace what cannot be measured, while the Fire is of His justice, exalted is He; and his statement that it is unsuitable for the context of threat together with what it contains of prohibition, is refuted by the fact that the discourse is built on contrast, and that it is in the pattern of response (mushakala) in their saying ﴿Which of the two groups is better in station and finer in assembly?﴾. So His promise to these is not merely for threatening those, but is intended for its own sake, as stated in al-Kashf.

The author of al-Fara'id said: What al-Zamakhshari said is far from natural speech and usage, and there is nothing in their discourse that supports it. It is possible to say: the meaning is that the reward of righteous deeds in the Hereafter is better than their reward in this world, which is what they obtained from it of good according to their claim, and of the wealth, status and benefits that come from them. End. His denial of it was rejected, because al-Zajjaj mentioned it in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity promised to the righteous?﴾, and because it has parallels. Remoteness from natural speech is within the realm of prohibition.

Some of the scholars of verification (muhaqqiqin) said: the form af'al (comparative) in the verse is to indicate attribution of the event and absolute increase, as was said about Yusuf, peace be upon him: "the best of his brothers," and this is one of his four states which some scholars of Arabic mentioned. So the meaning is that their reward and their return are characterized by increase in goodness over one who is characterized by it, regardless of these who take pride in their worldly life. Therefore it does not necessarily follow that they share in the goodness, so reflect.

According to what Abu al-Su'ud held, the sentence, under both possibilities of resumption and conjunction with what precedes it, is a new sentence revealed from Him, exalted is He, to explain the excellence of the deeds of the guided. It is not included within the scope of the speech imparted (mulaqqan) in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And Allah increases in guidance those who are guided﴾. It contains a consolation for the hearts of the believers against whatever pride of the disbelievers might stir in them, just as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿until, when they see﴾ — to — (troops), is a completion of their threat. Both are part of the command to answer their saying: ﴿Which of the two groups is better in station and finer in assembly?﴾, and the expression "better" is taken as in the pattern of response. That this is part of the answer is what comes first to mind, but the apparent sense of the address rejects it, and it may be forced to fit. Perhaps we have already given in this surah what benefits you regarding this matter, so remember.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 77:

﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs?﴾ That is, in Our signs, among which are the signs of resurrection. Al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Tabarani, Ibn Hibban and others narrated from Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, who said: "I was a blacksmith (qayn), and al-'As ibn Wa'il owed me a debt. I came to him to demand it, and he said: 'No, by Allah, I will not pay you until you disbelieve in Muhammad ﷺ.' I said: 'No, by Allah, I will not disbelieve in Muhammad ﷺ, not even when you die and are resurrected.' He said: 'When I die and am resurrected, I will come to you, and I will have wealth and children there, and I will pay you.' So Allah the Exalted revealed: (Have you seen...) etc."

In another narration, Khabbab said to him: "No, by Allah, I will not disbelieve in Muhammad ﷺ, whether alive or dead, or even when you are resurrected." Al-'As said: "When I am resurrected, I will come to you..." etc. In another narration, "some men from the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ came to him demanding a debt they were owed by him. He said: 'Do you not claim that in Paradise there is gold, silver, silk, and fruits of every kind?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Your appointment is the Hereafter. By Allah, I will be given wealth and children, and I will be given the like of your book which you have brought.'" Then it was revealed. It was also said that it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who had statements resembling this. Abu Muslim said: it is general to everyone who has this attribute. The first account is the one established in the books of the Sahih.

The hamza is for expressing wonder at the state of that disbeliever and for announcing that it is so strange and abominable that it should be seen and that wonder should be felt at it. The fa' is for coordination with an implied element required by the context, meaning: "Have you looked, and seen the one who disbelieved in Our manifest signs, which everyone who has come upon them should believe in," (and he said), mocking them, prefacing his speech with the wicked oath, "By Allah, I will be given" in the Hereafter, though it is in this world, as al-Tabarsi related from some of them. The authentic reports reject this, unless the giving is understood, as was said, as continuous giving until the Hereafter, meaning: "I will indeed be given continuous giving," ﴿wealth and children﴾. The intended meaning is: look at him and be amazed at his wondrous state and his shameful boldness.

It was also said that seeing is metaphorical for informing, by way of mentioning the cause and intending the effect, and the interrogative is metaphorical for a command to do it, because what is meant by phrases such as "What did you do?" is "Tell me." So it is a performative utterance used metaphorically for another performative utterance, and the fa' remains in its original sense.

The meaning is: "Inform us of the story of this disbeliever following the account of those who said: ﴿Which of the two groups is better in station?﴾" (the verse). It was also said: following the account of the one who said: ﴿Will I, when I have died, be brought forth alive?﴾ etc. What we have mentioned regarding the meaning of the verse is the more apparent, and it was chosen by the scholar Abu al-Su'ud.

The second view has been criticised with the statement: You know that the well-known usage of (ara'ayta) is in the sense of "tell me" by way of interrogation, remaining in its original sense or moved to a meaning suited to it, not by way of a command to inform another and intending "tell me" here by way of interrogation, remaining in its original sense or moved to a meaning suited to it, not by way of a command to inform another and intending "tell me" here, which hardly holds, as is not hidden.

It was also said: the intended meaning is "I will be given in this world," but the occasion of revelation contradicts this. The scholar said: except that the giving may be understood as continuous giving until the Hereafter, in which case it fits this. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash, Talha, Ibn Abi Layla and Ibn 'Isa al-Isfahani read (wuldan) with a dammah on the waw and sukun on the lam. It was said that it is the plural of walad, like asad and usud, and they cited as evidence the verse:

"Indeed I have seen people who have multiplied wealth and offspring (wuldan)."

It was also said that it is a dialectal form of walad, like al-'Arab and al-'Urb, and they cited as evidence the verse:

"Would that so-and-so had been in his mother's belly, and would that so-and-so had been the offspring (walad) of a donkey."

The truth is that it occurs in Arabic speech both as a singular and as a plural, and both are valid here. 'Abd Allah, Yahya ibn Ya'mur read (widan) with a kasrah on the waw and sukun on the lam, and it has the same meaning.

The statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Has he gained knowledge of the unseen?﴾ is a refutation of his monstrous words and a demonstration of their falsehood, following the expression of wonder at them that was indicated earlier. The clause is therefore resumptive (mustaʾnafah) and has no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis). It has also been said that it is in the accusative position, occupying the place of a second object of ﴿أرأيت﴾ (ara'ayta, "have you seen?"), with the meaning of "tell me." But this is, as you see, far-fetched. The hamzah is interrogative (hamzat al-istifham). The original form is أاطّلع (a-ittala'a), and the connective hamzah (hamzat al-wasl) was dropped for lightness. One reading has إطّلع (ittala'a) with a kasrah on the hamzah and the interrogative hamzah omitted, because the particle أم (am) indicates it, as in the line of poetry: "Did you throw the pebbles with seven, or with eight?" The verb is transitive by itself, and it may also take عَلى (ʿala, "over"). It is not intransitive, so the verse does not involve the omission and transfer of a particle. The meaning of al-ittila' (ittila', "gaining sight of") here is manifestation in a manner of elevation and possession. For this reason it was chosen over an expression such as "knowledge," and the meaning is: Has he reached such a height of grandeur that he has attained knowledge of the unseen, which the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, may His majesty be exalted, has reserved for Himself, to the extent that he claimed he would be given wealth and children in the Hereafter and swore an oath to it?

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that the meaning is: look into the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). ﴿Or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?﴾ He said: "There is no god but Allah," by which he hopes for that. It is related from Qatadah: "The covenant is the righteous deed for which Allah the Exalted has promised reward." So the meaning is: "Has he known the unseen, or has he performed a deed by which he hopes for that in return?" Some scholars said: "The covenant is on its apparent meaning."

The meaning is: Has he known the unseen, or has Allah the Exalted given him a covenant and a firm pledge, and said to him that this will certainly come to pass? This was related from al-Kalbi. This is a concession to the eye (muja­rah maʿa al-ʿayn) according to the literal sense of his speech, just as his words are of that kind. The mention of the title al-Rahmaniyyah (the Most Merciful) is to indicate that mercy is the cause for granting what he claims.

[Page 131]

﴿Nay﴾ is a rebuke and a deterrent against uttering that monstrous claim, and in it is an admonition regarding his error. This is the view of al-Khalil, Sibawayh, al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad, and the majority of the Basran grammarians concerning this particle, and there are other views on it which we will, God willing, point out. This is the first place in the Qur'an where it occurs. It is repeated in the second half of the Qur'an, occurring in thirty-three places. Abu al-Abbas did not permit pausing (waqf) on it at any place.

Al-Farra' said: It falls into four categories. The first is where it is good to pause on it and good to begin with it. The second is where it is good to pause on it but not good to begin with it. The third is where it is good to begin with it but not good to pause on it. The fourth is where neither of the two is good.

As for the first category, it occurs in ten places: this verse (﴿Nay. We will record what he says﴾); His saying, ﴿that they may be a source of honour for them﴾ ﴿Nay﴾; His saying, ﴿that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind﴾ ﴿Nay﴾; His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿those you have attached to Him as partners﴾ ﴿Nay﴾; His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He, ﴿that he should enter a Garden of Bliss﴾ ﴿Nay﴾; His saying, Majestic and Exalted is He, ﴿that I should increase﴾ ﴿Nay﴾; His saying, Mighty is His name, ﴿scrolls unrolled﴾ ﴿Nay﴾; His saying, Glorified and Exalted is He, ﴿my Lord has humiliated me﴾ ﴿Nay﴾; His saying, Blessed is His name, ﴿that his wealth will make him immortal﴾ ﴿Nay﴾; and His saying, Exalted is His majesty, ﴿then He will save him﴾ ﴿Nay﴾. Whoever makes it a rejection of what precedes it pauses on it, and whoever makes it mean "indeed" (alla), which is used for alerting, or mean "truly" (haqqan), begins with it, and the word admits of that in these places.

As for the second category, it occurs in two places: the saying of Majestic is His majesty, recounted: ﴿So I fear they will kill me﴾ ﴿He said: Nay﴾; and the saying of Mighty is His affair, ﴿Indeed we are overtaken﴾ ﴿He said: Nay﴾.

As for the third category, it occurs in nineteen places: the saying of Exalted is His affair: ﴿Nay, indeed it is a reminder﴾; ﴿Nay, by the moon﴾; ﴿Nay, but you deny the Recompense﴾; ﴿Nay, when it reaches the collarbones﴾; ﴿Nay, there is no refuge﴾; ﴿Nay, but you love the hasty life﴾; ﴿Nay, they will soon know﴾; ﴿Nay, He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him﴾; ﴿Nay, rather, what they have earned has covered their hearts﴾; ﴿Nay, but you do not honour the orphan﴾; ﴿Nay, indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾; ﴿Nay, indeed the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyin﴾; ﴿Nay, indeed they, from their Lord that Day, will be veiled﴾; ﴿Nay, when the earth is pounded﴾; ﴿Nay, indeed man transgresses﴾; ﴿Nay, if he does not desist﴾; ﴿Nay, do not obey him﴾; ﴿Nay, you will soon know﴾; ﴿Nay, if you knew with certain knowledge﴾. It is in these that it is not good to pause on it, because it is a rejection of what is in them.

As for the fourth category, it occurs in two places: ﴿Then nay, you will soon know﴾ and ﴿Then nay, they will soon know﴾. It is not good to pause on "then" (thumma) because it is a conjunction, nor on "nay" (kalla), because the benefit lies in what comes after it.

Some have said: it is good to pause on "nay" throughout the Qur'an, because it means "desist" (intahi ila) in one place, which is His saying, ﴿Nay, by the moon﴾, since it is connected to the oath, in the sense of your saying "i.e., by my Lord." ﴿We will record what he says﴾, i.e., We will make manifest that We have written his saying, like the saying of the poet:

When we trace our lineage, no base mother bore me, nor will you find any way but to acknowledge it.

That is: when we trace lineage, you will know and it will become clear that I am not the son of a base mother. Or it means: We will take vengeance on him, the vengeance of one who writes down the crime of the offender and preserves it against him, for the very act of recording such things is hardly delayed from the speech, according to His saying: ﴿He utters no word but that there is with him an observer ready﴾, and His saying, Glorified, Majestic and Exalted is He, ﴿and Our messengers with them record﴾. The basis of the first is treating the manifestation of a hidden thing as the bringing into existence of a non-existent matter, by the common feature that each is a bringing out from concealment into visibility. So it is an implicit metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah) founded on likening the manifestation of writing before the eyes of witnesses to its occurrence. The basis of the second is naming a thing by the name of its cause, for the recording of a criminal's crime is certainly a cause of his punishment. This was stated by Abu al-Su'ud. It was also said: the writing in the second sense is a metaphor for a threat of vengeance, but this is obscure. Some have said: there is no metaphor in the verse, but the "sin" (sin) is for emphasis (ta'kid), and what is meant is "We write now." This was refuted on the grounds that when the sin emphasizes, it emphasizes only a promise or a threat, and indicates that it will certainly occur in the future. As for its emphasizing what is meant to refer to the present, that is not so. Thus it is said; let it be examined.

Al-A'mash read (sa-yuktabu) with the initial letter ya' and the passive form. And it is reported from ʿAsim: ﴿and We will extend for him of the punishment an extension﴾, in place of what he claims for himself of being aided with wealth and children, i.e., We will prolong for him of the punishment what he deserves, or We will increase his punishment and multiply it for him from the extension. It is said: "madda-hu" and "amadda-hu" have the same meaning. And the reading of ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, supports this: (wa-numiddu) with a damma. In this sense it may be used with the lam and without it, and its meaning according to the first is "We will bring about the extension for him." It is more emphatic than "We will extend him," and it is reinforced with the verbal noun (masdar), to signify the intensity of God's wrath against him for his disbelief, his fabrication against God, Glorified is He, and his mockery of His mighty signs. We seek refuge in God, Mighty and Majestic, from what necessitates wrath.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 80:**

﴿And We shall inherit from him what he says﴾. That is, We shall strip him of that and take it from him at his death, as an heir takes what he inherits. What is meant by "what he says" is its referent and its actual object, namely the wealth and children he was given in this world. A man says, "I own such-and-such," and God says, "Rather, I have more than what you say." The meaning is in the past tense, and so is "says" in the preceding clause. This implies that what he claimed has no actual referent apart from what was mentioned. The word "what" (*ma*) is either a substitution for the pronoun, a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*), or an object. In that case the meaning is: We shall inherit from him what We gave him in this world. ﴿And he will come to Us﴾ on the Day of Resurrection ﴿alone﴾, not accompanied by wealth or children, which he had as a surplus. That is, he will be brought there with nothing extra. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "And We shall inherit from him what he has, and he will come to Us alone, having no wealth and no children," which clearly supports the meaning mentioned. It has also been said that the meaning is: We shall deprive him of what he claimed he would obtain in the Hereafter of wealth and children, and give it to others among the deserving. This was reported from Abu Sahl. Interpreting inheritance in this way is an interpretation by necessary consequence. "What he says" is also meant here in the sense of its referent. The child given to another must be the child of that other person whom he had in this world, and the giving of it to him would be by joining the two together as he desires. This is based on the view that there is no procreation in Paradise.

The scholars have differed on this. A group, including Mujahid, Tawus and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, held that there is no procreation, citing the lengthy hadith of Laqit (may Allah be pleased with him), which carries such majesty, dignity and the light of prophethood that it calls out to its authenticity. Abu Abdullah ibn Mandah said of it: "None denies it except a rejecter or an ignorant person." A group of imams of the Sunnah have transmitted it, from his words: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, will we have wives there, or will there be righteous ones among them?' He (ﷺ) said: 'The righteous women for the righteous men; you will delight them and they will delight you, just as your pleasures in this world, except that you will not procreate.'" They also cite what was reported from Abu Dharr al-Uqayli, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The people of Paradise will not have children."

Another group held that there is procreation, citing what al-Tirmidhi included in his Jami' from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When a believer desires a child in Paradise, its pregnancy, birth and growth will occur in a single hour, just as he desires." He said: "Hasan gharib." They also cite what Abu Nu'aym reported, also from Abu Sa'id: "It was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, will children be born to the people of Paradise, for a child is part of complete joy?' He, peace be upon him, said: 'Yes, by Him in whose hand is my soul, and it will be no more than the time it takes for one of you to wish: its pregnancy, nursing and youth.'"

Those who held the first view replied to the above by saying that what is meant is the denial of procreation or children in the familiar manner known in this world. It was objected that the last hadith is weak, as al-Bayhaqi said.

As for the first hadith, al-Saffarini said about it: "The best of its chains is the chain of al-Tirmidhi, and he judged it to be gharib, that it is not known except through the narration of Abu al-Siddiq al-Tajji. Its wording has also been disturbed: sometimes it is narrated from him as 'when the child is desired,' sometimes as 'he desires a child,' and sometimes as 'a man among the people of Paradise will have a child born to him.'" And if we say that it has a fair chain according to the earlier narration, as al-Tirmidhi indicated, then someone may say that it contains a conditional clause, and that it may not occur. And although "idha" (when) is apparent in the certain, it is sometimes used merely for a more general conditional. As for the answer to the two previous hadiths given in the way mentioned, it is weaker than a spider's web, as is evident. In sum, the view preferred by the majority is that there is no procreation. Al-Saffarini preferred this view on ten grounds, but there is room for discussion regarding most of them. And Allah knows best.

It has also been said that what is meant by "what he says" is the very statement mentioned, not its referent. The meaning is: he says this statement only so long as he is alive; but when We take him, We shall prevent him from saying it, and he will come to Us abandoning it, alone and separated from it.

This was objected to on the grounds that it is based on the statement being uttered by him as a matter of belief, and that it continues while he keeps uttering it, hoping for its content to come about. There is no doubt that this is impossible for one who disbelieved in the resurrection; he only said what he said as mockery.

It was answered: we do not accept that the interpretation is built on this, since it is possible that what is meant is that he says this and mocks only so long as he is alive; but when We take him, We shall prevent him from mocking, through what will be revealed to him and what will befall him. Or it may be said that the basis of what was mentioned is accommodation with the accursed one, as was explained earlier.

It has also been said that the meaning is: We shall preserve his statement in order to strike his face with it on the standing place (of judgment) and reproach him with it, and he will come to Us in his poverty and humiliation, alone, without wealth or children, to whom We did not grant his request or give him what he wished for. Thus two matters converge upon him: the consequence and burden of his statement, and the loss of what he hoped for. Al-Nahhas went to the interpretation of inheritance as preservation, and he cited from it: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets," meaning the preservers of what they said. You know well that the preservation of his statement is already known from the saying of the Exalted: ﴿We shall write down what he says﴾.

In al-Kashshaf it is said: it is possible that he desired and hoped that Allah would give him wealth and children in this world, and his greed reached the point that he swore an oath about it. So the Glorified said: Suppose We gave him what he desired; will We not inherit it from him in the end, and he will come to Us tomorrow alone, without wealth or children? This is like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾. So his desire and his oath will not benefit him. End of quotation. It is not hidden that this is a very remote possibility in itself, and in terms of the occasion of revelation, and forcing it to fit this interpretation does not bring it nearer, as is clear.

﴿Alone﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) according to all the views. But it has been said that it is a future circumstantial clause (*hal muqaddarah*), when the intention is to deprive him of wealth and children and to give that to its rightful recipient, because being alone at that point implies a difference between the misguided and the guided. And that happens only after the standing place, unlike the case where something other than that is intended from what the views contain, since it does not imply a difference between them, and the aloneness of the standing place suffices for validity even though it is shared. Some have claimed that the circumstantial clause is future on all the views, because what is meant is the continuation of separateness from wealth and children, or from the statement mentioned; and continuation is not established at the moment of arrival but is anticipated, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Enter it, abiding forever﴾. There is no concealing what is in this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 81:

﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah﴾ is a report of a general transgression that applies to all, one which is followed by the opposite of what they hope to result from it, following the report of the statement of the well-known disbelieving man and its being followed by the contrary of its content. That is: the disbelieving wrongdoers took idols, or whatever includes them and all other false objects of worship, as gods, exceeding Allah, exalted is He, ﴿that they might be for them a source of might﴾, meaning that they might gain strength through them, by their being for them a means of access to Him, mighty and majestic is He, and intercessors before Him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 82:

﴿Kalla﴾ is a rebuke and a restraint for them from that, and it contains a denial of the occurrence of what their vain hopes were attached to. ﴿They will deny their worship [of them]﴾, i.e., the gods will disown the worship of those disbelievers for them, and Allah Most High will make speak those among them who were not speaking, so they will all say, "You did not worship us," just as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And when those who associated others with Allah see their associates, they will say, "Our Lord, these are our associates whom we used to invoke besides You." But they will throw back at them the word, "Indeed, you are liars."﴾ Or the disbelievers will deny, when they witness the consequence of the evil of their disbelief, their worship of them, just as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Then their trial will be only that they will say, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not those who associated others with Allah."﴾

The meaning of His, Exalted is He, saying ﴿and they will be against them opposed (diddan)﴾ according to the first interpretation, as has been said, is that the gods in whom they hoped to find might (ʿizz) will be opposed to that might, i.e., [a source of] humiliation and disgrace, or helpers against them, as has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and this is more apparent than the previous explanation. Their being helpers against them is because they will curse them. It has also been said: because their worship was a cause of punishment.

It has been objected that this did not occur on the Day of Resurrection, whereas the apparent meaning of the verse is that it occurs on that Day, and the matter is simple in this regard. It has also been said: because they will become an instrument of their punishment, when they are made fuel of the Fire and the pebbles of Hell. This is not possible except on the assumption that by "the gods" idols are meant. The use of "opposed" (didd) for "helper" is because a man's helper opposes his enemy and contradicts him by assisting him against him. According to the second interpretation, the disbelievers will be "against" the gods, i.e., enemies of them, from the expression of people: "The people are against you" (ʿalaykum), i.e., your enemies. From this comes the saying: "O Allah, be for us and not against us opposed (didd)," i.e., contradicting what they used to be upon, disbelieving in them after they used to worship them. Thus ʿalayhim, according to what has been said, is the predicate of "yakūnūn," and "diddan" is an emphatic circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), while the enmity is intended by what precedes it. It has also been said that it is the predicate and ʿalayhim is in the position of a circumstantial phrase. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk explained it as "enemies" (aʿdāʾ), and according to what is reported from al-Akhfash, it is like "ʿaduww," which is used both in the singular and the plural.

The author of al-Qamus said likewise and considered the word here to be plural. Some have denied that it is used of both the singular and the plural, and said it is only for the singular. It was made singular here because of the unity of the meaning on which their opposition revolves, for they are by that like one thing, as in his, ﷺ, saying related by al-Nasa'i: "They are one hand against whoever is other than them." The author of al-Fara'id said: it was made singular because it is mentioned in contrast to His saying (ʿizzan), which is a verbal noun (maṣdar) suitable to be a plural, so this, although it is not a verbal noun, is suitable to be a plural when considering what is meant by it, which is humiliation.

This holds if it is complete, but it is complete only on the first meaning. Al-Bahr has explicitly stated that on that interpretation it is a verbal noun that is used as a description of the plural just as it is of the singular, so let it be consulted.

Abu Nuhayk read here and in what preceded "kallan" with a fatḥa on the kaf and tanwin. It has been said that it is the particle of restraint, except that he intended to pause on it, so its alif became like the alif of extension (alif al-iṭlāq), and then it was replaced with tanwin. It is also possible that he did not intend a pause, but the alif was treated like the alif of extension, because the alif of an indeclinable word has no origin, and it could not be the rhyme letter. This is called the tanwin of the exaggerator (tanwīn al-ghālī), and it attaches to letters and other things and combines with alif and lam, as in your saying:

"Restrain your blame, O censurer, and the rebuke, / And say, if I am right, indeed he has been right."

This is not like "qawārīran" (in the verse "qawārīr"), as is not hidden, contrary to those who claimed it. In Ibn Jinni's al-Muhtasab it is stated that "kallan" is a verbal noun from "kalla al-sayf" when it became blunt, and it is accusative by a verb implied from its own word, and the estimate here is "all this opinion and belief is kallan," and the meaning is that it became weak, a weakness. It has also been said that it is an object, with the estimate "they bore kallan." Something similar is said about what preceded. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is an attribute of "ālihah," and the meaning is the heavy burden that has no good in it, and the singular is because it is in the form of a verbal noun. And as you see, this is [weak]. The meaning favors what preceded, even though it has been said there is a verbal (lafẓī) strain in it, and that it entails affirming tanwin, which is an error, as in similar cases.

Abu ʿAmr al-Dani related from Abu Nuhayk that he read "kullan" with a ḍamma on the kaf and tanwin, and on this reading it is accusative by a verb omitted that is indicated by "sa-yakfurūna," so that it is of the type of ishtighal, like: "Zaydan, I passed by him," i.e., "they will deny kullan," i.e., the worship of each of the gods. There is then an omitted genitive, though it may not be estimated. al-Ṭabarī related from him that he read "kullun" with a ḍamma on the kaf and raf', and on this reading it is a subject (mubtada'), and the sentence after it is its predicate.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 83–84:

﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with full incitement?﴾ We have appointed them as their companions (qara'in) and made them dominant over them; or We have empowered them over them and enabled them to lead them astray. ﴿They incite them with a strong inciting﴾: they stir them up and agitate them towards sins with intense agitation, through all kinds of embellishments (taswilat) and whisperings (waswasa), for azz (incitement), hazz (shaking) and istifzaz (provoking) are sisters in meaning, signifying intense agitation. The clause ﴿tauzzuhum﴾ is either a conditioned circumstantial clause (hal muqaddara) from the devils, or a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that came as an answer to what arose from the beginning of the speech, as if it were said: "What do the devils do to them?" So it was said: "They incite them," etc. The purpose of the verse is to express the wonder of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at what the preceding noble verses contained, from His words, glorified is He, ﴿And man says: "When I am dead, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?"﴾ up to here, and what He related of these disbelievers, the deviants and the stubborn rebels, of the various kinds of vile sayings and deeds, persistence in error, immersion in misguidance, excess in obstinacy and insistence upon disbelief, without any deterrent that turns them back or any compassion that restrains them, and their unanimous obstruction of the truth after its clarification, and the complete absence of any association with it. It is also an indication that all of this is due to the misguidance and seduction of the devils, not because there is any deficiency in the conveyance (of the message) or any valid excuse in principle. In it there is also consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so it is a conclusion (tadhyil) to those verses for what has been mentioned. The purpose is not to express his wonder, upon him be blessings and peace, at the sending of the devils upon them, as the linking of the vision to it might suggest, but rather at what has been mentioned of their conditions insofar as they are effects of the devils' seduction, as His words, glorified is He, ﴿They incite them with a strong inciting﴾ indicate. ﴿So do not hasten against them﴾, that they should be destroyed in accordance with what their crimes require, and that they should be wiped out to the last of them, and the earth be cleansed of their filth. The fa' (so) indicates that what precedes it is a likely occasion for the forbidden act, requiring the prohibition, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this is an enemy to you and to your wife, so let him not expel you both from the Garden﴾.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We count for them a counting﴾ are a justification for the cause of the prohibition, by explaining that their destruction is near, for nothing remains for them but days and breaths which We count, a counting, that is, few, as was said regarding His words, exalted is He: ﴿a few counted dirhams﴾. This does not contradict what has passed, that it is extended for one who is in error, i.e., it lengthens, because it is relative to the apparent state in their view, and it is little when considered in its outcome and in the sight of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It was said: the justification by what has been mentioned indicates that their breaths and days end with the ending of the counting, and there is no doubt that, despite their multitude, they are exhausted in counting swiftly; so by this meaning he expressed the few, as if it were said: there is between you and their destruction only limited days and counted breaths, as though in swiftness they are passed in the hour in which they are counted, were they to be counted. This is not based on the principle that everything that is counted is few. End of quote. The first is the apparent meaning, and this is more remote in its purport.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that when he recited this verse he wept and said: "The last of the count is the going out of your breath; the last of the count is the parting from your family; the last of the count is the entering of your grave."

It is related from Ibn al-Sammak that he was in the presence of al-Ma'mun and recited it, and he said: "When breaths are by count and have no replenishment, how swiftly they are exhausted."

And by Allah, how well said is the one who said:

Indeed the beloved among the loved ones is one who is snatched away; no gatekeeper or guard prevents death.

And how can one rejoice in the world and its pleasures, a young man whose words and breaths are counted against him?

It was also said: the purpose is that We count their deeds, so that We may recompense them for them.
