On the Day We shall gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation (﴿يَوْمَ نَحْشُرُ المُتَّقِينَ إلى الرَّحْمَنِ وفْدًا﴾), meaning riders, as a group reported on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, has been related by a number of transmitters. Ibn Abi al-Dunya related it in his work on the description of Paradise, and Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related it through various chains from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this verse, and I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is the delegation anything other than riders?' He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: ('By Him in whose hand is my soul, when they come forth from their graves they will be met with white she-camels that have wings, upon which are saddles of gold, the straps of their sandals a shining light, each step of which is as far as the eye can see, and they will reach the gate of Paradise.') …" The hadith continues. These she-camels are from Paradise, as has been stated in a report narrated by 'Abd Allah ibn al-Imam Ahmad and others, as a statement (mawquf) attributed to 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face.

It is related from 'Amr ibn Qays that they will ride upon images of their righteous deeds, which are of the utmost beauty.

It is also reported that each of them will ride whatever he wishes, of camels, horses, or ships that come swimming with them. The root of al-Wafd (الوَفْدُ, "delegation") is the plural of wafid (وافِدٌ), like wufud (الوُفُودُ) and awfad (الأوْفادُ). Al-Wafd derives from wafada ilayhi and 'alayhi, yafidu, wafdan, wufudan, wifadatan and ifadatan, meaning he came and arrived.

(Page 136)

In al-Nihayah (a lexicon of hadith terms by Ibn al-Athir): al-Wafd (الوَفْدُ) are people who gather and travel to countries, the singular being wafid (وافِدٌ). This likewise applies to those who go to rulers for a visit, to seek gifts (istirfad), to seek pasture (intija'), or for other purposes. Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: al-Wafd and al-Wufud are those who come before kings seeking the fulfilment of their needs. From this comes "al-wafd min al-ibil" (الوَفْدُ مِنَ الإبِلِ), meaning the camel that goes ahead of the others. This meaning that he mentioned is the well-known one. From here it has been said that the word al-wafd implies honour and esteem, since it indicates a comparison of the state of the God-fearing with the state of the delegations of kings. The intended meaning is not the literal sense of wifada in all its aspects, because that includes departing from the one visited, whereas the God-fearing abide forever in the reward of their Lord, Mighty and Majestic. The statement is elliptical, meaning "to the honour of the Most Merciful," or "to His reward, which is Paradise," or "to the abode of His honour," or something similar. It has been said that gathering "to the Most Merciful" is a notice that they will be assembled from scattered places and distant regions to Him who will show them mercy. Al-Qadi said: The choice of "al-Rahman" in this surah has a significance, and perhaps it is that the context of the discourse in it is to enumerate the great blessings and to describe the state of those who give thanks for them and those who deny them. So it is as if it were said here: on the Day We gather the God-fearing to their Lord, who had already enveloped them with His mercy, and embraced them with His compassion. Its sum is: on the Day We gather them to the One who accustomed them to mercy. In this there is a great glad tiding, and what it contains.

And He (Glorified is He) has paired that with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will drive the criminals﴾, as cattle are driven, ﴿to Hell, a thirsty herd﴾. That is, thirsty, as narrated from Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan, Qatada and Mujahid. Its origin is the verbal noun of *warada*, meaning he went to the water. The reciter said:

*Ridi, ridi, wirda qatatin samma / kudriyyatin a'jabaha bardu al-ma'*
(Back, back, the drinking of a dove that is deaf, of the *kudriyya* kind, whom the coolness of the water pleased.)

Its application to the thirsty is a metaphor (*majaz*, figurative usage) through the relation of necessity (*'alaqat al-luzum*), because whoever comes to the water comes only from thirst. It is also permitted that *al-warid* means the animals that come to the water, and the speech is then a simile, meaning: We drive them like the animals that come to the water. In *al-Kashshaf*, the use of the word *al-warid* contains great mockery and contempt, especially since He has made its destination (*mawrid*) Hell, from which Allah the Exalted protect us by His mercy. So let one consider the great difference between the two sentences. Al-Hasan and al-Jahdari read ﴿The righteous are gathered and the criminals are driven﴾ with both verbs in the passive voice.

The verse has been cited as evidence that the terrors of the Resurrection are specific to the criminals, because the righteous are honoured from the beginning, so how could hardship befall them afterwards? In *al-Bahr al-Zahir*, it is said that the gathering of the righteous to the Merciful as a delegation (*wafdan*) is after the conclusion of the reckoning and the separation of the two groups. Ibn al-Jawzi related this from Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, and al-Nisaburi mentioned it as a possibility in examining the previous argument.

You know that this does not hold according to what you have heard in the report transmitted from Ali, may Allah honour his face, for it is explicit that they ride when they come out of their graves and reach the gate of Paradise, and it is clear that they are not called to account.

Some have said: the intended meaning of "the righteous" is those described with complete piety, and it is not far-fetched that they enter Paradise without reckoning, for reports have been authenticated that a group of this Ummah enter Paradise in this manner. In the two *Sahihs* from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us one day and said: "The nations were shown to me. A prophet would pass with one man, a prophet with two men, a prophet with no one, and a prophet with a company. Then I saw a great mass and hoped it was my Ummah. It was said: 'This is Musa and his people.' Then it was said: 'Look.' I saw a great mass and it was said: 'These are your Ummah, and with them seventy thousand who will enter Paradise without reckoning.'" Then the people dispersed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not explain it to them. His companions discussed it, saying: "As for us, we were born in polytheism, but we have believed in Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ). These are our children." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "They are those who do not seek incantation (*istirqa'*), do not seek cauterization (*iktiwa'*), do not practise augury (*tiyara*), and upon their Lord they rely." The hadith is long.

Al-Tirmidhi transmitted, and graded it good, from Abu Umama, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: My Lord promised me that He would admit seventy thousand of my Ummah into Paradise without reckoning or punishment. With each thousand, seventy thousand, and three handfuls from the handfuls of my Lord."

Imam Ahmad, al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani transmitted from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "My Lord has given me seventy thousand of my Ummah who will enter Paradise without reckoning." Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Why did you not ask Him for more?" He said: "I did ask Him, and He gave me this," and he spread apart his hands, stretched out his arms and gathered himself up.

Hisham said: "This is from Allah, Mighty and Majestic; its number is not known."

Al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Amr ibn Hazm al-Ansari, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) delayed from us for three days; he did not come out except for the prescribed prayer and then returned. When it was the fourth day he came out to us (ﷺ), and we said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you delayed from us until we thought some event had occurred.' He said: 'Nothing new happened. My Lord promised me that He would admit seventy thousand of my Ummah into Paradise without reckoning, and during these three days I asked my Lord for more, and I found my Lord Generous and Bountiful, so He gave me with each one seventy thousand.'" The report continues. Beyond these there are other reports, and in some of them are mentioned those who enter Paradise without reckoning, described as: those who praise Allah, exalted is His state, in ease and in hardship; those whose sides forsake their beds; those whom neither trade nor commerce distracts from the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He; one who dies on the road to Makkah, going or returning; the seeker of knowledge; the wife obedient to her husband; the child dutiful to his parents; the merciful and patient one; and others. The reconciliation between the reports is evident. Restricting "the righteous" to those described with complete piety entails either that the disobedient believers are included among the criminals, or that the verse does not admit of describing their condition. Some have used the verse as evidence for the report that the righteous are not brought to be present on their knees around Hell, so that what indicates generality is specified by such a thing. So reflect, and Allah is the Granter of success.

The word ﴿day﴾ (*yawma*, يوم) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*zarf*), governed by a deleted verb placed after it, meaning: on the day We gather and drive, We shall deal with the two groups in such actions that speech cannot contain their description. It has been said that it is in the accusative as an object governed by a deleted word placed first, addressed to the master of the addressed, (ﷺ), meaning: mention to them, by way of encouragement and warning, the day We gather, and so on. It has been said that it is an adverb of time governed by *na'udd* (We count), in view of the sense of recompense. It has been said that it is governed by the saying of the Exalted and Glorified: ﴿They will deny their worship of them﴾. It has been said it is governed by the saying of the Exalted, Majestic: ﴿and they will be against them as adversaries﴾. And it has been said it is governed by the saying of the Exalted, whose state is great:

[Page 137]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 87:

﴿They will not have power of intercession﴾. What the momentousness of the context requires, and the eloquence of the revelation demands, is that it (the phrase) be in the accusative (naṣb) according to one of the first two readings, and that this be a resumptive clause (isti'nāf) clarifying some of the matters of that Day that indicate its terror. The pronoun of plurality refers to a general group encompassing both the pious and the criminals, that is, the servants in general. It was also said that it refers to the pious, and it was said that it refers to the criminals among the people of faith and the people of disbelief. (As for "al-shafā'ah" [intercession]), according to the first two views it is the verbal noun of the active form, and according to the third view it should be the verbal noun of the passive form.

And His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿except him who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ is a connected exception (istithnā' muttaṣil) from the pronoun according to the first view. The position of the excepted element is either nominative, as a substitute (badal), or accusative, according to the original principle of exception. The meaning is: the servants do not have the power to intercede for others, except for one among them who has the qualities that make him worthy to intercede, and this is what is meant by "the covenant." Ibn 'Abbas interpreted it as the testimony that there is no god but Allah. The disavowal of power and strength is the non-hope in anyone except Allah, exalted is He. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh [Page 138] and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited the verse and said: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, says on the Day of Resurrection: 'Whoever has a covenant with Me, let him stand up.' None will stand except those who said this in the world: 'O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, I covenant with You in this worldly life that if You leave me to myself, You will bring me near to evil and distance me from good, and I trust in nothing but Your mercy. So make it a covenant with You which You will fulfill for me on the Day of Resurrection, for indeed You do not break the promise.'" Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Muqatil that he said: "The covenant is righteousness," and something similar was narrated from al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj. Al-Layth said: "It is the preservation of the Book of Allah, exalted is He." Calling what has been mentioned a "covenant" is by way of metaphor (tashbīh). It was also said: the intended meaning of "the covenant" is the command and permission, from the expression: "The ruler made a covenant (ʿahida) to so-and-so with such-and-such," when he commanded him to do it. That is: the servants do not have the power to intercede except for one whom Allah, mighty and majestic, has permitted to intercede and commanded to do so, for he has the power to do that. And the word "ʿinda" (with) does not at all refuse the sense of "ittikhādh" (taking), for just as one says "I took permission (akhadhtu al-idhn) to do such-and-such," one can say "ittakhadhtuhu" (I took it). Yes, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with the Most Merciful﴾ there is a kind of refusal of this, although the majority hold the first view. The meaning of intercession according to both views is what encompasses intercession for entry into Paradise and intercession for other matters. The Mu'tazilah (a theological school that denies this) disputed this, and did not permit intercession for entry into Paradise, but the reports refute them. On the authority of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed a man from my community will intercede for a multitude of people, and they will enter Paradise through his intercession, and indeed a man will intercede for a man and his household, and they will enter Paradise through his intercession.'" Ibn 'Atiyyah allowed that by intercession is meant the general intercession in the judgment of the decision, and by "the one whom the Prophet (ﷺ) took" [a covenant with], and by "the covenant," the promise of that in His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾; but this is very contrary to the apparent meaning. According to the second view regarding the plural pronoun, the exception is from the intercession with an implied genitive (muḍāf maḥdhūf), and it is also connected.

As for the excepted element, there are the two previously mentioned possibilities: that is, the pious do not have the power of intercession except the intercession of one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful, and the intended meaning of that is faith, and the verbal noun is annexed to its object. It was also said: on this view the excepted element (al-mustathnā minhu) is omitted, meaning: the pious do not have the power of intercession for anyone except one who has taken, etc., that is, except for one who is characterized by faith. It is also permitted that the exception be from the intercession with an implied genitive according to the first view regarding the pronoun, and that the verbal noun be annexed to its agent or annexed to its object. It is also permitted on this view that the excepted element be omitted, as you have heard. And according to the third view, the exception is from the pronoun and is also connected, and regarding the excepted element there are the two possibilities: that is, the criminals do not have the power to have intercession made for them except for one who was a believer, for he has the power to have intercession made for him. It was also said: the exception, on the assumption that the pronoun returns to the criminals, is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ), because the intended ones are the disbelievers; and interpreting this as referring to sinners and disbelievers is far-fetched, as Abu Hayyan said. In that case the excepted element is obligatorily accusative according to the Hijazis, while in the view of the Tamim tribe its accusative case is permitted, as is its substitution.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the waw in ﴿they will not have power﴾ be the sign of the plural, like that in "akalūnī al-barāghīth" (the fleas ate me), and that the agent be ﴿him who has taken﴾, because it has the sense of the plural. Abu Hayyan criticized him by saying: "The Qur'an should not be interpreted according to this rare dialect, especially with the clear reading of the waw as a pronoun." Al-Ustadh Abu al-Hasan ibn 'Usfur mentioned that it is a weak dialect. Furthermore, the waw, alif and nun which are used as signs cannot be relied upon to be followed by an agent except with explicit plurality or explicit duality, or coordination. Either it comes in a singular word that is used for a plural or dual, and then its establishment requires transmission (naql); but as for the return of pronouns in the dual and plural to a singular in form that is intended to mean the dual or plural, this is well-known and attested in the speech of the Arabs, so it is possible to analogize these signs to those pronouns; but the safer course is not to say that except by hearing. End. Ibn al-Munir also criticized him, saying: "In this there is artificiality, for if one makes the waw a sign of the plural and then returns a pronoun in the singular to its form, namely 'ittakhadha' (he took), this is a summary after a clarification, and it is a reversal in the method of eloquence, which is clarification after summary. The waw, in its grammatical role, even if it does not refer back to 'man', nevertheless reveals its meaning just as a pronoun referring to it reveals it. Then he said:

"So be alert to this criticism, for it is more marketable than currency,
and it is admired on the neck of the beautiful woman, the necklace."

End. From this it is known that the view permitting the pronoun to return to it first according to its meaning and second according to its form is not free from turbidity.

"And they say: 'The Most Merciful has taken to Himself a son.'" This is a narration of the crime of those who said, "Uzayr is the son of Allah," "Isa is the son of Allah," and "the angels are the daughters of Allah," from among the Jews, the Christians and the Arabs—exalted is He above what they say, a great exaltation. It follows the narration of the crime of those who worshipped what was worshipped besides Him, mighty and majestic is He, by way of joining one story to another story. So the pronoun refers to those you already know of, even though it has not been mentioned explicitly, because the matter is clear.

It has been said: it refers to the criminals; it has been said: to the disbelievers; it has been said: to the wrongdoers; it has been said: to the servants, as indicated by the mention of the two groups, the God-fearing and the criminals. And in it there is the attribution of what belongs to some to all of them, although they did not approve of it, and the discussion of this has already passed.

Al-Alusi's commentary on Surah Maryam (19), verse 89:

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed you have produced something monstrous﴾ is a rejection of their false claim and an amplification of its gravity, by way of iltifat (the shift) from the third person (absence) to the second person (address), which indicates the utmost wrath and the intensity of anger, expressing the extreme of reproach and condemnation, and recording against them the utmost in shamelessness, ignorance and audacity. It has also been said: there is no iltifat, and the speech is with an implied "Say to them": "Indeed you have produced..." etc.

The word iddan (إدًّا), with a kasra on the hamza, as in the reading of the majority (al-Jumhur), and with a fatha on it, as Al-Sulami read it, means "a wonder," as said by Ibn Khalawayh. It has also been said that it means "a great evil" or "a grave denial." Al-Iddah means "severity," and adda al-amr and ada al-amr (meaning "the matter became difficult/burdensome") and aadani al-amr ("the matter weighed on me and was grave to me").

Al-Raghib said: al-idd is "the denounced thing (al-munkar) which contains a clamour," from the saying of the people: addat al-naqatu taidu, meaning the she-camel repeated her moaning with intense modulation.

It has also been said: iddun with a fatha is a verbal noun (masdar), and with a kasra it is a noun (ism), meaning "you have done a strange matter or a severely denounced thing whose magnitude cannot be measured." Thus, ja'a and ata are used in the sense of fa'ala (to do), and so they take the same transitive construction as fa'ala.

Al-Tabarsi said: this is from the category of elision and transference (al-hadhf wal-iesal), meaning: "you have come with a thing of iddun."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 90:**

﴿The heavens are about to be torn apart because of it.﴾ This is in the position of a qualifier (ṣifah, "attribute") of *iddan* (a monstrous thing), or it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the magnitude of its gravity and horror. *Al-tafaṭṭur* (being split apart), as most scholars have stated, is simply *al-tashaqquq* (cracking). According to what al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) says, it is cracking lengthwise, since he explained *al-fatr*, which is the root of this word, as splitting in that same way. The usage of the word does not require restricting it to what has been mentioned. It has been said that usage requires *al-fiṭr* (rupture) to be one of the properties of a solid body, for one says "a vessel that is cracked" (*ināʾun maftūr*) but does not say "a garment that is cracked" (*thawbun maftūr*), but rather "torn" (mashqūq). In my view this belongs to the conventions of rejection and acceptance. On this basis, the attribution of *tafaṭṭur* to the heavens and of *infishaq* (splitting) to the earth in the Most High's words ﴿and the earth is split open﴾ indicates that the heaven is harder than the earth. The intensification (*takthir*) indicated by the form *tafaʿʿul* has been attributed to the verb itself, because that is most fitting to the context. It has also been said that it refers to its object, and this is preferred because Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, Abu Bakr (from ʿAsim), Yaʿqub, Abu Bahriyya, al-Zuhri, Talha, Humayd, al-Yazidi and Abu ʿUbayd read ﴿yanfaṭirna﴾ (the imperfect of *infaṭara*), and the agreement of the two readings requires this. Also, *infiʿal* (the reflexive/passive form) has been preferred in ﴿the earth is split open﴾, where there is no plurality in the object. For this reason ﴿and of the earth, the like of them﴾ has been interpreted as "regions" and the like, as will come, God willing. Some scholars explained the difference in form, on the view that the intensification lies in the verb, by saying: since the heavens are sanctified, and God has never been disobeyed in them at all, not even in any sort of disobedience, they have not been accustomed to sin; the earth, however, is affected by the enormity of sin in a way that the heavens are not affected.

Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿yatasaddaʿna﴾ (be split asunder). Al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit*) said: "It should be taken as an explanation (tafsir), not as a reading, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf on which there is consensus, and because reliable transmitters report from him that he read like the majority." End of quotation. It is not hidden from you that in any case this supports the view of those who claim that *al-fatr* is one of the properties of a solid body, based on what is in the *Qamus* (al-Firuzabadi's dictionary) that *al-sadʿ* is a crack in a solid thing.

[p. 140]

Nafi', al-Kisa'i, Abu Haywa and al-A'mash read ﴿yakādu﴾ with a *yāʾ* from below, ﴿and the mountains collapse﴾, meaning they fall and crumble, *hadd*an (crumbling). It is in the accusative because it is a cognate object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) of *takharru*, since it has the meaning of "crumbles," as we have indicated. This is the view of Ibn al-Nahhas. He also permitted that it be a cognate object of an implied *tanhaddu* (crumbles), the clause being in the position of a circumstantial (*hal*). It has been said that it is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, in the accusative as a circumstantial, from *hadda* in its transitive use, meaning "being crushed." It has also been permitted that it be an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), meaning "because they crumble," taking it as from *hadda* in its intransitive use, meaning "collapsed." Its coming as intransitive is something Abu Hayyan, who is an imam in language and grammar, has explicitly stated, so no weight is given to one who denies it. In that case the crumbling is an action of the mountains, so the subject of the verbal noun and the verb that is the cause coincide. It has also been said that it is not their action, but when someone crushes them, crumbling results for them, so it is correct for it to be an object of purpose. The speech contains an affirmation that this is *idd*, and the "almost" (*kaydūdah*) in it is taken in its literal sense of approaching a thing. Al-Akhfash interpreted it here, and also in the Most High's words ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ (20:15), as "intending," and he cited as evidence the verse of the poet:

*"She almost, and I almost, and that is the best intention, if there returned from the time of passion what has passed."*

But there is no proof for him in it. The meaning is that the horror of that ugly word and its magnitude are such that, if it were imagined in a sensible form, these great bodies would not bear it and their parts would scatter from its intensity. Or the meaning is that the right of that word, if those great inanimate things understood it, would be that they split, break apart, and collapse from its atrocity. It has also been said the meaning is "the Resurrection almost occurred," for these things will in reality happen on the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said that the speech is a metaphor (kinayah) for God's anger against the speaker of that word, and that were it not for His forbearance, glorified and exalted is He, that would have happened and the speaker and others would have perished, meaning: "I almost did that out of anger, were it not for My forbearance."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: "Shirk (polytheism) caused the heavens, the earth, the mountains and all creation to be frightened of it, except the two species (humans and jinn), and they almost ceased to exist because of it, glorifying God." In this is an affirmation of a kind of understanding in those bodies and substances appropriate to them. This has already been discussed.

In *al-Durr al-Manthur*, in the discussion of this verse, it is reported that Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn al-Mubarak, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-ʿAzama*, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shuʿab al-Iman*, through the chain of ʿAwn, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "A mountain calls to another mountain by its name: 'O so-and-so, has anyone passed by you today who remembered God, the Most High?' If it says 'Yes,' it rejoices." ʿAwn said: "Then do they not hear falsehood when it is said, and do they not hear good? They are more attentive to good." And he recited (the verses) "and they say..." etc. End of quotation. It is clearly apparent in understanding.

Ibn al-Munir said: "There appears to me a meaning in the verse that I have not seen from anyone else. God, glorified and exalted, has metaphorically used the indication of these bodies to His existence, mighty and majestic, as described by the perfect attributes that are necessary for Him, by making them glorify Him with His praise. The Most High said: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him, and there is not a thing but glorifies Him with His praise﴾ (17:44). Among what the heavens, the earth, the mountains, and indeed every atom of them indicate is that God, the Most High, is exalted above being attributed a son:

*'And in everything there is a sign that indicates that He is One.'*

So the one who believes that a son is attributed to Him, mighty and majestic, has nullified the indication of these existing things to the glorification and sanctification of God, the Most High. Thus, to nullify what is in them of the spirit of the indication for which they were created, their forms are made to be nullified by splitting, cracking and breaking." End of quotation.

[p. 141]

It was objected to this that existing things indicate a Creator who is powerful, knowing and wise, since an effect indicates its agent and the capacity to act indicates the thing acted upon, and the perfection of knowledge indicates knowledge and wisdom. As for their indicating oneness, there is no basis for this, and such a thing is not established by poetry. It was answered that if they did not indicate it, the argument of mutual prevention (*hadith al-tamanuʿ*, the argument from mutual hindrance) would not come, as the Mawla al-Khayali (Mawla al-Khayali) verified in his glosses on the commentary of al-Nasafi's *ʿAqaʾid* by al-ʿAllama al-Thani (the Second Scholar, i.e., al-Taftazani).

Some said: they indicate the greatness of His state, may He be exalted, that nothing resembles Him or comes near Him, so it follows that He has no partner and no son, for if He were like that, He would have an equal, mighty and majestic. Therefore this indication was expressed by glorification and transcendence.

Perhaps what we have indicated is more preferable and more precise. The attribution of a son to Him, mighty and majestic, does not mean anything but polytheism, so reflect. The majority hold that the speech is to explain the abomination of that word, in the sense that if the inanimate things understood it, they would consider it hugely grave and would crumble from its abomination. Similar to this is a well-known style among the Arabs. The poet said:

*"When the news of al-Zubayr arrived, the walls of Medina humbled themselves, and the humble mountains."*

And another said:

*"So the valley of Mecca became shuddering, as if the earth had no Hisham in it."*

And another said:

*"Did you not see a manifest crack in the sky over the son of Lubayna, al-Harith ibn Hisham?"*

And so on, beyond these. This is a type of hyperbole, and it is accepted when accompanied by something like *kada* (almost), as in the noble verse. This has been explained in its proper place.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verses 91–92:

﴿That they ascribe a son to the Most Merciful﴾, with the lam of causation (al-lam al-ta'liliyyah, the lam expressing reason) understood. After its deletion, its position is in the accusative according to Sibawayh, and in the genitive according to al-Khalil and al-Kisa'i. It is the cause for the causality contained in (minhu) [from Him], but in terms of what the situation indicates, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful that He should take a son﴾. It has also been said that it is the cause for (takadu) [they are about to], etc. This was objected to: that (takadu) being caused by this is already known from (idda) [a monstrous thing], so it would entail repetition. It was answered with something that is not free from scrutiny. It has also been said that it is the cause for this, and this is the cause for the collapsing. It has been said that there is no implied lam at all, rather (anna) and what follows it are in the sense of a genitive verbal noun (masdar majrur), in apposition (badal) to the pronoun in (minhu), as in the poet's saying:

"In a state where, were Hatim among the people, despite his generosity he would withhold water, O Hatim."

Here (Hatim) is genitive by apposition to the pronoun in (judihi) [his generosity]. Abu Hayyan deemed this improbable because of the separation by two clauses between the substitute (badal) and the substituted-for (mubdal minhu). It has also been said that the verbal noun is nominative, as the predicate of an elided subject, meaning: what necessitates that is their calling upon the Most Merciful to have a son. Regarding this there is discussion. It has also been said that it is nominative as the subject of (hadda), and is considered a verbal noun in the active sense, meaning: their calling upon the Most Merciful to have a son demolished it. Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying that it is far-fetched, because the apparent reading is that this verbal noun is emphatic (ta'kidi), and an emphatic verbal noun does not govern. Even if it were supposed to be non-emphatic, it would not govern by analogy except when it is an imperative such as (darban Zaydan) [strike Zayd], or after an interrogative such as (idribā Zaydan). What is here is neither of the two, and what has come governing where neither applies is like the saying:

"Standing by them, my companions upon their mounts."

This is rare. Insisting that what is here is among the rare cases does not remove the distance. Perhaps what we have mentioned is the most refined of the opinions and the most preferable, so reflect upon it. And God, exalted is He, is the Guide to the straight path.

(Waladan) [a son], according to most scholars, means "greatness" (sumuwwan). The verb (da'a) in the sense of naming takes two objects directly, as in the poet's saying:

"Umm 'Amr called me her brother, though I was not her brother, and I had not nursed at her milk."

It may also take the second object with (bi), so one says: "I named my son Zayd" (da'awtu waladi bi-Zayd). Here it is limited to the second object, and the first is omitted to indicate generality and comprehensiveness, covering every son that they ascribed to Him, mighty and majestic is He, such as those ascribed to Jesus, Ezra, peace be upon them both, and others. It is also permitted that it be from (da'a) in the sense of (nasaba) [to attribute lineage], whose reflexive form (mutawai') is what is in the saying of the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him: ("Whoever claims to be [the son] of other than his masters...").

And the saying of the poet:

"We are the sons of Nahshal; we are not called after a father other than ourselves, nor do the sons sell us."

Here it takes one object. The prepositional phrase (wa-al-jarr wa-al-majrur) may be permitted to be related to an elided element which functions as a circumstantial clause (hal) from (waladan), and may be related to what precedes it. The clause (ma yanbaghi) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of (da'aw) [they called]; it has also been said from the subject of (qalu) [they said]. (Yanbaghi) is the present tense of (inbaghaa), the reflexive of (baghaa) in the sense of "to seek"; its past tense has been heard, so it is a fully conjugable verb in general. Ibn Malik counted it in al-Tashil among the verbs that are not conjugable, and Abu Hayyan faulted him for this. It may be said that his meaning is that it is not fully conjugable. The phrase (an yattakhidha) is in the sense of a verbal noun of its agent, and the meaning is: it is not fitting for Him, glorified is He, to take a son, nor does He seek one, exalted and majestic, because that is impossible in itself, since it entails being a part or being of the same kind, and every such matter is impossible. Placing (al-Rahman) in the position of the pronoun serves to indicate the cause of the ruling, by alerting that everything other than Him, exalted is He, is either a blessing or one upon whom a blessing is bestowed. How can that be compared with the One who is the origin of blessings and the patron of their roots and branches?

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verses 91–92:

﴿That they ascribe a son to the Most Merciful﴾, with the lam of causation (al-lam al-ta'liliyyah, the lam expressing reason) understood. After its deletion, its position is in the accusative according to Sibawayh, and in the genitive according to al-Khalil and al-Kisa'i. It is the cause for the causality contained in (minhu) [from Him], but in terms of what the situation indicates, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful that He should take a son﴾. It has also been said that it is the cause for (takadu) [they are about to], etc. This was objected to: that (takadu) being caused by this is already known from (idda) [a monstrous thing], so it would entail repetition. It was answered with something that is not free from scrutiny. It has also been said that it is the cause for this, and this is the cause for the collapsing. It has been said that there is no implied lam at all, rather (anna) and what follows it are in the sense of a genitive verbal noun (masdar majrur), in apposition (badal) to the pronoun in (minhu), as in the poet's saying:

"In a state where, were Hatim among the people, despite his generosity he would withhold water, O Hatim."

Here (Hatim) is genitive by apposition to the pronoun in (judihi) [his generosity]. Abu Hayyan deemed this improbable because of the separation by two clauses between the substitute (badal) and the substituted-for (mubdal minhu). It has also been said that the verbal noun is nominative, as the predicate of an elided subject, meaning: what necessitates that is their calling upon the Most Merciful to have a son. Regarding this there is discussion. It has also been said that it is nominative as the subject of (hadda), and is considered a verbal noun in the active sense, meaning: their calling upon the Most Merciful to have a son demolished it. Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying that it is far-fetched, because the apparent reading is that this verbal noun is emphatic (ta'kidi), and an emphatic verbal noun does not govern. Even if it were supposed to be non-emphatic, it would not govern by analogy except when it is an imperative such as (darban Zaydan) [strike Zayd], or after an interrogative such as (idribā Zaydan). What is here is neither of the two, and what has come governing where neither applies is like the saying:

"Standing by them, my companions upon their mounts."

This is rare. Insisting that what is here is among the rare cases does not remove the distance. Perhaps what we have mentioned is the most refined of the opinions and the most preferable, so reflect upon it. And God, exalted is He, is the Guide to the straight path.

(Waladan) [a son], according to most scholars, means "greatness" (sumuwwan). The verb (da'a) in the sense of naming takes two objects directly, as in the poet's saying:

"Umm 'Amr called me her brother, though I was not her brother, and I had not nursed at her milk."

It may also take the second object with (bi), so one says: "I named my son Zayd" (da'awtu waladi bi-Zayd). Here it is limited to the second object, and the first is omitted to indicate generality and comprehensiveness, covering every son that they ascribed to Him, mighty and majestic is He, such as those ascribed to Jesus, Ezra, peace be upon them both, and others. It is also permitted that it be from (da'a) in the sense of (nasaba) [to attribute lineage], whose reflexive form (mutawai') is what is in the saying of the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him: ("Whoever claims to be [the son] of other than his masters...").

And the saying of the poet:

"We are the sons of Nahshal; we are not called after a father other than ourselves, nor do the sons sell us."

Here it takes one object. The prepositional phrase (wa-al-jarr wa-al-majrur) may be permitted to be related to an elided element which functions as a circumstantial clause (hal) from (waladan), and may be related to what precedes it. The clause (ma yanbaghi) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of (da'aw) [they called]; it has also been said from the subject of (qalu) [they said]. (Yanbaghi) is the present tense of (inbaghaa), the reflexive of (baghaa) in the sense of "to seek"; its past tense has been heard, so it is a fully conjugable verb in general. Ibn Malik counted it in al-Tashil among the verbs that are not conjugable, and Abu Hayyan faulted him for this. It may be said that his meaning is that it is not fully conjugable. The phrase (an yattakhidha) is in the sense of a verbal noun of its agent, and the meaning is: it is not fitting for Him, glorified is He, to take a son, nor does He seek one, exalted and majestic, because that is impossible in itself, since it entails being a part or being of the same kind, and every such matter is impossible. Placing (al-Rahman) in the position of the pronoun serves to indicate the cause of the ruling, by alerting that everything other than Him, exalted is He, is either a blessing or one upon whom a blessing is bestowed. How can that be compared with the One who is the origin of blessings and the patron of their roots and branches?

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on surah 19, verse 93:

Already indicated by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾. That is, there is none of them, of the angels and of the two species (humans and jinn), but that he is a slave belonging to Him, exalted and majestic, who returns to Him in servitude and submission to His decree and His predestination, glory be to Him and exalted. So the "coming" is figurative (ma'nawi). It was also said that it is literal (hissi), and that what is meant is: none but comes to the place of His judgment, which is the land of the Gathering (ardh al-mahshar), submissive, not claiming for himself anything of what they attributed to Him. But this is not the case, as is not hidden.

(Man) is a relative pronoun meaning "the one who" (alladhi), and (kull) ("every") is prefixed to it because what is intended by it is the category (jins), as was said regarding His saying, exalted: ﴿And the one who brought the truth (alladhi jaa bi-s-sidq)﴾, and the line of poetry: "And every one that has burdened me, I bear it." It was also said that man is a relative clause with an indefinite antecedent (mawsufah), because it occurs after (kull) in the indefinite form, as it occurs after (rubba) in the line of poetry:

Rubba man anḍajtu ghayzan ṣadrahu / qad tamannā lī mawtan lam yuṭi'

Al-Zamakhshari, in the first of the two readings (al-Bahr), preferred that its occurrence as a qualified noun (mawsufah) is rare compared with its occurrence as a relative pronoun (mawsulah).

ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), Ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Haywa, Talha, Abu Bahriyya, Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Ya'qub read (ātin) with tanwin, and (al-Raḥmāna) in the accusative, according to the original form.

(ʿAbdan) is in the accusative in both readings as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). The verse has been used as evidence that a father does not own his child, and that he is freed upon him if he comes to own him.

**Verse 94:** ﴿Indeed, He has enumerated them and counted them with an exact counting.﴾

﴿لَقَدْ أحْصاهُمْ﴾ (He has enumerated them): He has confined them and encompassed them, such that none of them can escape from the grasp of His knowledge and the fist of His power, exalted is His majesty.

﴿وعَدَّهم عَدًّا﴾ (and counted them with an exact counting): that is, He counted their persons, their breaths, and their deeds, for everything with Him, exalted is He, is by a measure.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 95:**

﴿And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone.﴾ That is, singled out from followers and helpers, wholly devoted to Allah, the Exalted, and utterly in need of His help and mercy. How then could he be of His kind or comparable to Him, so as to take Him as a son or to associate partners with Him? Glorified is He, exalted far above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation.

It has also been said: that is, each one of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, the worshippers and the worshipped, will come to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, separate from the other. So the worshippers will be separated from the gods they claimed were helpers or intercessors, and the worshipped will be separated from the followers who worshipped them. This requires the absence of benefit, and by this the likeness to the One in whose hand is the dominion of everything is negated, blessed and exalted is He.

In (ātīhi) there is an indication of their coming in that manner, definitely, which is not present in yaʾtīhi. For this reason it was chosen, and it is the predicate of (kulluhum). When kull is annexed to a definite noun that is pronounced, as in kulluhum or kullu l-nās, it is related that it is permissible to return the pronoun to it in the singular, observing its wording, so one says kullukum dhāhib (each of you is going), and it is permissible to return it in the plural, observing its meaning, so one says kullukum dhāhibūn (each of you are going).

Ibrahim ibn Asbagh, in the book Ru'us al-Masa'il, reported consensus on the permissibility of both forms. Abu Zayd al-Suhayli said: when kull is placed at the beginning and is annexed in form to a definite noun, it is only good to use the singular predicate, taking the meaning into account, because the meaning of kullukum dhāhib, for example, is "each one of you is going," and this is not observing the wording. Otherwise it would be permissible to say al-qawm dhāhib, because kull is from kull, and al-qawm is a collective noun singular in form. End of quote.

In al-Bahr it is stated that establishing kullukum dhāhibūn in the plural requires a transmission from the Arabs. Al-Zamakhshari, in his tafsir of this verse, used the plural, and the good assumption about him is that he found this in their speech. When the definite noun annexed to kull is omitted, what is heard from the Arabs is both forms, and there is no dispute about this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 96:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection (wudd)﴾. That is: affection in hearts, because of their faith and their righteous deeds. The well-known view is that this appointment takes place in this world.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, 'Abd ibn Humayd and others related from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah loves a servant, He calls Jibril, saying: 'I have loved so-and-so, so love him.' Then he calls out in the heaven, and then love for him is placed upon the earth." That is the saying of Allah, ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾, to the end of the verse.

The mention of the title "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahman) is because what is promised is among its effects. The sin (in sawfa, "will") is because the surah is Meccan, and they were despised at that time among the disbelievers, so Allah, glorified is He, promised them this; then He fulfilled it when Islam increased and grew strong after the Hijrah. It is also mentioned that the verse was revealed concerning the emigrants to Abyssinia along with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and that He, glorified is He, promised to place affection for them in the heart of the Negus (al-Najashi).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf that when he emigrated to Medina he felt distress at being separated from his companions in Mecca, among them Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah and Umayyah ibn Khalaf, so Allah revealed this verse. According to this, the verse is Medinan.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami related from al-Bara' who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to 'Ali, may Allah honour his face: Say, 'O Allah, make for me a covenant with You, and make for me affection (wudd) in the breasts of the believers.' Then Allah, glorified is He, revealed this verse." Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: You will not find a believer except that he loves 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, and his household.

The Imamiyyah narrated the report of its revelation concerning 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Baqir, and they supported this with what is authentic in their view: "that he, may Allah honour his face, said: Even if I struck the nose of a believer with this sword of mine, on condition that he hate me, he would not hate me; and even if I poured the whole world upon a hypocrite, on condition that he love me, he would not love me. That is because it was decreed and it passed, upon the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: 'No believer hates you, and no hypocrite loves you.'"

The intended meaning is the lawful love which is free of excess. Some Christians claimed love for him, may Allah honour his face. The linguist imam Radi al-Din Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Yusuf al-Ansari al-Shatibi recited for Ibn Ishaq the Christian al-Rash'ani:

"'Udayy and Taym, I do not seek to mention them with evil, but I am a lover of Hashim;

And what concerns me regarding 'Ali and his kin, when they are mentioned, is that in Allah they fear no blame of a blamer.

They say: What is the matter with the Christians that you love them, while the people of intellect, of Arabs and non-Arabs,

So I said to them: Indeed I reckon their love has spread among the creatures, even the animals."

You know that if the hadith is authentic, its falsehood is established. I think the attribution of these verses to the Christian has no basis, and they are among the verses of the Shi'ah who composed the lie; and they have many such schemes, as was made clear in the Twelver Tuhfah. Apparently, according to this, the verse is also Medinan. Then, regarding all the other narrations about the occasion of revelation, the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion.

al-Jubba'i held that this refers to the Hereafter; it was said: in Paradise, when they will be brothers on couches facing one another; and it was said:
[page 144]
when their good deeds are presented before the heads of the witnesses. The matter of the sin (in sawfa) is clear according to this. Perhaps singling out this promise among what they will be granted on the Day of Resurrection of noble honours is because the disbelievers will then fall into mutual hatred, enmity, severance and mutual cursing. It has been mentioned as the connection (of this verse): when the ugly conditions of the disbelievers were detailed, it was followed by mention of the good conditions of the believers. It may also be said, on the basis that this refers to the Hereafter: when He, majestic is His glory, informed that all of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth will come to Him, glorified is He, alone on the Day of Resurrection, He comforted the believers by saying that He, majestic and exalted, will make for them affection on that day. Ibn 'Atiyyah explained it in this sense as His love for them, and by it he meant His honouring them and His forgiving their sins, glorified and exalted is He. It is permissible that the promise is the appointing of affection in both this world and the Hereafter, and I do not see this as far from the truth. Neither this nor what precedes it prevents the mention of the title "the Most Merciful", since it is permissible to call the generality: indeed "O Merciful of this world and the next" has come, and "Compassionate of both."

Abu al-Harith al-Hanafi read "wuddan" with a fatha on the waw. Jannah ibn Hubaysh read "widdan" with a kasra on it. All of these are dialectal forms of it, and likewise in "al-widad".

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 97:

﴿So We have only made it easy﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, by sending it down ﴿in your tongue﴾ (bi-lisanika), i.e., in your language. This is a well-known metaphor (majaz mashhur) in that regard. The ba' (in bi-lisanika) is in the sense of ʿala ("upon"), or it retains its original sense of attachment (al-ilsaq), since the verb "yassarnā" ("We made easy") is construed as containing the meaning of "anzalnā" ("We sent down"), meaning: We made it easy by sending it down to you in your language. The fa' (in "fa-innamā") gives the reason for a matter to which the noble context leads, as if it were said: after the revelation of this noble surah, convey this message, give glad tidings with it, and warn with it, for We have only made it easy in your clear Arabic tongue ﴿that you may give glad tidings thereby to the God-fearing﴾, those characterized by taqwa (God-consciousness) in order to act upon what it contains of commands and prohibitions, or those who are heading towards it, on the basis that this is a metaphor of the first kind ﴿and warn thereby a people most contentious﴾, who do not believe in it out of obstinacy and stubbornness. The word *ludd* is the plural of *alladd*, which, as al-Raghib said, is "the fierce opponent who is most intractable," and its root meaning is "the intensely hard," *al-ladid*, i.e., the side of the neck; this is because he cannot be turned away from what he intends.

And from Qatadah: *al-ludd* are those who are vehement in falsehood in argument, who take up every side (ladid), i.e., every direction, in disputation. From Ibn ʿAbbas, *al-ludd* is interpreted as "those in darkness." From Mujahid, it is interpreted as "the wicked (fujjar)." From al-Hasan, it is interpreted as "the deaf." From Abu Salih, it is interpreted as "the crooked." All of these are interpretations by way of a necessary concomitant (tafsir bi-l-lazim). The intended people are the people of Makkah, as related from Qatadah.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 19, verse 98:

﴿How many generations have We destroyed before them?﴾ This is a promise to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) included within the threat of destruction against these people, and an encouragement to him, peace be upon him, to warn. That is: We destroyed many generations before these obstinate ones. ﴿Do you perceive any of them, or hear from them a whisper?﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) confirming the content of what came before it. The interrogative carries the sense of negation: that is, you do not perceive any one of them.

Abu Haywa, Abu Bahriyya, Ibn Abi Ablah and Abu Ja'far al-Madani read (تَحُسُّ) with a fatha on the taʾ and a damma on the ḥāʾ. ﴿or hear from them a rikz﴾: that is, a faint sound. The root of the word is concealment, and from it comes rakz al-rumh (the planting of a spear) when its tip is buried in the earth, and al-rikaz (buried treasure) for hidden wealth. Some scholars restricted rikz to a faint sound without the articulation of letters or speech, but most hold the first meaning. The faint sound was singled out because it is the most basic and common form, and because if a faint trace disappears, the disappearance of other things is all the more so.

The meaning is: We destroyed them completely and uprooted them, such that you see none of them and hear from them not even a faint sound, let alone anything more. It was also said: the meaning is that We destroyed them completely, such that you neither see any of them nor hear anyone who reports about them or reminds of them with a faint sound. The sum is: We destroyed them, so there is neither trace nor report. The address is either to the master of those addressed, ﷺ, or to everyone fit to be addressed.

Hanzala read (تُسْمَعُ) as the present tense of (أُسْمِعْتُ) in the passive voice. And Allah knows best.

* * *

(From the path of allusion in the verses) ﴿And mention in the Book Abraham; indeed he was a siddiq, a prophet﴾: this is a command to the Beloved to mention the Friend (Khalil) and what Allah, exalted is He, bestowed upon him of the requirements of friendship, so that those who aspire may be encouraged to adorn themselves with as much of it as they can. The siddiq, according to what Ibn 'Ata' said, is one who stands with his Lord, glorified is He, upon the threshold of truthfulness at all times, such that no opposition ever contests his truthfulness in any state. Abu Sa'id al-Kharraz said: the siddiq is one who takes the fullest share of every lofty station, until he draws near to the ranks of the prophets, peace be upon them. Some said: he upon whom the lights of witnessing and certainty have successively descended, and whom the lights of infallibility encompass.

The Qadi said: he is the one whose soul ascends at times by the ladders of reflection on proofs and signs, and at other times by the stairways of purification and discipline, to the zenith of gnosis, until he perceives things and reports of them as they truly are. The station of siddiqiyya is said to be beneath the station of prophethood, with no station between them.

From al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, [the view is] the affirmation of a station between them, and he mentioned that it was attained by Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him.

Among the Companions, the one most famously known by this description is Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, but this is not restricted to him. Abu Nu'aym in al-Ma'rifa, Ibn 'Asakir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from the hadith of Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from his father Abu Layla al-Ansari, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The siddiqun are three: Habib al-Najjar, the believer of the family of Ya-Sin, who said: ﴿O my people, follow the messengers﴾; and Hizqil, the believer of the family of Pharaoh, who said: ﴿Will you kill a man because he says: My Lord is Allah﴾; and Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him and honour his face, and he is the best of them."

﴿When he said to his father: O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees, and which avails you nothing?﴾ and so on. In it is of gentleness in calling to follow the truth and guiding to it, what is not hidden. This is sought in enjoining good and forbidding evil, especially when it is with relatives and the like. He said ﴿Peace be upon you﴾. This is the peace of turning away from strangers and the gentleness of the righteous with the ignorant. Abu Bakr ibn Tahir said: when there appeared from Azar in his address what appears only from an ignorant person, [Abraham], peace be upon him, made his reply peace, because Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say: Peace﴾. ﴿And I will withdraw from you and what you call upon besides Allah﴾, that is: I will migrate away from you with my religion. From this is understood the recommendation of shunning the wicked.

From Abu Turab al-Nakhshabi: "The company of the wicked begets bad opinion of the good." The textual evidences and experience have converged that their company begets hardness and discourages from good.

﴿And I will call upon my Lord; perhaps I will not be in my supplication to my Lord unfortunate﴾: in it is an indication of his, peace be upon him, extra courtesy toward his Lord, mighty and majestic, of which there is much. The station of friendship requires this, for one who has no courtesy is not fit to be taken as a friend.

﴿So when he had withdrawn from them and what they worshipped besides Allah, We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾. It seems that this was a replacement for those from whom he withdrew of his father and people, so that his heart would not be constricted, as it has been said: When our Prophet (ﷺ) withdrew from the whole of existence, "his gaze did not swerve nor transgress," he was compensated, peace be upon him, when He, glorified is He, said to him: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are actually pledging allegiance to Allah; the hand of Allah is over their hands﴾.

(And mention), O Beloved, ﴿in the Book, Moses﴾, the Interlocutor, ﴿indeed he was mukhlas﴾, sincere to Allah, exalted is He, in all his affairs. Al-Tirmidhi said: the truly sincere (mukhlas) is one like Moses, peace be upon him, who went to al-Khidr, peace be upon him, to be disciplined by him, and did not let slide anything that appeared to him from him. ﴿And We called him from the right side of the mount, and brought him near in intimate conversation﴾. They said: the call is the beginning and the intimate conversation is the end. The call is the station of longing, and the intimate conversation is the station of unveiling secrets. ﴿And We granted him, out of Our mercy, his brother Aaron as a prophet﴾. It was said: Allah, exalted is He, knew the burden of secrets upon Moses, peace be upon him, so He chose for him his brother Aaron as a repository for them. Thus Aaron, peace be upon him, was the repository of the secret of Moses, peace be upon him.

﴿And mention in the Book Ishmael; indeed he was true to his promise﴾, through patience in giving up his soul, or through what his readiness was promised of perfect piety toward his Lord, exalted and high is He, and adornment with the morals that please Him, glorified is He. ﴿And mention in the Book Idris; indeed he was a siddiq, a prophet﴾. ﴿And We raised him to a lofty station﴾. This is a kind of nearness to Allah, exalted is He, which was bestowed upon him, peace be upon him. It was said: the fourth heaven, and that favour upon him is due to what it contains of unveiling some secrets of the realm of sovereignty. Those are the ones upon whom Allah bestowed of the great blessings that the bounds of enumeration cannot encompass: ﴿When the verses of the Most Merciful are recited to them, they fall down prostrating and weeping﴾, because of what He unveiled to them of His signs, exalted is He. It has been mentioned that the Qur'an is the greatest manifestation of Allah, mighty and majestic is He. (And weeping) from the abundance of their joy at what they found, or from fear that what they had attained of manifestation would not endure:

"We weep when they are far, out of longing for them, and we weep when they draw near, out of fear of separation."

﴿And for them is their provision therein, morning and evening﴾. It was said: the provision here is the witnessing of the Truth, glorified is He, and the vision of Him, mighty and majestic is He. This is for the general population of the Garden. As for those who are beloved and longing, the witnessing does not cease from them for a moment, and if they were veiled, they would die from the pain of the veil. ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them; so worship Him and be steadfast in His worship. Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾, meaning any equal worthy of being turned to and asked for anything. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: Does anyone deserve to be named with one of His names, exalted is He, in the true sense?

﴿And there is none of you but will arrive at it [Hell]; it is upon your Lord an inevitable decree﴾. This is so that the greatness of His dominance, glorified is He, and the traces of His might over all His creation, mighty and majestic is He, may be manifest. ﴿Then We will save those who feared Allah﴾, as recompense for their piety, ﴿and We will leave the wrongdoers therein on their knees﴾, as recompense for their wrongdoing. This verse has caused many eyes to shed tears.

From Abd Allah ibn Rawaha, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to weep and say: "I know that I will arrive at the Fire, and I do not know how I will leave after arrival." From al-Hasan: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when they met, one would say to his companion: "Has it reached you that you will arrive [at Hell]?" He would say: "Yes." He would say: "Has it reached you that you will emerge?" He would say: "No." He would say: "Then why the laughter?"

﴿Say: Whoever is in error, the Most Merciful will extend for him an extension﴾. When they boasted of the portions of this world, which only those of low aspiration boast of, Allah, exalted is He, answered them that this is a lure into ruin, not an honour. The allusion in it is that everything that preoccupies one away from Allah, exalted is He, and from turning toward Him, mighty and majestic is He, is evil for its possessor.

﴿On the Day We will gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾, riders upon the swift steeds of light. Ibn 'Ata' said: "It has reached me from al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: riders upon the backs of gnosis."

﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾: poor, humbled, submissive, stripped of selfhood entirely.

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection﴾ in the hearts that are created upon love of Allah, exalted is He. That is the effect of His love for them, glorified is He. In the hadith: "My servant does not cease to draw near to Me through voluntary acts until I love him; and when I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, and his sight with which he sees," and so on.

It is not objectionable to this that we see many of those who believe and do righteous deeds being hated, because those who hate them have hearts created upon evil, though they do not perceive that. From here it is known that hatred of the righteous is a sign of corruption of the inner self.

﴿Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not put in our hearts any rancour toward those who believe﴾. It was said: the meaning of ﴿the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection﴾ is that He will appoint for them delight and sweetness in obedience. The reports support what has preceded. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best, and to Him belongs praise for completing the commentary on surah Maryam. We ask Him, glorified is His majesty, for success in completing the commentary on the rest of the surahs of His Glorious Book, by the sanctity of His Prophet (ﷺ).
